The lecture of this chapter (figures built as it is explained)

We start this chapter with bodies that spin: a shaft with a disk in a turbine, a pump or a fan. We can already describe their motion in two separate parts, which figure 24.1 shows. The first part is a shaft that vibrates but does not spin. From the straight position it bends and returns to it. The shaft is a beam from chapter 5, which we compute with finite elements by chapter 12. The vibration of masses and springs was treated in chapters 9 and 10, and the bending vibration of a beam and the torsional vibration of a shaft with a disk in chapter 13. The second part is a rigid body that spins but does not vibrate, in the figure a disk on a rigid shaft that spins with angular velocity \(\Omega\). The equations of motion of a rigid body and its kinetic energy were written in chapter 8. Here we join the two kinds of knowledge and ask what changes when the shaft spins while it vibrates.

The chapter name has two words. A rotor (rotor) is, in mechanics, any body that turns about its own axis, here the shaft together with the disks mounted on it. Dynamics (dinamika) is the part of mechanics that computes motion under forces. Rotordynamics is therefore the computation of the motion of spinning shafts with disks, and above all of their vibrations across the axis, which the spin excites and changes. The rotor does not only vibrate, it also spins about its own axis, and its axis also circles about the bearing axis, the line through the two bearings. In the figure we see this at the disk centre \(S\), which goes round the bearing axis on a closed path. We will call this circling motion whirl (vrtinčenje).

Every fast machine shows why this matters. A turbine wheel, a pump rotor or a fan turns at a speed where even a small unbalance bends the shaft and loads the two bearings. The unbalance of chapter 23 here means that the centre of mass \(G\) of the disk is not exactly at the disk centre \(S\) on the shaft axis, but slightly to one side. When the disk spins, \(G\) circles about the axis and therefore has an acceleration toward the axis. Only the shaft can give it the force for this. By Newton's third law the disk therefore pulls the shaft outward, the shaft bends and the two bearings hold it. The displacement of the disk centre from the axis grows strongly at certain speeds. This is the resonance of chapter 9: the unbalance pulls the shaft in a direction that turns once per revolution, and when the spin speed matches the natural frequency of the shaft with the disk, the displacement builds up until damping limits it. So the designer must know where these speeds lie and either take the rotor through these ranges during run-up or avoid them, so that the machine runs far from them.

For a steel shaft with a disk of mass \(49\) kg, which we will compute in the chapter as example R1, \(G\) lies only \(0{,}05\) mm from \(S\), which is \(1/4000\) of the disk radius. Yet at the peak of the response at \(1484\) rev/min the disk centre moves \(1{,}25\) mm away from the bearing axis and each bearing carries \(739\) N, \(3{,}07\) times as much as under the weight of the disk, \(240\) N.

A spinning disk can also carry only a limited speed itself, because the spin stretches it. Each piece of the disk circles about the axis and has an acceleration toward the axis of size \(\Omega^2 r\), where \(\Omega\) is the angular velocity of the disk and \(r\) the distance of the piece from the axis. Only the neighbouring material, which pulls it, can give it the force for this, so the material of the disk is stretched. At twice the speed the acceleration is four times as large, and since the stress in a linear elastic disk grows in proportion to the load, the stress is four times as large too: at the centre of disk R1 it is \(12{,}70\) MPa at \(3000\) rev/min and \(50{,}8\) MPa at \(6000\) rev/min. At some speed the stress reaches what the material can still carry.

The chapter promises the following. First we take the simplest model, one disk at the middle of a shaft, and solve it completely, then compute the response to unbalance and the speed at which the response peaks. Then we look at how a disk that tilts resists the tilting, and how the whirl frequencies therefore change with the spin speed. Next we divide the shaft into finite elements and so treat rotors with several masses. We will show how damping in the spinning material can make a rotor unstable, how a rotor is balanced, and how stresses set the speed limit of a spinning disk. At the end we connect everything with the other chapters.

24.1 The Jeffcott rotor and free whirl

Take a slender steel shaft held by two bearings, with a thick disk at its middle: a turbine wheel, a pump rotor, a fan. If we knock the disk sideways, the shaft vibrates like the beam of chapter 5 with a mass at the middle. But the shaft usually also turns. The disk can then vibrate in one plane, or it can circle around the line joining the two bearings, and we ask whether the turning changes the frequency and the shape of this motion. The word rotor (rotor) comes from the Latin verb rotare, to turn, and in mechanics it means any body that turns about its axis, here the shaft with the disk. We start with the simplest model that still poses the question and solve it to the end. Each further ingredient of a rotor comes in its own section.

24.1.1 The model

Figure 24.3 shows the model we will compute. First the two bearings at the ends, a distance \(L\) apart (the length \(L\) is drawn below them). The bearings are short and rigid: we take them as pinned supports, so the shaft can tilt in them but cannot move sideways. Through the middle of both bearings runs the bearing axis, which we call the axis \(x\), as in chapter 5. When the disk is at rest and weight is ignored, the shaft lies on this axis. Under load the shaft is curved along a curve that we compute below. It is steel, has a circular cross section and is massless in the model. At the middle sits the disk of mass \(m\), drawn from the side. In the side view the disk centre is displaced from the axis by \(v\). The force of the shaft on the disk \(k\,v\) starts at the disk centre and points toward the axis, because the bent shaft tries to straighten (the arrow lies on the line along which the force acts).

The disk can leave the axis in two directions at once, so on the right half of the figure we look along the axis. We draw the plane perpendicular to the axis, with the axes \(v\) and \(w\) and the point \(O\) where the bearing axis pierces the plane. The axes are turned so that \(x\), \(v\), \(w\) form a right-handed system, so the sense that turns counterclockwise in this view is positive about the axis \(x\). We draw the disk as a circle with centre \(S\), the centre of the shaft in this plane, and we turn it with a constant spin speed \(\Omega\), positive counterclockwise. The symbol \(\Omega\) is the excitation frequency of chapter 9: in the machine of example 9.76 it was the speed with which the unbalanced mass turns, and here it is the speed of the shaft. The centre \(S\) is displaced from \(O\) by the vector \(p\), which has the components \(v\) and \(w\). While vibrating, the point \(S\) circles around \(O\), and we write \(\omega\) for the angular velocity with which it circles. We separate the two symbols: \(\Omega\) is the turning of the disk about its own axis, \(\omega\) is the circling of its centre about the bearing axis.

Notation. The whirl frequency \(\omega\) is related to the natural angular frequency \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) of chapter 9. The bold \(\boldsymbol\omega\) of chapter 8 is the angular velocity vector of a body and does not appear in this section. The letter \(p\) is the complex displacement \(v + \mathrm{i}\,w\) (in chapter 11 \(p\) is a pressure, not used here). The stiffness \(k\) at the disk is the stiffness of the shaft under a force at the middle, not the stiffness of the foundation in chapter 9.

Now we write the model as a definition.

Definition 24.1 Jeffcott rotor (Jeffcottov rotor)

A Jeffcott rotor is a rigid disk of mass \(m\) fixed at the middle between the bearings on a shaft with a circular cross section. The shaft is massless, linearly elastic and lies in two rigid short bearings that hold it as pinned supports (chapter 5), a distance \(L\) apart. The disk turns with a constant spin speed \(\Omega\) about its own axis, which is the tangent of the shaft at the point of attachment. The lateral displacements of the disk centre from the equilibrium position are \(v\) and \(w\), perpendicular to the axis \(x\) and to each other (figure 24.3).

Source: FPGL section 3.9 (PDF pp. 131-132): rigid short bearings that treat the shaft as simply supported, one disk and a small shaft mass compared with the disk, which is therefore neglected, and the disk at midspan as the Jeffcott rotor. In FPGL the axis of rotation is \(z\), here it is \(x\), as in chapter 5.

Three assumptions are named here and each has its limit. The first is the massless shaft. In example R1 (below) the shaft has a mass equal to 20 % of the disk mass, so the model overestimates the frequency by 4.5 %, which we compute in example 24.5. The second is small slopes of the shaft: by the deflection curve the slope at the bearing is \(3\,|p|/L\) (step 2 of the proof of theorem 24.2), at \(|p| = 3{,}33\) mm it equals \(0{,}01\), the square of this slope is \(10^{-4}\), and by that much (up to a factor \(3/2\)) the true curvature term differs from the linear \(v''\), so the linear stiffness \(k\) is good enough here. The third is the constant \(\Omega\), which the motor maintains and the model takes as prescribed, as in example 9.76. When \(\Omega\) changes (run-up, shut-down), the equation of free motion stays the same, because \(\Omega\) does not appear in it, so \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) is the same too. The assumption fails only when \(\Omega\) enters as an excitation (imbalance, section 24.2), because then the run-up affects the response.

24.1.2 Equations of free motion

We look for the equations by which the disk centre moves if we release it. The disk is at the middle of the shaft, where the slope of the shaft under symmetric loading is zero, so the disk will only translate and not tilt. We prove this in the first steps, and it is the reason why the spin does not change the equations.

Theorem 24.2 Equations of motion of the Jeffcott rotor (gibalne enačbe Jeffcottovega rotorja)

Let the Jeffcott rotor of definition 24.1 be undamped and balanced (the centre of mass of the disk is on the shaft axis), with a constant spin speed \(\Omega\). Let the disk have zero tilt and zero tilt rate at the start. Let the bearing axis be horizontal, and let \(v\) and \(w\) be measured from the equilibrium position under weight. Let \(k = 48EI/L^3\) be the stiffness of the shaft under a force at the middle (chapter 5) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \sqrt{k/m}\). Then:

  1. The disk does not tilt during the motion: the slope of the shaft at the middle is zero, in both planes, and the shaft gives the disk no moment.
  2. The equations of motion in the real coordinates \(v\) and \(w\) are
    \[m\ddot v + k\,v = 0 , \qquad m\ddot w + k\,w = 0 , \tag{24.1}\]
    and in the complex coordinate \(p = v + \mathrm{i}\,w\) (definition 9.24) one equation
    \[m\ddot p + k\,p = 0 . \tag{24.2}\]
  3. The spin speed \(\Omega\) does not appear in the equations, so \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) does not depend on it either.
Proof

We must show that the middle of the shaft stays without slope, that the equations are Lagrange's equations for the energies \(T\) and \(V\), and that we combine them into the complex form with the displacement \(p\).

  1. If a force \(F\) (the disk at the middle) acts at the middle of a simply supported shaft in the plane \(x v\), equation (5.60) gives \(v(x) = -F\,x\,(3L^2 - 4x^2)/(48EI)\) on \([0, L/2]\). The derivative is \(v'(x) = -F\,(3L^2 - 12x^2)/(48EI)\) and at \(x = L/2\) we get \(3L^2 - 3L^2 = 0\), so the graph of the slope crosses the axis there. So the tangent to the deflection curve at the middle, where the disk sits, is horizontal, the slope of the shaft is zero and the force at the middle needs no moment. The same holds in the plane \(x w\), because \(I\) about every axis through the centre of a circle is the same (definition 5.26), and by lemma 5.60 the two loadings add. A disk that only translates with its axis in the same direction and turns with a constant \(\Omega\) about its own axis needs only a force from the shaft: by equation (8.77) its moment about the centre of mass is zero. We split the acceleration of every particle into two parts. The first part is the same for all particles, the acceleration \(a_{\mathrm{S}}\) of the centre of mass, and gives no moment, because by the definition of the centre of mass the sum of the masses times their positions relative to it is zero. The second part is the acceleration \(\Omega^2\rho\) toward the axis of a particle at distance \(\rho\) from the axis. A particle of mass \(\Delta m\) at distance \(z\) from the middle plane of the disk therefore has the moment \(\Delta m\,\Omega^2\rho\,z\) about \(S\) in one direction. In a round homogeneous disk, on the opposite side of the axis there is a particle of the same mass with the same lever arm \(z\), which has the opposite acceleration and so the opposite moment, and the two moments cancel. A force at the middle, in turn, causes no slope, as the horizontal tangent shows. So the motion without tilt satisfies both equations (8.77), and since the disk has zero tilt and zero tilt rate at the start, by the uniqueness of the solution (theorem 8.107) it is the only motion. This is point 1.
  2. The displacement under a force \(F\) at the middle is \(F/k\) with \(k = 48EI/L^3\), the same in both planes. By the same equation the slope at the bearing is \(v'(0) = -FL^2/(16EI) = -3(F/k)/L\), that is \(3|p|/L\) at the displacement \(|p| = F/k\). The shaft is massless and acts on the disk as a spring with the forces \(-k\,v\) and \(-k\,w\). The potential energy is \(V = \tfrac12 k\,(v^2 + w^2)\). The weight of the disk is a constant force on a linear spring. The line of the total vertical force of the shaft and the weight as a function of \(w\) is therefore parallel to the line of the shaft force alone, with the same slope \(-k\), and is only shifted so that its zero is at \(w = -mg/k = -0{,}41\) mm (R1, below). So the weight only shifts the equilibrium position and does not change the stiffness. The shaft force points toward the axis in every direction and has the same size, because the stiffness is the same in every direction across the axis, so it is opposite to the weight only vertically below the axis, and the equilibrium position is there. We measure the coordinates \(v\) and \(w\) of the left view from it, the displacement \(p\) from the point \(O'\) (as in example 9.76, step 3).
  3. The disk is a rigid body (chapter 8). By theorem 8.92 its kinetic energy is the sum of the energy of the centre of mass, \(\tfrac12 m(\dot v^2 + \dot w^2)\), and the energy of rotation about the centre of mass. The axis of the disk keeps its direction (point 1) and the spin speed \(\Omega\) is constant, so the energy of rotation is constant and does not appear in the derivatives with respect to \(v\), \(w\), \(\dot v\), \(\dot w\). So \(T = \tfrac12 m(\dot v^2 + \dot w^2) + \text{const.}\) and \(\Omega\) is only in the constant.
  4. By theorem 8.101 (\(Q^{\mathrm{nc}} = 0\)), for the coordinate \(v\): \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\big(\partial T/\partial\dot v\big) - \partial T/\partial v + \partial V/\partial v = 0\). Here \(\partial T/\partial\dot v = m\dot v\), \(\partial T/\partial v = 0\) and \(\partial V/\partial v = k\,v\), in size the force of the shaft. We get \(m\ddot v + k\,v = 0\). For \(w\) the calculation is the same and gives the second equation (24.1).
  5. We multiply the second equation by \(\mathrm{i}\) and add it to the first: \(m(\ddot v + \mathrm{i}\,\ddot w) + k\,(v + \mathrm{i}\,w) = 0\). This is equation (24.2) for the complex displacement \(p\), because \(\ddot p = \ddot v + \mathrm{i}\,\ddot w\) (derivative by components, definition 9.32).
  6. In steps 2 to 5 there is no term with \(\Omega\), which is point 3.

Source: FPGL section 3.9 (PDF pp. 131-133): there are four coordinates \(u\), \(v\), \(\theta\), \(\psi\) and a relation with the stiffness matrix. For a disk at the distances \(a\) and \(b\) from the bearings, equation (3.85) (PDF p. 133) gives the coupling coefficient \(k_{\mathrm{C}} = 3EI(a^2 - b^2)/(a^2b^2)\), which is zero for a disk at the middle (\(a = b\)), so the equations for the two displacements separate from those for the two tilts, and \(k_{\mathrm{T}} = 3EI(a^3 + b^3)/(a^3b^3)\), which at \(a = b = L/2\) equals our \(k = 48EI/L^3\). Our step 1 shows this split with the deflection curve of chapter 5.

The theorem holds only if the disk really sits at the middle. That is the condition without which the conclusion that \(\Omega\) is not in the equations fails. Take the same shaft R1 and a disk at \(x = L/4\). A force \(F\) there gives, by the deflection curve of a simply supported beam (SymPy confirms the calculation), the displacement \(3FL^3/(256EI)\) and the slope \(FL^2/(32EI)\), that is a slope equal to \(8/3\) times the displacement divided by \(L\). At a displacement of \(1\) mm and \(L = 1\) m the slope is \(0{,}00267\), not zero. Such a disk also tilts when it moves, and while it tilts its spinning contributes a moment that depends on \(\Omega\) and that this section does not yet contain. So a disk away from the middle has frequencies that change with \(\Omega\) (section 24.3). The free whirl that follows belongs only to a disk at the middle.

24.1.3 Whirl and circular orbits

Equation (24.2) is the equation of the undamped oscillator in a complex variable \(p\), from chapter 9. Solutions of this kind are complex exponential functions. Before we write them down, we name the motions that we get.

Definition 24.3 Whirl and orbit (vrtinčenje in orbita)

The orbit is the curve that the disk centre \(p(t) = v(t) + \mathrm{i}\,w(t)\) traces in the plane \(v w\). Whirl is the motion of the disk centre about the bearing axis along an orbit. The motion \(p(t) = P\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}\) with a complex \(P \ne 0\) and a real \(\omega \ne 0\) is a circular whirl with radius \(|P|\) and angular velocity \(|\omega|\) (theorem 9.34, point 2). For \(\omega > 0\) the centre circles in the sense of positive rotation about the axis \(x\), that is the sense in which the disk turns at \(\Omega > 0\), and the whirl is forward (vrtinčenje naprej, prednje vrtinčenje). For \(\omega < 0\) it circles the opposite way and the whirl is backward (vrtinčenje nazaj, obratno vrtinčenje).

Source: FPGL section 3.6.1 (PDF pp. 117-118): the direction of whirl from the phase between \(u\) and \(v\), and the words forward and backward for the sense of the shaft's spin or the opposite, circular orbits with amplitudes \(r_{\mathrm{u}} = r_{\mathrm{v}}\) and phase \(\pm\pi/2\). Our \(\omega\) is a signed frequency that already contains this direction.

The word whirl comes from a whirlpool, in which particles of water circle about a centre, as the disk centre circles about the bearing axis. Both whirls have the same centre of circling, the point \(O\), and differ only in direction. Whirl is not the turning of the disk: the disk turns with the speed \(\Omega\) about its own axis, while whirl is the motion of its centre. The relation between \(\omega\) and \(\Omega\) shows itself with unbalance in section 24.2.

Lemma 24.4 Free motion is the sum of a forward and a backward circular orbit (prosto gibanje je vsota krožnih orbit naprej in nazaj)

Let \(p(t)\) be a solution of equation (24.2). Then:

  1. There are exactly determined complex numbers \(A\) and \(B\) such that
    \[p(t) = A\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t} + B\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t} , \qquad A = \tfrac12\Big(p(0) + \frac{\dot p(0)}{\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}}\Big) , \quad B = \tfrac12\Big(p(0) - \frac{\dot p(0)}{\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}}\Big) , \tag{24.3}\]
    and every such sum is a solution.
  2. The first term is a circular forward whirl with radius \(|A|\), the second a circular backward whirl with radius \(|B|\), both with angular velocity \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\).
  3. If \(A\) and \(B\) are not both zero, the orbit of the sum is an ellipse with semi-axes \(|A| + |B|\) and \(\big||A| - |B|\big|\), which the centre traverses forward if \(|A| > |B|\), backward if \(|A| < |B|\), and which is a line segment if \(|A| = |B|\). If \(B = 0\) or \(A = 0\) it is a circle. The period is \(T = 2\pi/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) in all cases.
Proof

We must show that the sum solves the equation and has the given initial condition, that there is no other solution, and that its orbit is an ellipse with the stated properties.

  1. In the left figure with its axes the pointers start at \(O\). By theorem 9.34 (point 3), \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t} = \pm\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t}\) and the second derivative is \(-\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\,\mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t}\). So the derivative of a rotating pointer is a pointer turned by a right angle forward and multiplied by \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), and it lies on the tangent of its circle. The second derivative is turned by one more right angle, by two in all, and points from the tip of the pointer back toward \(O\), multiplied by \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\). For the opposite rotation the first derivative is turned by a right angle the other way, and the second derivative again points toward \(O\). The sum of the second derivatives is therefore \(-\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\) times the sum of the pointers, \(\ddot p = -\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 p\), and \(\ddot p + \omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 p = 0\) holds for every \(A\) and \(B\), which is equation (24.2) divided by \(m\).
  2. At \(t = 0\) the pointers are just the numbers \(A\) and \(B\), so \(p(0) = A + B\) and \(\dot p(0) = \mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}(A - B)\), that is \(A - B = \dot p(0)/(\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}})\). These are the diagonals of the parallelogram with sides \(A\) and \(B\). We add the two equations and divide by \(2\) to get \(A\), subtract them and divide by \(2\) to get \(B\), which is equation (24.3). In the right figure with its axes this is the midpoint of the diagonals \(\tfrac12 p(0)\), from which half of the other diagonal forward reaches the tip of \(A\), and half backward the tip of \(B\). So for every \(p(0)\) and \(\dot p(0)\) there is a sum with one pair of numbers \(A\), \(B\).
  3. The characteristic polynomial of the equation \(\ddot p + \omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 p = 0\) is \(s^2 + \omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\), with leading coefficient \(1 \ne 0\). By theorem 9.41 the equation has exactly one solution for given \(p(0)\) and \(\dot p(0)\). So every solution is the sum of step 2, and \(A\), \(B\) are determined by the initial values. This is point 1.
  4. By definition 24.3 the term \(A\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t}\) is a circular whirl with radius \(|A|\) (theorem 9.34, point 2) and with \(\omega = +\omega_{\mathrm{n}} > 0\), so forward. The term \(B\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t}\) has \(\omega = -\omega_{\mathrm{n}} < 0\), radius \(|B|\), so backward. If \(A = 0\) or \(B = 0\) one term remains. This is point 2.
  5. In the left figure with its axes the pointers start at \(O\). Write \(A = |A|\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\alpha}\) and \(B = |B|\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\beta}\) and take \(\gamma = (\alpha + \beta)/2\) and \(\varphi = \omega_{\mathrm{n}} t + (\alpha - \beta)/2\). Then \(A\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t} = |A|\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\gamma + \varphi)}\) and \(B\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t} = |B|\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\gamma - \varphi)}\), since the exponents \(\gamma + \varphi = \alpha + \omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) and \(\gamma - \varphi = \beta - \omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) agree with the given ones. So the pointers are mirror images about the line at the angle \(\gamma\), the first by \(\varphi\) on one side, the second by \(\varphi\) on the other. Along the line their parts \(|A|\cos\varphi\) and \(|B|\cos\varphi\) point the same way, across it their parts \(|A|\sin\varphi\) and \(|B|\sin\varphi\) point opposite ways. So
    \[p(t) = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\gamma}\Big[(|A| + |B|)\cos\varphi + \mathrm{i}\,(|A| - |B|)\sin\varphi\Big] , \tag{24.4}\]
    because \(\cos\varphi + \mathrm{i}\sin\varphi = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi}\) and \(\cos\varphi - \mathrm{i}\sin\varphi = \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\varphi}\) (definition 9.33).
  6. In the right figure with its axes the expression in the bracket is the point \((a\cos\varphi,\ b\sin\varphi)\) with \(a = |A| + |B| > 0\) and \(b = |A| - |B|\). Its orbit is an ellipse with semi-axes \(a\) and \(|b|\) along the coordinate axes (a line segment at \(b = 0\)), and multiplication by \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\gamma}\) turns the ellipse by the angle \(\gamma\) about \(O\). Since \(\dot\varphi = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), the velocity of the point is \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}(-a\sin\varphi,\ b\cos\varphi)\). The cross product of position and velocity in the plane (the signed area of the parallelogram they span), the first component of the position times the second of the velocity minus the second times the first, is \(a\cos\varphi \cdot \omega_{\mathrm{n}} b\cos\varphi - b\sin\varphi \cdot (-\omega_{\mathrm{n}} a\sin\varphi) = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\,a\,b\), and the turn by \(\gamma\) does not change it. For \(b > 0\) it is positive and the point circles counterclockwise (forward), for \(b < 0\) the opposite way (backward). Because \(\varphi\) grows with \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\), the period is \(2\pi/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\). This is point 3.

Source: FPGL section 3.6.1 (PDF pp. 117-118): the orbit of \(u\) and \(v\) with a phase difference is an ellipse, the semi-axes from the eigenvalues of the matrix \(H = TT^{\mathsf T}\), the direction from the sign of the phase difference, a circle at \(r_{\mathrm{u}} = r_{\mathrm{v}}\) and phase \(\pm\pi/2\). Our proof comes from the complex form and is shorter because equation (24.2) has one frequency.

Two cases show what the lemma says. First we ask whether the ellipse that the disk centre traces for a general initial condition is a third kind of whirl besides forward and backward. It is not. Take example R1 with \(v(0) = 1\) mm, \(w(0) = 0\), \(\dot v(0) = 0\) and \(\dot w(0) = 0{,}2\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) mm, so \(p(0) = 1\) mm. Then \(\dot p(0) = \mathrm{i}\cdot 0{,}2\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) mm. By equation (24.3), \(A = \tfrac12(1 + 0{,}2) = 0{,}6\) mm and \(B = \tfrac12(1 - 0{,}2) = 0{,}4\) mm, both real. The orbit is an ellipse with semi-axes \(|A| + |B| = 1{,}0\) mm and \(|A| - |B| = 0{,}2\) mm, and because \(|A| > |B|\) the centre traverses it forward. SymPy confirms the same result: \(v = \cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) and \(w = 0{,}2\sin\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) (in mm) solve both equations (24.1) with the given initial conditions (both residuals are zero). Figure 24.10 shows an early moment, \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t = 50^\circ\).

We build the figure step by step. We draw the axes \(v\) and \(w\) through \(O\). The first term, \(A\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t}\), is an arrow from \(O\) of length \(|A|\) (0.6 mm, 1.8 cm at the scale of the figure) and angle \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) counterclockwise: a centre that moved only along it would circle forward. At its end we attach the second term, \(B\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t}\), an arrow of length \(|B|\) (0.4 mm, 1.2 cm) that turns the opposite way, clockwise. The sum of these two arrows is the point \(p\) we look for, at \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t = 50^\circ\) at \(0{,}643 + 0{,}153\,\mathrm{i}\) mm. As time runs, the point \(p\) traces the ellipse, which at every time is the sum of two turning arrows, and its semi-axes are the sum and the difference of their lengths: when the arrows are parallel the distance from \(O\) is largest, \(|A| + |B| = 1{,}0\) mm, when they are opposite it is smallest, \(|A| - |B| = 0{,}2\) mm. Both arrows have the same frequency \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), so their relative position repeats every \(2\pi/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) and the orbit is a closed curve.

The same initial position with another initial velocity gives other whirls. At \(\dot w(0) = 0\) we have \(\dot p(0) = 0\) and \(A = B = 0{,}5\) mm: the two arrows are equally long, the sum is \(\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) on the real axis, and the orbit is a line segment from \(-1\) mm to \(1\) mm on the axis \(v\), that is vibration in one plane (\(w \equiv 0\)), which is the sum of both whirls with equal radii. At \(\dot w(0) = -0{,}2\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) mm we have \(A = 0{,}4\) mm and \(B = 0{,}6\) mm: the ellipse is the same, but the centre traverses it backward. The first ellipse is thus a sum and not a third whirl, and a sum of two circular orbits differs from a single circle only in that both \(A\) and \(B\) are nonzero. The reason that the circular orbits are solutions and have the same frequency is the equal stiffness in both planes. With unequal bearing stiffness the vibrations in the planes \(v\) and \(w\) have different frequencies \(\omega_{\mathrm{v}}\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{w}}\) (section 24.2), the circular orbits are no longer solutions, and the free orbit is in general no longer an ellipse.

24.1.4 Example R1: numbers and a check of the massless shaft

Example 24.5 Steel shaft with disk R1 (jeklena gred z diskom R1)

The shaft has diameter \(d = 40\) mm and length between the bearings \(L = 1\) m, the disk has diameter \(D = 400\) mm and thickness \(h = 50\) mm. The steel has \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³. We look for the stiffness, the natural frequency and the effect of the shaft mass.

  1. The second moment of area of the section is \(I = \pi d^4/64 = 1{,}2566\cdot 10^{-7}\) m\(^4\) (definition 5.26) and \(EI = 24\,630{,}1\) N m\(^2\).
  2. The stiffness at the middle is by equation (5.60) \(k = 48EI/L^3 = 1{,}1822\cdot 10^{6}\) N/m. Check: a cantilever of length \(L/2\), clamped at the middle, with a force \(F/2\) at its end, has the deflection \((F/2)(L/2)^3/(3EI) = F L^3/(48EI)\), because \(\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac18\cdot\tfrac13 = \tfrac1{48}\). This is the same value.
  3. The mass of the disk is \(m = \rho\,\pi D^2 h/4 = 49{,}009\) kg, the mass of the shaft \(m_{\mathrm{s}} = \rho\,\pi d^2 L/4 = 9{,}802\) kg, so \(20{,}0\) % of the disk mass.
  4. The natural angular frequency of the disk on the spring is \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \sqrt{k/m} = 155{,}32\) 1/s. That is \(f = 24{,}719\) Hz, period \(T = 40{,}45\) ms and \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\cdot 60/(2\pi) = 1483{,}2\) rev/min.
  5. The static sag under weight is \(mg/k = 0{,}407\) mm. The slope of the shaft at the bearing is \(3|p|/L\) (theorem 24.2, step 2), for \(|p| = 3{,}33\) mm that is \(0{,}01\).
  6. Check of the massless shaft with the Rayleigh quotient. The static deflection curve on one half, \(v = p\,(3\xi - 4\xi^3)\) with \(\xi = x/L\) and \(p\) the displacement of the middle, is an admissible field of the simply supported beam (definition 13.76, chapter 13). The derivative at \(\xi = 0\) is \(3p/L\), which gives the slope at the bearing of step 5. The kinetic energy of the shaft is \(\tfrac12\rho A L\,\dot p^2\cdot 2\int_0^{1/2}(3\xi - 4\xi^3)^2\mathrm{d}\xi\). The integral is \(17/70\), times two \(17/35\) (SymPy), so it is proportional to \(\tfrac{17}{35}\,m_{\mathrm{s}}\), not to the whole mass. The strain energy of this shape is \(\tfrac12 k\,p^2\). The quotient is \(\omega^2 = k/(m + \tfrac{17}{35}m_{\mathrm{s}})\), which gives \(\omega = 148{,}28\) 1/s or \(1416{,}0\) rev/min.
  7. Theorem 13.81 says that the quotient with an admissible field is at least \(\omega_1^2\), but it is proved for a beam without a disk. For the shaft with the disk we therefore check the bound with the frequency equation. By equation (13.42) with \(q = 0\), the shape of a vibration with frequency \(\omega\) on the half \([0, L/2]\) is \(a\sin\beta x + c\sinh\beta x\) with \(\beta^4 = \rho A\,\omega^2/(EI)\), because the displacement and the moment at the bearing are zero. The disk moves only in symmetric shapes, since antisymmetric ones have zero displacement at the middle, so at the middle the slope is zero, and the shear forces on both sides of the disk together accelerate the disk: \(-2EI\,v'''(L/2) = m\,\omega^2 v(L/2)\), with the derivative taken from the left. For a massless shaft this condition with the shape \(3\xi - 4\xi^3\) gives exactly \(\omega^2 = k/m\). The smallest \(\omega\) at which both conditions have a solution \((a, c) \ne (0, 0)\) is \(\omega_1 = 148{,}27\) 1/s (NumPy), just below the quotient \(148{,}28\) 1/s, as the bound requires. The frequency of the massless model is larger than the true one: \((155{,}32 - 148{,}27)/155{,}32 = 0{,}045\). The model of a massless shaft overestimates the frequency by \(4{,}5\) % of its value.
  8. By lemma 24.4, at \(p(0) = 1\) mm and \(\dot p(0) = 0\) the motion is a line segment, at \(\dot p(0) = \mathrm{i}\cdot 0{,}2\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) mm it is an ellipse with semi-axes \(1{,}0\) and \(0{,}2\) mm, in both cases with the frequency \(1483{,}2\) rev/min. What happens if the shaft turns at exactly this speed is shown in section 24.2.

The Rayleigh quotient of step 6 is thus only \(0{,}006\) % above the true frequency of step 7, because the static deflection curve is close to the shape of the first mode. For a quick check the quotient is therefore enough, and the frequency equation shows that in this example the bound also holds for the shaft with the disk. A shaft with \(20\) % of the disk mass is not negligible, and the numbers of the massless model must be read with this deviation.

From history

The model is named after Jeffcott and De Laval: FPGL writes that it is called a Jeffcott (Jeffcott, 1919) or a De Laval rotor in honour of Henry Jeffcott and Carl De Laval, who conducted some of the earliest studies of the dynamics of flexible rotors (FPGL, PDF p. 131). Jeffcott's work is listed in the references of FPGL as The lateral vibration of loaded shafts in the neighbourhood of a whirling speed: The effects of want of balance, in the journal Philosophical Magazine (FPGL, PDF p. 528). The title shows why the name belongs to this model: the paper dealt with the lateral vibration of a loaded shaft near the speed at which it whirls, and with the effect of unbalance, which is the question of the next section. For De Laval FPGL gives no dates, so we write none.

The main finding is therefore this. The Jeffcott rotor has two independent vibrations with the same frequency \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), in the planes \(v\) and \(w\), and the complex coordinate \(p\) combines them into equation (24.2). Every free motion is the sum of a circular forward and a circular backward whirl, and the spin speed does not appear in the equations. When the disk gets an unbalance, the spin speed will enter as an excitation, and in section 24.2 we ask at which speed the shaft bends most.

24.2 Rotor unbalance and the critical speed

A car wheel that has a little more mass at one place on its rim a little more mass than elsewhere starts to shake the steering wheel at one road speed and calms down again at a higher one. That is why the garage clips a small weight to the rim (figure 24.14). The same happens in a turbine, a fan or an electric motor, except that there a shaft turns thousands of times a minute and rests on two bearings. Why does a small fault in the distribution of mass cause a force on the bearings, why is this force especially large at one speed, and why does the shaft settle down again above that speed?

The model is the Jeffcott rotor (Jeffcottov rotor) of section 24.1 (definition 24.1): a rigid disk of mass \(m\) at midspan of a massless shaft that rests in two rigid short bearings. Our running example R1 is a steel shaft of diameter \(40\) mm with the bearings \(L = 1\) m apart, carrying a disk of diameter \(400\) mm and thickness \(50\) mm. The disk has mass \(m = 49{,}009\) kg. By the deflection curve of a simply supported beam under a central force (equation (5.60)) the stiffness of the shaft at midspan is \(k = 48EI/L^3 = 1{,}1822 \cdot 10^6\) N/m. The second moment of area \(I = \pi d^4/64\) holds about every axis through the centre of the circle, because a circle is symmetric about every diameter (definition 5.26). The natural circular frequency of free vibration is \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \sqrt{k/m} = 155{,}32\) 1/s, which is \(1483\) revolutions per minute (rev/min). The disk sits at midspan, where the slope of the deflection curve is zero by symmetry (figure 5.143), so it does not tilt when the shaft bends. The tilt of the disk comes in section 24.3. The shaft turns at a constant spin speed \(\Omega\) (chapter 9: this is what we called the frequency of the forcing), kept up by a motor. This holds while the motor can supply the power to keep the shaft turning: at run-up and shutdown \(\Omega\) is not constant, the force gets a further term with \(\dot\Omega\), and the theorem below does not apply, so such passages are treated in section 24.6.

So far the disk moved only because of bending. Now we give it a fault that makes the shaft shake even though the only cause is the turning. We look at the disk in a plane perpendicular to the shaft, along the shaft.

We draw the axes \(v\) and \(w\) through the point \(O\) where the bearing axis, the line through the centres of the two bearings, pierces the plane of the disk. At rest the shaft would be straight and the centre of the disk would lie at \(O\). When the shaft turns it bends and the disk centre \(S\) moves from \(O\) by the displacement \(p = v + \mathrm{i}\,w\) (section 24.1, complex number: definition 9.24). The vector from \(O\) to \(S\) is \(p\). The centre of the disk is the point where the axis of the shaft pierces the disk, so in this plane it is also the centre of the shaft. The centre of mass \(G\) of the disk may lie elsewhere. If the disk is not perfectly round or homogeneous (cast metal with a bubble, a keyway, a bolt on the rim), it is not at \(S\). From \(S\) to \(G\) we draw the vector of length \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\). The disk is a rigid body that turns with the shaft at angular velocity \(\Omega\), so this vector turns with it, and its angle \(\Omega t\) is measured from the direction of the axis \(v\). The turning goes from the axis \(v\) towards the axis \(w\). The centre of mass is then at \(p + a_{\mathrm{u}}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) and the dashed line from \(O\) to \(G\) shows its position relative to the bearing axis.

Why does the position of the centre of mass matter, and not the centre? By Newton's second law the sum of the external forces on a body equals its mass times the acceleration of its centre of mass. If we held the centre \(S\) at \(O\) (as for a rigid shaft), the centre of mass \(G\) would go round a circle of radius \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\) with angular velocity \(\Omega\), with acceleration \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2\) towards \(O\) (figure 24.16). For this acceleration the shaft must act on the disk with a force \(m\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2\), and by the law of action and reaction the disk acts with such a force on the shaft and through it on the bearings. The force turns with the disk. For the disk R1 with \(a_{\mathrm{u}} = 0{,}05\) mm at \(3000\) rev/min, which is \(\Omega = 314{,}16\) 1/s, it is \(49{,}009 \cdot 0{,}05 \cdot 10^{-3} \cdot 314{,}16^2 = 241{,}8\) N (NumPy), about half the weight of the disk, \(mg = 480{,}8\) N. We made the same calculation for a machine with an unbalanced mass in example 9.76, where only a small mass \(m_{\mathrm{u}}\) at radius \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\) was unbalanced. Here the whole disk is unbalanced, so its whole mass enters the product.

Definition 24.6 Unbalance (neuravnoteženost)

Let a rigid disk of mass \(m\) be fixed on a shaft that turns about its axis at constant angular velocity \(\Omega > 0\) in the sense of increasing angle from the axis \(v\) towards the axis \(w\). Let \(S\) be the point where the axis of the shaft pierces the plane of the disk and \(G\) the centre of mass of the disk. The vector \(\overrightarrow{SG}\) lies in the plane of the disk and turns with it. The disk is unbalanced (neuravnotežen) if \(G \ne S\). The number

\[a_{\mathrm{u}} = |SG| \ge 0 \tag{24.5}\]

is the eccentricity (izsrednost) and the vector

\[\vek U = m\,\overrightarrow{SG} , \qquad U = m\,a_{\mathrm{u}} \tag{24.6}\]

is the unbalance of the disk. It is a vector in the plane of the disk, measured in kg m (in practice g mm), and the disk carries it round. The disk is balanced (uravnotežen) if \(\vek U = \vek 0\). Here \(m\) is the total mass of the turning part. If a mass \(m_{\mathrm{d}}\) is added at distance \(a\) from the axis of a balanced disk, the unbalance of the whole is \(U = m_{\mathrm{d}}\,a\) (example after this block).

Source: FPGL section 6.2.1 (PDF p. 248-250): there the eccentricity is \(\varepsilon = |SG|\) (figure 6.2) and the equivalent added small mass \(m_0\) has \(m_0 a = m\varepsilon\) (PDF p. 250). FPGL has the axis of turning as z, ours is the shaft axis \(x\), as in chapter 5. The notation \(U = m a_{\mathrm{u}}\) is the product \(m_{\mathrm{u}} a_{\mathrm{u}}\) of example 9.76 (chapter 9), here with the whole disk as \(m_{\mathrm{u}}\).

Notation. The spin speed \(\Omega\) is the forcing frequency \(\Omega\) of chapter 9, and the same number for unbalance. The whirl frequency will be written \(\omega\) (the bold \(\boldsymbol\omega\) of chapter 8 is the angular velocity vector and does not appear here). The letter \(p\) is the complex displacement \(v + \mathrm{i}\,w\). The ratio \(r = \Omega/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) is the frequency ratio of chapter 9. \(G\) is the centre of mass in this section (the shear modulus is the italic \(G\) elsewhere).

The word balanced says that the masses are distributed around the axis so that their effects on the axis cancel, as the weights on the two arms of a balance cancel. With \(G = S\) the acceleration of the centre of mass is zero while the centre stays still, and the bearings receive no force from the turning. With \(G \ne S\) this condition is lost. Let the disk R1 be balanced and let us bolt a mass \(m_{\mathrm{d}} = 14\) g on it at radius \(a = 175\) mm, inside the disk of radius \(200\) mm (figure 24.17). The centre of mass of everything is then \(m_{\mathrm{d}}\,a/(m + m_{\mathrm{d}}) = 14 \cdot 175/49\,023\) mm \(= 0{,}04998\) mm from \(S\), and the total unbalance is \((m + m_{\mathrm{d}})\cdot 0{,}04998\) mm \(= 2450\) g mm, which is the product \(m_{\mathrm{d}}\,a = 2450\) g mm. Unbalance is thus a product of a mass and an arm, and neither factor alone fixes the force. For that reason we describe the rotor in every calculation by one number \(U\) and a direction, that is by \(a_{\mathrm{u}} = U/m\). For R1 we take \(a_{\mathrm{u}} = 0{,}05\) mm, \(U = 2450{,}4\) g mm. This is very little: the ratio of \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\) to the radius of the disk is \(2{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4}\), and yet the force will be large, because \(\Omega\) enters squared.

Now we compute how the shaft responds. The centre \(S\) moves with the bending of the shaft, so with two coordinates \(v\) and \(w\) (figure 24.15), and the centre of mass \(G\) is away from it by the turning vector \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\). The kinetic energy of the disk therefore depends on the velocity of the point \(G\). We derive the equations by Lagrange, as for the machine in example 9.76, but in two directions.

Theorem 24.7 Response of the Jeffcott rotor to unbalance (odziv Jeffcottovega rotorja na neuravnoteženost)

Let the Jeffcott rotor of definition 24.1 be a disk of mass \(m\) at midspan of a massless shaft that has the same stiffness \(k\) at the disk in both planes \(v\) and \(w\), and two rigid short bearings. Let the disk have unbalance with eccentricity \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\) (definition 24.6), a constant spin speed \(\Omega > 0\) and an external viscous damping with coefficient \(c \ge 0\): a force \(-c\,\dot p\) acts on the disk centre, opposite to its velocity, as for the damper of definition 9.1, only equally in every direction of the plane. Notation: \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \sqrt{k/m}\), \(\zeta = c/(2\sqrt{km})\), \(r = \Omega/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\). Then:

  1. The equations of motion in the real coordinates \(v\) and \(w\) are
    \[\begin{aligned} m\ddot v + c\dot v + k v &= m\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2\cos\Omega t , \\ m\ddot w + c\dot w + k w &= m\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2\sin\Omega t , \end{aligned} \tag{24.7}\]
    and as one complex equation for \(p = v + \mathrm{i}\,w\)
    \[m\ddot p + c\dot p + k p = m\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t} . \tag{24.8}\]
  2. If \(c > 0\) or \(r \ne 1\), one solution is \(p(t) = P\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) with the complex number
    \[P = a_{\mathrm{u}}\,\frac{r^2}{1 - r^2 + 2\mathrm{i}\,\zeta r} , \qquad |P| = a_{\mathrm{u}}\,r^2 D(r) , \tag{24.9}\]
    where \(D\) is the dynamic factor (definition 9.64). The disk centre goes round a circle of radius \(|P|\) along it, once per revolution of the shaft, in the sense of the turning of the shaft, that is in forward whirl (definition 24.3).
  3. If \(\zeta > 0\), every solution of equation (24.8) approaches the solution of item 2 as time goes on (figure 24.19).
Proof

We must show three things: the equations from Lagrange's equations, the solution of item 2 from theorem 9.62 in each plane separately, and their joining into the complex form.

  1. The centre of the disk is at the point \((v, w)\) of the plane of the disk. The centre of mass is away from it by \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\) in the direction of angle \(\Omega t\) (definition 24.6), so \(x_{\mathrm{G}} = v + a_{\mathrm{u}}\cos\Omega t\) and \(y_{\mathrm{G}} = w + a_{\mathrm{u}}\sin\Omega t\).
  2. The disk is a rigid body (chapter 8). By theorem 8.92 its kinetic energy is the sum of the energy of the centre of mass, \(\tfrac12 m(\dot x_{\mathrm{G}}^2 + \dot y_{\mathrm{G}}^2)\), and the energy of the turning about the centre of mass. It does not tilt (section 24.1) and turns about its own axis with constant \(\Omega\), so the energy of the turning is constant and does not enter the derivatives with respect to \(v\) and \(\dot v\). The angle \(\Omega t\) is prescribed (a rheonomic constraint, as in example 9.76). So
    \[T = \tfrac12 m\big[(\dot v - a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega\sin\Omega t)^2 + (\dot w + a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega\cos\Omega t)^2\big] + \text{const.}\]
  3. By the split of theorem 8.97, \(T_2 = \tfrac12 m(\dot v^2 + \dot w^2)\), \(T_1 = m\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega(-\dot v\sin\Omega t + \dot w\cos\Omega t)\) and \(T_0 = \tfrac12 m\,a_{\mathrm{u}}^2\Omega^2 + \text{const.}\) The coordinates \(v\) and \(w\) themselves do not enter \(T\).
  4. The force of the shaft on the disk is \(-k\,v\) in the direction \(v\) and \(-k\,w\) in the direction \(w\): the shaft has no mass, so it acts on the disk as a spring, and by equation (5.60) the deflection under a force \(F\) at midspan is \(F/k\), the same in each plane because \(I\) is the same about every axis through the centre of the section, and by lemma 5.60 the displacements in the two planes add. The potential energy is \(\tfrac12 k(v^2 + w^2)\). The weight of the disk only moves the equilibrium position by \(mg/k = 0{,}41\) mm (R1), and \(v\) and \(w\) are measured from it, as in example 9.76, step 3.
  5. The damping force on the disk centre has the components \(-c\,\dot v\) and \(-c\,\dot w\). The position of the centre is \((v, w)\), so its derivative with respect to \(v\) is the unit vector of the \(v\) axis and with respect to \(w\) the unit vector of the \(w\) axis. By definition 8.51 the generalized forces are \(Q_{\mathrm{v}} = -c\,\dot v\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{w}} = -c\,\dot w\).
  6. By theorem 8.101 for the coordinate \(v\): \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\big(\partial T/\partial\dot v\big) - \partial T/\partial v + k\,v = -c\,\dot v\). Here \(\partial T/\partial\dot v = m\dot v - m\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega\sin\Omega t\), its time derivative is \(m\ddot v - m\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2\cos\Omega t\), and \(\partial T/\partial v = 0\). The torque that keeps up \(\Omega t\) does no virtual work (example 9.76, step 5). This gives the first equation (24.7).
  7. For \(w\), \(\partial T/\partial\dot w = m\dot w + m\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega\cos\Omega t\), its derivative is \(m\ddot w - m\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2\sin\Omega t\), and we get the second equation (24.7). SymPy confirms steps 6 and 7.
  8. We multiply the second equation by \(\mathrm i\) and add it to the first. Since \(\cos\Omega t + \mathrm i\sin\Omega t = \mathrm e^{\mathrm i\Omega t}\) (definition 9.33), this is equation (24.8). This is item 1.
  9. The first equation (24.7) is equation (9.64) with \(Q_0 = m\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2\). For \(c > 0\) or \(r \ne 1\), by theorem 9.62 (item 1) one solution is \(v_{\mathrm{p}} = X\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)\) with \(X = Q_0|H(\Omega)|\) and \(\varphi = \arg(k - m\Omega^2 + \mathrm i\,c\Omega)\) (in the theorem this is the \(\arg\) of the polynomial at \(\mathrm i\Omega\), not our amplitude \(P\)).
  10. The second equation has the same left side and the force \(Q_0\sin\Omega t = Q_0\cos(\Omega t - \pi/2)\), which is the force of the first equation delayed by \(\tau = \pi/(2\Omega)\) (figure 24.20). The coefficients are constant, so \(w_{\mathrm{p}}(t)\) \(= v_{\mathrm{p}}(t - \tau) = X\cos(\Omega t - \varphi - \pi/2) = X\sin(\Omega t - \varphi)\).
  11. So \(p_{\mathrm{p}} = v_{\mathrm{p}} + \mathrm i\,w_{\mathrm{p}} = X\,\mathrm e^{\mathrm i(\Omega t - \varphi)}\) (definition 9.33): a circle of radius \(X\) that the point runs round with angular velocity \(\Omega > 0\), so in the sense of the turning of the shaft.
  12. The radius is \(X = m\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2|H| = a_{\mathrm{u}}\,(m\Omega^2/k)\,k|H| = a_{\mathrm{u}}\,r^2 D(r)\), because \(m\Omega^2/k = r^2\) and \(D = k|H|\) (definition 9.64). By step 4 of the proof of theorem 9.62 the complex number \(P = X\mathrm e^{-\mathrm i\varphi}\) equals \(m\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2\,H(\Omega)\) with \(H = 1/(k - m\Omega^2 + \mathrm i\,c\Omega) = 1/\big(k(1 - r^2 + 2\mathrm i\zeta r)\big)\), since \(c\Omega/k = 2\zeta r\). This proves item 2.
  13. The remainder \(p - p_{\mathrm{p}}\) solves the free equation \(m\ddot p + c\dot p + k p = 0\), that is the free equations of both real coordinates (theorem 9.62, item 2), and for \(\zeta > 0\) it tends to zero (item 3 of the same theorem). This is item 3.

Source: FPGL section 6.2.1 (PDF p. 248-250) gets equations (6.5) from the free-vibration equations (3.63) by substituting the displacement of the centre of mass, section 6.2.2 (PDF p. 252-253) gives equation (6.16) and the complex amplitude \(r_0\) from (6.17) to (6.19), which is \(P\) in equation (24.9), and section 6.2.3 (PDF p. 259) states that (6.16) holds for the Jeffcott rotor too. The derivation from Lagrange's equations in steps 1 to 8 is ours, as in example 9.76. The radius \(|P|\) is \(|r_0|\) of FPGL (figure 6.5, PDF p. 254).

The theorem says that under unbalance the disk centre goes round (figure 24.15). It goes round a circle because in the plane \(w\) the force is the same as in the plane \(v\) but delayed by a quarter of a period (step 10), and always in the sense of the turning of the shaft, because the force itself turns in that sense. The radius of the circle is \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\,r^2 D(r)\). In chapter 9 we obtained the same formula for a machine with an unbalanced mass, \(X = (m_{\mathrm{u}} a_{\mathrm{u}}/M)\,r^2 D(r)\) (equation (9.74)), only with a mass ratio. Here the whole disk is unbalanced and the mass ratio is \(1\).

We read the upper graph from the left. On the horizontal axis is the ratio \(r = \Omega/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), on the vertical one the radius \(|p|\) in units of the eccentricity, shown by the blue curve. At low speed, \(r = 0{,}5\), \(|p| = 0{,}3332\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\), because the force \(m a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2\) is small and the spring holds it. The radius grows and at \(r = 1\) reaches \(25{,}000\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\), which is \(1/(2\zeta)\), because at \(r = 1\) the spring force \(k|P|\) and the inertia force \(m\Omega^2|P|\) on the disk cancel (\(k = m\Omega^2\)) and the force \(m\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2\) is opposed only by the damping \(c\Omega|P|\). From \(c\Omega|P| = m\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2\) we get \(|P| = a_{\mathrm{u}}m\Omega/c = a_{\mathrm{u}}/(2\zeta)\), and indeed only the term \(2\mathrm i\zeta r\) is left in the denominator of equation (24.9). The peak of the curve, the orange dot, lies a little to the right of \(r = 1\) and a little higher, which we compute exactly below. At \(r = 0{,}9\) it is still \(4{,}1886\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\) and at \(r = 1{,}1\) it is \(5{,}6394\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\) (SymPy). After that the radius falls. At \(r = 2\) it is \(1{,}3329\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\), at \(r = 5\) it is \(1{,}0416\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\), and it tends to the value \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\). The vertical axis is logarithmic because the values \(0{,}1\) and \(25\) differ by more than two orders of magnitude. The lag \(\varphi\) is near zero for small \(r\) (at \(r = 0{,}5\) it is \(1{,}5^\circ\)), at \(r = 1\) it is \(90^\circ\) and for large \(r\) it is near \(180^\circ\). What that means in the plane of the disk is shown by figure 24.22.

We take three snapshots. In each we take the moment when the vector from \(S\) to \(G\) points along the axis \(v\). The centre \(S\) goes round the blue circle, the centre of mass \(G\) round the dashed orange one. At \(r = 0{,}5\) the points \(S\) and \(G\) lie almost in the same direction from \(O\) and the centre of mass is farther from the axis than the centre: \(|p_{\mathrm{G}}| = 1{,}3331\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\) against \(|p| = 0{,}3332\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\). The disk goes round with a small radius and the centre of mass outside it. At \(r = 1\) the point \(S\) is below the axis and \(G\) is \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\) to the right of it, a distance \(|SG| = a_{\mathrm{u}}\) that is barely visible against the radius \(25\) times larger (in this panel \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\) is only \(0{,}08\) cm). At \(r = 2\) the point \(S\) is to the left of \(O\) and \(G\) lies between \(S\) and \(O\), so the centre of mass is closer to the axis: \(|p_{\mathrm{G}}| = 0{,}3343\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\). The centre of mass is now inside the orbit of the centre. At \(r = 5\) it would be \(|p_{\mathrm{G}}| = 0{,}0425\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\).

Definition 24.8 Critical speed (kritična hitrost)

For a Jeffcott rotor with unbalance, the critical speed (kritična hitrost) \(\Omega_{\mathrm{c}} > 0\) is the spin speed at which the radius \(|P|\) of the circular orbit of theorem 24.7, as a function of \(\Omega\), is largest, if such a largest value exists. We write \(r_{\mathrm{c}} = \Omega_{\mathrm{c}}/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), the position of the peak on the horizontal axis of figure 24.21, and usually give \(\Omega_{\mathrm{c}}\) in rev/min. A more general definition for several masses is in section 24.6.

Source: FPGL section 6.2.2 (PDF p. 254): "When the amplitude of whirl is a maximum, the corresponding rotor speed is called the critical speed." The more general definition is in section 6.7 (PDF p. 293), not used here.

The word critical says that at such a speed turning is no longer safe. FPGL (PDF p. 247) writes that if a machine runs continuously at a critical speed, damage can occur very quickly, and (PDF p. 254) that it is unlikely that the rotor can be operated safely at a steady speed near it. Where is this speed? Without damping the denominator of equation (24.9) is zero at \(r = 1\). There is no circular solution there, and as \(r\) approaches \(1\) the radius \(|P| = a_{\mathrm{u}}r^2/|1 - r^2|\) grows beyond every bound. With little damping the peak is somewhere near \(r = 1\), as the orange dot of figure 24.21 shows for \(\zeta = 0{,}02\). The theorem gives the exact answer.

Theorem 24.9 Critical speed of the Jeffcott rotor (kritična hitrost Jeffcottovega rotorja)

In the setting of theorem 24.7 with \(\zeta \ge 0\) the following holds for the curve \(|P|\):

  1. If \(0 < \zeta < 1/\sqrt2\), then \(|P|\) as a function of \(r > 0\) has exactly one largest peak at
    \[r_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 2\zeta^2}} , \qquad |P|_{\max} = \frac{a_{\mathrm{u}}}{2\zeta\sqrt{1 - \zeta^2}} . \tag{24.10}\]
  2. If \(\zeta \ge 1/\sqrt2\), then \(|P|\) is strictly increasing on \((0, \infty)\) and tends to \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\) without reaching it: there is no critical speed.
  3. If \(\zeta = 0\), then \(|P| \to \infty\) as \(r \to 1\) (figure 24.23).
Proof

We must show where \(|P|\) is largest. We write it as \(a_{\mathrm{u}}/\sqrt{g}\) with one function \(g\) and find the smallest value of \(g\) by completing the square (figure 24.24).

  1. By equation (24.9), \((|P|/a_{\mathrm{u}})^2 = r^4/\big((1 - r^2)^2 + 4\zeta^2r^2\big)\). We divide numerator and denominator by \(r^4\) and introduce \(u = 1/r^2 \in (0, \infty)\): \((|P|/a_{\mathrm{u}})^2 = 1/g(u)\) with \(g(u) = (u - 1)^2 + 4\zeta^2u\).
  2. With \(b = 1 - 2\zeta^2\) we have \(g(u) = u^2 - 2bu + 1 = (u - b)^2 + 1 - b^2\) and \(1 - b^2 = (1 - b)(1 + b) = 2\zeta^2\cdot 2(1 - \zeta^2) = 4\zeta^2(1 - \zeta^2)\).
  3. Since \(u = 1/r^2\) is smaller at larger \(r\), \(|P|\) is largest where \(g\) is smallest. If \(b > 0\) (that is \(\zeta < 1/\sqrt2\)), \(u = b\) is admissible and \(g_{\min} = 4\zeta^2(1 - \zeta^2)\) at \(r_{\mathrm{c}}^2 = 1/b\). This is also the only minimum of \(g\), because the square \((u - b)^2\) is positive for \(u \ne b\). Hence \(|P|_{\max}\) of equation (24.10) for \(\zeta > 0\). This is item 1.
  4. If \(b \le 0\) (that is \(\zeta \ge 1/\sqrt2\)), then for every \(u > 0\) \(g(u) - 1 = u(u - 2b) > 0\) and \(g\) is increasing on \((0, \infty)\), because \((u - b)^2\) is increasing there. So \(|P|/a_{\mathrm{u}} = g^{-1/2}\) is decreasing in \(u\), that is increasing in \(r\), and \(g \to 1\) as \(u \to 0\) (that is \(r \to \infty\)), hence \(|P| < a_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(|P| \to a_{\mathrm{u}}\). This is item 2.
  5. For \(\zeta = 0\), \(g(u) = (u - 1)^2 \to 0\) as \(u \to 1\) and \(|P| \to \infty\). This is item 3.

Source: FPGL section 6.2.2 (PDF p. 253): from \(|r_0|\) in equation (6.20) the maximum is found by differentiating \(|r_0|^2\) with respect to \(R^2\), with the result \(R^2 = 1/(1 - 2\zeta^2)\) in the unnumbered equation below it. The proof by completing the square is not from the source.

So the critical speed \(\Omega_{\mathrm{c}}\) does not coincide exactly with the natural frequency \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\). For R1 with \(\zeta = 0{,}02\), \(r_{\mathrm{c}} = 1{,}00040\), that is \(\Omega_{\mathrm{c}} = 1483{,}75\) rev/min against \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 1483{,}16\) rev/min, and the peak is \(25{,}005\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\) against \(25{,}000\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\) at \(r = 1\). So we may equate the critical speed with the natural frequency, but only for small damping. At \(\zeta = 0{,}1\) it is \(r_{\mathrm{c}} = 1{,}0102\) and at \(\zeta = 0{,}3\) already \(1{,}1043\). In chapter 9 the peak of the dynamic factor \(D(r)\) was at \(r = \sqrt{1 - 2\zeta^2} < 1\) (theorem 9.66, item 1), here it is at \(r > 1\). The reason is the factor \(r^2\) in theorem 24.7: the force \(m a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2\) grows with speed, so the response keeps growing even where \(D\) already falls. At slow turning the force is small, at \(r = 0{,}5\) it is only a quarter of the force at \(r = 1\).

A critical speed is not a property of every rotor. At damping \(\zeta = 0{,}6\) the theorem (item 1) gives \(r_{\mathrm{c}} = 1{,}8898\) with a peak \(1{,}0417\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\), barely above \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\), and the peak has almost gone (figure 24.21 shows the case \(\zeta = 0{,}02\), where it is still large). At \(\zeta = 0{,}8\), by item 2, \(|P| = 0{,}9647\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\) at \(r = 3\), \(0{,}9972\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\) at \(r = 10\) and \(0{,}99997\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\) at \(r = 100\), always less than \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\) and with no peak (SymPy, NumPy). Above the limit \(\zeta = 1/\sqrt2\) there is no critical speed. For R1, \(\zeta = 0{,}02\), far below the limit \(1/\sqrt2 \approx 0{,}707\), so R1 has a sharp peak at the critical speed.

Where does the centre of mass go? Figure 24.21 has also the blackwhite curve: the distance of the centre of mass from the bearing axis, \(|p_{\mathrm{G}}|\). The centre of mass is at \(p_{\mathrm{G}} = p + a_{\mathrm{u}}\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\Omega t} = a_{\mathrm{u}}\,(1 + H_{\mathrm{u}})\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\Omega t}\) with \(H_{\mathrm{u}} = P/a_{\mathrm{u}} = r^2/(1 - r^2 + 2\mathrm i\zeta r)\). For large \(r\) the curve goes to zero, for small \(r\) to \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\), because there \(|p|\) is small and the centre of mass is almost \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\) from the centre.

Corollary 24.10 Self-centring (samocentriranje)

In the setting of theorem 24.7 the distance of the centre of mass from the bearing axis is

\[|p_{\mathrm{G}}| = a_{\mathrm{u}}\,\frac{\sqrt{1 + 4\zeta^2r^2}}{\sqrt{(1 - r^2)^2 + 4\zeta^2r^2}} . \tag{24.11}\]

As \(r \to \infty\), \(|p_{\mathrm{G}}| \to 0\) and \(|p| \to a_{\mathrm{u}}\). For \(\zeta = 0\) and \(r \ne 1\), \(|p_{\mathrm{G}}| = a_{\mathrm{u}}/|1 - r^2|\) and \(|p| = a_{\mathrm{u}}r^2/|1 - r^2|\), so \(|p_{\mathrm{G}}| = |p|/r^2\). Without damping the centre of mass is thus farther from the bearing axis than the disk centre for \(r < 1\) and nearer for \(r > 1\).

Proof

We must show the formula that follows from the theorem, and the limits.

  1. Let \(H_{\mathrm{u}} = P/a_{\mathrm{u}} = r^2/(1 - r^2 + 2\mathrm i\zeta r)\). By theorem 24.7, \(p = a_{\mathrm{u}}H_{\mathrm{u}}\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\Omega t}\). The centre of mass is \(p_{\mathrm{G}} = p + a_{\mathrm{u}}\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\Omega t}\) \(= a_{\mathrm{u}}(1 + H_{\mathrm{u}})\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\Omega t}\) (definition 24.6).
  2. From \(1 + H_{\mathrm{u}} = (1 - r^2 + 2\mathrm i\zeta r + r^2)/(1 - r^2 + 2\mathrm i\zeta r) = (1 + 2\mathrm i\zeta r)/(1 - r^2 + 2\mathrm i\zeta r)\) and \(|\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\Omega t}| = 1\) we get equation (24.11).
  3. As \(r \to \infty\) the numerator \(\sqrt{1 + 4\zeta^2r^2} \sim 2\zeta r\) for \(\zeta > 0\) (and \(1\) for \(\zeta = 0\)), while the denominator grows as \(r^2\), so the quotient tends to zero. The radius \(|p| = a_{\mathrm{u}}r^2D(r)\) has, after division by \(r^2\), the denominator \(\sqrt{(1/r^2 - 1)^2 + 4\zeta^2/r^2} \to 1\), hence \(|p| \to a_{\mathrm{u}}\).
  4. For \(\zeta = 0\), \(H_{\mathrm{u}} = r^2/(1 - r^2)\) and \(1 + H_{\mathrm{u}} = 1/(1 - r^2)\). From this \(|p_{\mathrm{G}}|\) and \(|p|\) and their ratio \(r^2\). The ratio \(|p_{\mathrm{G}}|/|p| = 1/r^2\) is larger than \(1\) exactly for \(r < 1\).

Source: FPGL section 6.2.2 (PDF p. 254-256, figures 6.6 and 6.7) describes the same as the figure: below the critical speed the heavy side is outside the orbit of the centre, above it inside, and at a very high speed the rotor turns about the heavy side. The proof is ours.

The reason for self-centring (figure 24.22, the panel \(r = 2\), where the centre of mass is inside the orbit of the centre) is Newton's second law, as at the start of the section. Without damping the only force on the disk is the force of the shaft \(-k\,p\). The centre of mass goes round with radius \(|p_{\mathrm{G}}|\) and angular velocity \(\Omega\), so its acceleration is \(\Omega^2|p_{\mathrm{G}}|\), hence \(m\,\Omega^2|p_{\mathrm{G}}| = k|p|\) and \(|p_{\mathrm{G}}| = |p|/r^2\), as the corollary says. For large \(r\) the number \(r^2\) is large, so \(|p_{\mathrm{G}}|\) must be small. Indeed the spring is stretched only by \(|p| \le |p_{\mathrm{G}}| + a_{\mathrm{u}}\), because \(S\) is \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\) away from \(G\). From \(r^2|p_{\mathrm{G}}| = |p| \le |p_{\mathrm{G}}| + a_{\mathrm{u}}\) we get for \(r > 1\) the bound \(|p_{\mathrm{G}}| \le a_{\mathrm{u}}/(r^2 - 1)\). A spring stretched this little gives no force for a large acceleration, so the centre of mass hardly moves and the disk turns about its centre of mass. At \(r = 3\), \(|p_{\mathrm{G}}| = 0{,}1259\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\) with damping \(\zeta = 0{,}02\) and \(0{,}1250\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\) without it.

Let us see what this means for the shaft and the bearings. The rotor R1 has \(a_{\mathrm{u}} = 0{,}05\) mm and \(\zeta = 0{,}02\). At \(r = 1\) the radius of the circle is \(|P| = a_{\mathrm{u}}/(2\zeta) = 1{,}250\) mm. The force of the shaft on the disk is \(k|P| = 1{,}1822\cdot10^6 \cdot 1{,}250\cdot10^{-3} = 1478\) N and points towards the bearing axis (theorem 24.7, step 4), and the disk acts with such a force \(F\) on the shaft.

We draw the shaft, bent under this force, and the bearing axis dashed. The shaft has no mass, so the equilibrium of forces and moments on it is the same as for a static load: at midspan the disk acts with the force \(F\) (away from the axis, by the law of action and reaction), and each of the bearings holds it with a force \(F/2\) in the opposite direction (symmetry, the sum of the forces on the shaft is zero). So each bearing carries \(F/2 = 739\) N, which is \(3{,}07\) times the static force under the weight of the disk (\(mg/2 = 240{,}4\) N). The moment at midspan is \(FL/4 = 369{,}5\) N m (figure 5.118, a beam with a force at midspan) and the bending stress in the fibre on the outer side of the bend by theorem 5.35 is \(\sigma = M\,(d/2)/I = 58{,}8\) MPa, while the weight alone gives \(19{,}13\) MPa.

The fibres of the shaft are not fatigued by alternating bending here. In the four pictures below the centre \(S\) of the section of the shaft is each time at another place on the dashed path round \(O\), but by theorem 24.7 the angle from \(O\) to \(S\) is \(\Omega t - \varphi\) and a fibre on the surface of the shaft has the angle \(\theta_0 + \Omega t\). Their difference \(\theta_0 + \varphi\) is independent of time, so the fibre is always on the same side of the bend (the drawn fibre on the outer side), and the stress in it is constant. With alternating bending it would swing between tension and compression. FPGL (PDF p. 265) writes that elliptical orbits cause alternating stresses and forward circular ones do not. The reason for ellipses follows in the lemma below.

The theorem assumes the same stiffness in both planes \(v\) and \(w\). With rigid bearings this assumption is met, because the cross-section of the shaft is round (step 4 of the proof of the theorem). In reality a bearing on a pedestal is not equally stiff in all directions, the horizontal stiffness is usually lower than the vertical one (FPGL, PDF p. 263). What then happens to the orbit? We replace the idealization of rigid bearings by bearings that have springs in series with the shaft. Let the disk R1 with the same unbalance lie on bearings with stiffness \(2\cdot10^6\) N/m in the direction \(v\) and \(6\cdot10^6\) N/m in the direction \(w\), each. Under a force \(F\) at midspan the shaft bends by \(F/k\) and each support sinks by \((F/2)/k_{\mathrm{b}}\) (figure 24.26), so the midspan sinks by \(F/k + F/(2k_{\mathrm{b}})\) (lemma 5.60: the displacement of a rigid body and the bending add). The stiffness at midspan is therefore \(1/k_{\mathrm{v}} = 1/k + 1/(2k_{\mathrm{b},\mathrm{v}})\), numerically \(k_{\mathrm{v}} = 9{,}1253\cdot10^5\) N/m and \(k_{\mathrm{w}} = 1{,}0762\cdot10^6\) N/m. The natural circular frequencies are \(\omega_{\mathrm{v}} = 136{,}45\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{w}} = 148{,}19\) 1/s, that is \(1303{,}0\) and \(1415{,}1\) rev/min. We neglect damping to keep the calculation clear.

Lemma 24.11 Unbalance with different stiffnesses (neuravnoteženost pri različnih togostih)

Let the Jeffcott rotor without damping of theorem 24.7 have stiffness \(k_{\mathrm{v}}\) at the disk in the plane \(v\) and \(k_{\mathrm{w}}\) in the plane \(w\), \(\omega_{\mathrm{v}} = \sqrt{k_{\mathrm{v}}/m} < \omega_{\mathrm{w}} = \sqrt{k_{\mathrm{w}}/m}\), and let \(\Omega \ne \omega_{\mathrm{v}}, \omega_{\mathrm{w}}\). Then:

  1. One solution is \(v = A_{\mathrm{v}}\cos\Omega t\), \(w = A_{\mathrm{w}}\sin\Omega t\) with \(A_{\mathrm{v}} = a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2/(\omega_{\mathrm{v}}^2 - \Omega^2)\) and \(A_{\mathrm{w}} = a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2/(\omega_{\mathrm{w}}^2 - \Omega^2)\). The disk centre moves on an ellipse with semi-axes \(|A_{\mathrm{v}}|\) and \(|A_{\mathrm{w}}|\) along the axes.
  2. The orbit is in forward whirl if \(A_{\mathrm{v}}A_{\mathrm{w}} > 0\) and in backward whirl if \(A_{\mathrm{v}}A_{\mathrm{w}} < 0\). The latter holds exactly for \(\omega_{\mathrm{v}} < \Omega < \omega_{\mathrm{w}}\).
  3. As \(\Omega \to \omega_{\mathrm{v}}\) and as \(\Omega \to \omega_{\mathrm{w}}\) one semi-axis tends to infinity: there are two critical speeds.
Proof

We must show the solution by checking it, the shape of the orbit and the sign of the turning.

  1. Steps 1 to 7 of the proof of theorem 24.7 with \(c = 0\) and potential energy \(\tfrac12(k_{\mathrm{v}}v^2 + k_{\mathrm{w}}w^2)\) give \(m\ddot v + k_{\mathrm{v}}v = m a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2\cos\Omega t\) and \(m\ddot w + k_{\mathrm{w}}w = m a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2\sin\Omega t\).
  2. For \(v = A\cos\Omega t\), \(\ddot v = -\Omega^2 v\) and \((k_{\mathrm{v}} - m\Omega^2)A = m a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2\), so \(A = a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2/(\omega_{\mathrm{v}}^2 - \Omega^2)\). Likewise for \(w\) with a sine. So \(A_{\mathrm{v}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{w}}\) are those of item 1. Every other solution differs from it by a free vibration in each plane (theorem 9.62, item 2), which does not decay without damping. This solution is the one that remains under however small a damping once the free vibration has died out: by the same theorem, with damping \(c\) the amplitude in the plane \(v\) is \(m a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2/|k_{\mathrm{v}} - m\Omega^2 + \mathrm i\,c\Omega|\), which tends to \(|A_{\mathrm{v}}|\) as \(c \to 0\), because \(k_{\mathrm{v}} - m\Omega^2 \ne 0\). The same holds in the plane \(w\).
  3. From \(\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1\) it follows that \((v/A_{\mathrm{v}})^2 + (w/A_{\mathrm{w}})^2 = 1\), an ellipse with semi-axes \(|A_{\mathrm{v}}|\) and \(|A_{\mathrm{w}}|\).
  4. Let \(\vartheta(t)\) be the angle from the \(v\) axis to the centre, so \(v = |p|\cos\vartheta\) and \(w = |p|\sin\vartheta\). Here \(|p| > 0\), because an ellipse with nonzero semi-axes does not pass through \(O\). By the product rule (lemma 1.82, item 3) and the chain rule (lemma 4.43), \(\dot v = \dot{|p|}\cos\vartheta - |p|\,\dot\vartheta\sin\vartheta\) and \(\dot w = \dot{|p|}\sin\vartheta + |p|\,\dot\vartheta\cos\vartheta\), so \(v\dot w - w\dot v = |p|^2\dot\vartheta\,(\cos^2\vartheta + \sin^2\vartheta) = |p|^2\dot\vartheta\). Here \(v\dot w - w\dot v = A_{\mathrm{v}}\cos\Omega t\cdot A_{\mathrm{w}}\Omega\cos\Omega t + A_{\mathrm{w}}\sin\Omega t\cdot A_{\mathrm{v}}\Omega\sin\Omega t = A_{\mathrm{v}}A_{\mathrm{w}}\Omega\), a constant. The angle \(\vartheta\) of the centre therefore grows (\(\dot\vartheta > 0\), turning in the sense of the shaft, forward whirl, definition 24.3) exactly when \(A_{\mathrm{v}}A_{\mathrm{w}} > 0\).
  5. The product \(A_{\mathrm{v}}A_{\mathrm{w}} = a_{\mathrm{u}}^2\Omega^4/\big((\omega_{\mathrm{v}}^2 - \Omega^2)(\omega_{\mathrm{w}}^2 - \Omega^2)\big)\) is negative exactly when the two factors in the denominator have opposite signs, that is for \(\omega_{\mathrm{v}}^2 < \Omega^2 < \omega_{\mathrm{w}}^2\), since \(\omega_{\mathrm{v}} < \omega_{\mathrm{w}}\).
  6. If \(\Omega \to \omega_{\mathrm{v}}\), then \(\omega_{\mathrm{v}}^2 - \Omega^2 \to 0\) and \(|A_{\mathrm{v}}| \to \infty\). The same for \(\omega_{\mathrm{w}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{w}}\).

Source: FPGL sections 6.2.5 and 6.2.6 (PDF p. 263-266): the orbit of a rigid rotor on anisotropic bearings is an ellipse and backward whirl occurs in speed ranges that, for damped bearings, are roughly between the two critical speeds (example 6.2.3, figure 6.13, PDF p. 265-266), and damping can remove it. The proof for the undamped model is ours.

Let us look at the three speeds on the horizontal axis \(\Omega\) of the previous figure.

At \(1042\) rev/min, below both natural frequencies, \(A_{\mathrm{v}} = 0{,}0887\) mm and \(A_{\mathrm{w}} = 0{,}0592\) mm are positive and the orbit is an ellipse in forward whirl. At \(1359\) rev/min, between \(1303\) and \(1415\) rev/min, \(A_{\mathrm{v}} = -0{,}6199\) mm and \(A_{\mathrm{w}} = +0{,}5935\) mm, and the orbit is almost a circle of large radius with backward whirl. The reason is physical: the plane \(v\) is already above its resonance, where the response opposes the force, while the plane \(w\) is still below it, where the response follows the force, and the two motions combine into the opposite sense. At \(1698\) rev/min, above both, both \(A\) are negative (\(-0{,}1216\) and \(-0{,}1637\) mm) and the orbit is forward again, but with the longer axis along \(w\). Theorem 24.7 therefore relies on equal stiffness in both planes. Without it there is no circle, no constant stress in a fibre (the centre moves unevenly while the fibre of the shaft turns evenly, so the angle between them changes) and no single critical speed.

We got to know the response to unbalance on the simplest model and saw that, as a function of the ratio \(r\), two numbers determine it, \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(\zeta\). The next section adds the tilt of the disk, which brings the gyroscopic moment (section 24.3). Running through a critical speed at start-up is treated in section 24.6, and the removal of unbalance with weights in section 24.8.

24.3 Gyroscopic couple of a disk

The Jeffcott rotor (Jeffcottov rotor) of section 24.1 has the disk at midspan of the shaft. There the disk only translates, because the middle of a symmetrically loaded shaft does not tilt. A disk that sits elsewhere tilts with the shaft, and a disk that turns answers a tilt differently from a disk at rest. Here we find the equation that describes this. We write it for the disk alone, with the forces and couples that the shaft exerts on it (their link with the shaft is made by the next section). The promise of chapters 8 and 13, that gyroscopic forces appear in turning bodies, is kept here.

24.3.1 A wheel that we tilt

Take a bicycle wheel, hold it by the axle at both ends and spin it. If we now move the axle parallel to itself, we feel nothing special. If we try to tilt it, for example the right end upwards, the wheel pushes us sideways: one hand feels a force forwards, the other backwards, as if the wheel wanted to turn the axle about the vertical instead of about the horizontal. A wheel at rest does not do this. The effect can be measured and we shall calculate it.

Figure 24.29 says what we shall calculate. First the axis \(x\) of the equilibrium position of the shaft and the two bearings at its ends. The shaft, taken here without mass (section 24.1), bends under load, in the plane \(x y\) by the function \(v(x)\) (top), in the plane \(x z\) by the function \(w(x)\) (bottom). The disk is fixed on the shaft, drawn from the side as a thick line, and sits perpendicular to the shaft. Because the shaft tilts at the disk, the axis of the disk, the tangent to the bent shaft, tilts with it. The disk therefore moves by the displacement \(v\) or \(w\) and its axis tilts from the position \(x\) by the angle \(\alpha\) in the plane \(x y\) and the angle \(\beta\) in the plane \(x z\). The angles are measured in radians. Transverse displacement and tilt are thus four numbers \(v\), \(w\), \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), all functions of time, and these numbers will be the coordinates of the disk.

For small tilts \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) equal the slopes of the shaft \(v'\) and \(w'\). By a more exact calculation (below, before lemma 24.14) the axis of the disk points in the direction \((\cos\alpha\cos\beta,\ \sin\alpha,\ \cos\alpha\sin\beta)\), so \(v' = \tan\alpha/\cos\beta\) and \(w' = \tan\beta\). At a tilt of \(0{,}01\) (0,57 degrees) \(v'\) exceeds \(\alpha\) by the relative amount \(8\cdot 10^{-5}\), at \(0{,}05\) by \(2\cdot 10^{-3}\). To the end of the section we assume that both tilts are smaller than \(0{,}01\) in absolute value, and wherever this says more than a word, we state what part of the value we neglected.

The word gyroscopic (žiroskopski) is taken from the physics of spinning tops. It comes from the Greek words for turning and observing, because a gyroscope is a device in which the turning is observed as the keeping of the direction of an axis. The same effect is present in a disk that we spin in a machine, and so its answer to a tilt is called gyroscopic.

24.3.2 The disk as a rigid body

For the calculation we need a model of the disk, its assumptions and two numbers that measure inertia. The disk is a rigid body (definition 8.39) and does not deform. This is an idealization: for our disk of diameter 0,4 m and thickness 0,05 m on a shaft of diameter 0,04 m we take its deformation to be negligible against the bending of the shaft. The book does not derive an estimate of this assumption, a full treatment would model the disk with finite elements (chapter 15). Its centre of mass lies on the axis perpendicular to the plate and stays on the shaft. The turning about the axis has a constant angular velocity \(\Omega\) that we prescribe, just as in chapter 9 in example 9.76 the angle \(\Omega t\) of the unbalanced mass is prescribed. We call \(\Omega\) the spin speed (hitrost vrtenja), because it is the speed with which the disk turns about its own axis. Its unit is \(1/\mathrm{s}\), and \(\Omega\) is positive in the sense from the axis \(y\) towards the axis \(z\) (right-hand screw about the axis \(x\)). The shape of the disk is described by a definition.

In the figure the disk is a cylinder. Through its centre of mass \(G\) passes the axis \(x\), which is the axis of the disk. We measure the radius \(R\) and the thickness \(h\). A rotation \(\varphi\) about the axis maps the disk onto itself, the rotation by \(\pi\) and the rotation by \(\pi/2\) are the special cases. The point with the small mass element is at \(\sqrt{y^2+z^2}\) from the axis, at \(x\) from the plane through \(G\) and at \(\sqrt{x^2+z^2}\) from the diameter \(y\).

Definition 24.12 Axisymmetric disk (osnosimetričen disk)

An axisymmetric disk is a rigid body (definition 8.39) with continuous density \(\rho > 0\) on a region \(B\) with nonempty interior, whose centre of mass \(G\) lies on a line \(a\), called the axis of the disk (os diska), and whose mass distribution does not change when it is turned about \(a\) by any angle. In the reference position the axis \(a\) is the axis \(x\) with the origin at \(G\), and the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) are measured perpendicular to this axis.

Source: FPGL (PDF p. 97): a uniform round disk that turns about an axis. The general definition by invariance of the mass distribution is not from the source.

The inertia tensor of the disk (definition 8.89) therefore simplifies.

Lemma 24.13 The two moments of inertia of a disk (vztrajnostna momenta diska)

Let the disk be axisymmetric by definition 24.12 and let \(\mat J_{\mathrm{G}}\) be its inertia tensor in the reference position. Then \(\mat J_{\mathrm{G}} = \mathrm{diag}(J_{\mathrm{p}},\ J_{\mathrm{t}},\ J_{\mathrm{t}})\) with

\[J_{\mathrm{p}} = \int_{\mathrm{B}}\rho\,(y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}V , \qquad J_{\mathrm{t}} = \int_{\mathrm{B}}\rho\,(x^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{B}}\rho\,x^2\,\mathrm{d}V + \tfrac12 J_{\mathrm{p}} , \tag{24.12}\]
