In figure 24.55 the plane \(xy\) and the plane \(xz\) each carry one element, in blue and orange, and each shows the displacements \(v_1\), \(v_2\) (respectively \(w_1\), \(w_2\)) and the slopes \(\varphi_1\), \(\varphi_2\) (respectively \(\psi_1\), \(\psi_2\)) of both nodes. The deflection between the nodes is a polynomial of third degree built from Hermite functions (definition 12.3), and the planes do not influence each other as long as the cross-section is round. In a turning shaft, however, a gyroscopic term couples them, and so we join them into one complex number, as in section 24.1: the point of the axis in the plane of the cross-section has the coordinates \(v\) and \(w\), and we assign to it \(p = v + \mathrm{i}\,w\). The slope of the complex point is \(p' = v' + \mathrm{i}\,w' = \varphi + \mathrm{i}\,\psi\). The nodal unknown (vozliščna neznanka) of node \(j\) is the pair of complex numbers \((p_{\mathrm{j}}, p_{\mathrm{j}}')\), and the whole unknown of the rotor is a column \(\vek q\) of them, ordered by nodes as for the beam: \(\vek q = \vek d_{\mathrm{v}} + \mathrm{i}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{w}}\), where \(\vek d_{\mathrm{v}}\) and \(\vek d_{\mathrm{w}}\) are the real columns of nodal quantities of the planes \(xy\) and \(xz\). The rotation \(\Omega t\) of the shaft about its axis does not appear in \(\vek q\), because only the cross-sections carry it and the axis stays in place (the axis is the same axis at every time).

24.5.2 Shaft element

What is the kinetic energy of a piece of a turning shaft? We know the disk from lemma 24.15: a rigid body of mass \(m\) and moments \(J_{\mathrm{p}}\) and \(J_{\mathrm{t}}\) has, for small slopes \(\alpha = v'\) and \(\beta = w'\), the energy \(T = \tfrac12 m(\dot v^2 + \dot w^2) + \tfrac12 J_{\mathrm{t}}(\dot\alpha^2 + \dot\beta^2) + \tfrac12 J_{\mathrm{p}}\Omega^2 - J_{\mathrm{p}}\Omega\,\alpha\dot\beta\). The shaft is spread along its length, so we cannot assign a single mass to it. But we can cut it into \(N\) pieces of length \(\ell = h/N\), take each for a rigid cylinder and add them up, and then let \(\ell\) go to zero. This is the same step as for a sum that passes into an integral (Riemann sum), and it contains no quantity that is itself "infinitely small". The lemma is derived on this path. The cut is shown in figure 24.56. The element of length \(h\) is cut into pieces, each of length \(\ell\). The enlarged piece is a round cylinder with the moment about the axis \(J_{\mathrm{p}}\) and the moment about a diameter \(J_{\mathrm{t}}\), and for a small slope it turns about a diameter as a rigid body. The axial distance \(s\) runs from \(-\ell/2\) to \(\ell/2\) along the piece.

Lemma 24.27 Element of a rotating shaft (element vrteče se gredi)

Let \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\) be a beam element of length \(h\) (definition 12.3), with a round cross-section of constant diameter \(d\), area \(A\) and second moment of area \(I\) (definition 5.26), with modulus \(E\) and density \(\rho\). The shaft turns with constant speed \(\Omega\) about the axis \(x\), the cross-sections stay plane and perpendicular to the axis (Rayleigh model), the slopes are small. The deflection of the axis in both planes is \(v_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat H_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{v}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat H_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{w}}\) with the nodal columns \(\vek d_{\mathrm{v}} = (v_1, \varphi_1, v_2, \varphi_2)^\T\) and \(\vek d_{\mathrm{w}} = (w_1, \psi_1, w_2, \psi_2)^\T\). Then:

  1. The polar second moment of area \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = \int (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}A\) is \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = 2I\). Both axes are equivalent in the circle, because a quarter turn maps it onto itself, and the sum \(y^2 + z^2\) is the square of the radius.
  2. The kinetic energy of the element is, up to the term \(\tfrac12\rho I_{\mathrm{p}}\Omega^2 h\), which does not depend on the displacements,
    \[T_{\mathrm{e}} = \tfrac12\,\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{v}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{e}}\,\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{v}} + \tfrac12\,\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{w}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{e}}\,\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{w}} - \Omega\,\vek d_{\mathrm{v}}^\T\,\mat G_{\mathrm{e}}\,\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{w}} , \qquad \mat M_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat m_{\mathrm{e}} + \mat m_{\mathrm{e}}^{\mathrm{r}} , \quad \mat G_{\mathrm{e}} = 2\,\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}^{\mathrm{r}} , \tag{24.27}\]
    where \(\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}^{\mathrm{r}}\) are the matrices of lemmas 12.43 and 13.92. The sum over pieces turns into an integral, as the column sum in figure 24.58 shows.
  3. The strain energy of the element is \(U_{\mathrm{e}} = \tfrac12\,\vek d_{\mathrm{v}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{v}} + \tfrac12\,\vek d_{\mathrm{w}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{w}}\) with the matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) of lemma 12.4. Each plane has its own energy, the plane \(xy\) and the plane \(xz\), both with the same stiffness matrix.

The matrices \(\mat M_{\mathrm{e}}\), \(\mat G_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) are real and symmetric. Each of these matrices is symmetric about its diagonal.

Proof

We must show three things: the polar moment of the circle, the kinetic energy as a limit of sums of rigid pieces, and the strain energy of both planes. For the energy we use the disk of lemma 24.15, every piece is such a disk.

  1. A circle is mapped onto itself by a rotation through a right angle, which takes \(y\) into \(z\), so \(\int y^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \int z^2\,\mathrm{d}A = I\) and \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = \int (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}A = 2I\). For \(d = 40\) mm, \(I = 1{,}2566\cdot 10^{-7}\) m\(^4\) and \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = 2{,}5133\cdot 10^{-7}\) m\(^4\). The circle stays the same under a quarter turn, so the strip on the \(y\) axis gives the same as the strip on the \(z\) axis.
  2. We cut the element into \(N\) pieces of length \(\ell = h/N\) with centres \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\). A piece is a round cylinder of mass \(\rho A\ell\). Its polar mass moment is \(J_{\mathrm{p}} = \rho I_{\mathrm{p}}\ell = 2\rho I\ell\) by step 1. The transverse moment about a diameter through the centre is \(\int\rho\,(y^2 + s^2)\,\mathrm{d}V = \rho\,(I\ell + A\ell^3/12)\), because \(s \in [-\ell/2, \ell/2]\) is the axial distance and \(\int_{-\ell/2}^{\ell/2} s^2\,\mathrm{d}s = \ell^3/12\). The piece is a cylinder of length \(\ell\), and its axial distance \(s\) gives the term \(A\ell^3/12\) in the transverse moment.
  3. By lemma 24.15 the piece has the energy \(\tfrac12\rho A\ell\,(\dot v^2 + \dot w^2) + \tfrac12\rho(I\ell + A\ell^3/12)\,(\dot v'^2 + \dot w'^2) + \tfrac12 J_{\mathrm{p}}\Omega^2 - 2\rho I\ell\,\Omega\,v'\dot w'\), all values at \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\). The sum over \(j\) is the kinetic energy of the element, provided the third-order pieces are not too large. The energy of the piece is made of the displacement, the slope and the spin about the axis.
  4. The functions \(\dot v_{\mathrm{h}}\), \(\dot w_{\mathrm{h}}\) and their derivatives in \(x\) are polynomials and therefore continuous. The sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} f(x_{\mathrm{j}})\,\ell\) of a continuous function goes, as \(\ell \to 0\), to \(\int_{\mathrm{x}_\mathrm{a}}^{x_{\mathrm{b}}} f\,\mathrm{d}x\) (Riemann sum). The term with \(A\ell^3/12\) is \(\tfrac{A\ell^2}{12I}\) times the term with \(I\ell\), so its sum is bounded by \(\ell^2\) times a constant and goes to zero. The limit is \(T_{\mathrm{e}} = \int_{\mathrm{x}_\mathrm{a}}^{x_{\mathrm{b}}}\big[\tfrac12\rho A(\dot v_{\mathrm{h}}^2 + \dot w_{\mathrm{h}}^2) + \tfrac12\rho I(\dot v_{\mathrm{h}}'^2 + \dot w_{\mathrm{h}}'^2) - 2\rho I\,\Omega\,v_{\mathrm{h}}'\dot w_{\mathrm{h}}'\big]\mathrm{d}x + \tfrac12\rho I_{\mathrm{p}}\Omega^2h\). The pieces are columns that narrow as \(\ell\) shrinks and fill the area under the curve, while the term with \(\ell^3\) becomes a thin sliver that vanishes.
  5. We insert \(v_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat H_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{v}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat H_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{w}}\). The first two terms give \(\tfrac12\dot{\vek d}^\T\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\dot{\vek d}\) for each plane (steps 1 and 2 of lemma 12.43), the next two give \(\tfrac12\dot{\vek d}^\T\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}^{\mathrm{r}}\dot{\vek d}\) (steps 1 and 2 of lemma 13.92). The mixed term is \(2\rho I\,\Omega\int v_{\mathrm{h}}'\dot w_{\mathrm{h}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = \Omega\,\vek d_{\mathrm{v}}^\T\big(2\int\rho I\,\mat H_{\mathrm{e}}'^\T\mat H_{\mathrm{e}}'\,\mathrm{d}x\big)\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{w}} = \Omega\,\vek d_{\mathrm{v}}^\T\,2\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}^{\mathrm{r}}\,\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{w}}\), because \(v_{\mathrm{h}}' = \mat H_{\mathrm{e}}'\vek d_{\mathrm{v}}\) and \(\dot w_{\mathrm{h}}' = \mat H_{\mathrm{e}}'\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{w}}\) are numbers. With the minus sign this is equation (24.27). The matrices are the sum of the beam matrix and the rotary matrix, and the gyroscopic matrix is twice the second.
  6. The axis of the shaft is a principal axis of the section in every direction (circle, step 1), so bending in the plane \(xy\) and in the plane \(xz\) each has its own energy \(\tfrac12\int EI\,(v_{\mathrm{h}}'')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(\tfrac12\int EI\,(w_{\mathrm{h}}'')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) without a mixed term (theorem 5.35 and lemma 5.60). By lemma 12.4 each integral is \(\tfrac12\vek d^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d\). Each plane has its own energy, the plane \(xy\) and the plane \(xz\), with the same stiffness matrix.
  7. Symmetry: \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\) are symmetric (lemmas 12.4 and 12.43), \(\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}^{\mathrm{r}}\) is symmetric because of equation (13.98). The symmetry shows in the matrices as a mirroring across the diagonal.

Source: The proof is not from the source. FPGL (section 5.4.5, PDF pp. 188 to 190, equations 5.53 to 5.60) derives the gyroscopic shaft element from the same energy as for the disk and says that the polar moment of a thin disk cut from the shaft is twice the transverse one, hence "the factor 2". The matrix there is skew-symmetric, and the signs of the terms follow from FPGL's axes (the axis \(z\) for the shaft, figure 5.4, PDF p. 187), not from our choice of the axis \(x\).

Figure 24.57 shows the polar moment. The section is a circle with axes \(y\) and \(z\). Each strip at height \(y\) contributes its share to the integral \(I = \int y^2\,\mathrm{d}A\). A quarter turn moves the \(y\) axis onto the \(z\) axis and the circle stays the same, so \(\int y^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \int z^2\,\mathrm{d}A = I\). A point on the radius \(r\) has \(r^2 = y^2 + z^2\), so \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = 2I\).

Figure 24.58 shows the limit of the proof. The horizontal axis is \(x\), the vertical one \(f\). Under the curve \(f\) stand columns of width \(\ell\) with heights \(f(x_{\mathrm{j}})\). As \(\ell\) falls the columns narrow and their sum approaches the area under the curve. The thin sliver on top of each column is the term with \(\ell^3\), smaller than the first term by a factor \(\ell^2\).

Figure 24.59 shows the element matrices. Each is a \(4\times 4\) square with rows \(v_1, \varphi_1, v_2, \varphi_2\). The matrix \(\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the bending matrix, \(\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}^{\mathrm{r}}\) the rotary matrix, and their sum is \(\mat M_{\mathrm{e}}\). The gyroscopic matrix is twice the second. The stiffness matrix is the third. Each is symmetric: an entry below the diagonal equals its mirror entry above it.

The lemma says how the shaft element is made: the mass matrix \(\mat M_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the bending matrix (lemma 12.43) with the addition of rotary inertia (lemma 13.92), and the gyroscopic matrix \(\mat G_{\mathrm{e}}\) is twice that addition. The factor two is not mysterious: for a round shaft \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = 2I\), so turning about the axis is twice as hard as turning about a diameter, which we already see for the disk drawn as a flat plate (\(J_{\mathrm{p}} = 2J_{\mathrm{t}}\) for a thin plate). In figure 24.59 the matrix \(\mat M_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the sum of \(\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}^{\mathrm{r}}\), and the matrix \(\mat G_{\mathrm{e}}\) is twice the second.

The disk and the bearing are elements too. For the disk, the energy is already given by lemma 24.15, and we write it in the form that we shall assemble. The disk and the bearings are already drawn in figure 24.54.

Definition 24.28 Disk and bearing element (element diska in ležaja)

A rigid disk of mass \(m\), transverse mass moment \(J_{\mathrm{t}}\) and polar mass moment \(J_{\mathrm{p}}\) is fixed to the shaft at node \(j\). Its element has matrices that act on the complex unknown \((p_{\mathrm{j}}, p_{\mathrm{j}}')\) and are real \(2\times 2\), The disk and the bearings are only extra blocks at a node.

\[\mat M_{\mathrm{d}} = \begin{pmatrix} m & 0 \\ 0 & J_{\mathrm{t}} \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \mat G_{\mathrm{d}} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & J_{\mathrm{p}} \end{pmatrix} , \tag{24.28}\]

so the mass acts on the displacement, and \(J_{\mathrm{t}}\) and \(J_{\mathrm{p}}\) act on the slope. A bearing with isotropic stiffness \(k_{\mathrm{b}}\) (N/m) at node \(j\) is a spring with energy \(\tfrac12 k_{\mathrm{b}}(v_{\mathrm{j}}^2 + w_{\mathrm{j}}^2)\). It adds \(k_{\mathrm{b}}\) to the term of the matrix \(\mat K\) at the displacement \(p_{\mathrm{j}}\) and nothing elsewhere.

Source: FPGL (section 5.3, PDF pp. 175 to 177, equations 5.7 to 5.9) derives the disk elements from the kinetic energy with \(I_{\mathrm{d}}\) and \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\) (our \(J_{\mathrm{t}}\) and \(J_{\mathrm{p}}\)), and adds the bearings (section 5.5, PDF p. 194) as diagonal terms.

The matrices of equation (24.28) have the same form as the matrices of a piece of shaft from lemma 24.27, when the piece is shrunk towards zero: there the mass is \(\rho A\ell\), \(J_{\mathrm{t}} = \rho I\ell + \ldots\) and \(J_{\mathrm{p}} = 2\rho I\ell\). This is also the reason why the shaft and the disk can be put into the same sum. A piece shrunk toward zero is a disk, and its block is added to the same sum.

24.5.3 Assembling the rotor

Now we have the elements. For the beam, theorem 12.9 said that the matrix of the whole is obtained from the matrices of the elements with selection matrices \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\), which pick out of the whole column of unknowns those that belong to the element. We do the same for the rotor, except that we also have a sum for the disks and the bearings, and that we make one complex equation out of two real ones. Figure 24.60 shows what this sum does. On the grid the nodes carry indices 0 to 4. The column of unknowns has two rows for each node. Each element picks four rows from it, and its \(4\times 4\) matrix sits on the diagonal. Neighbouring elements share a node, so their matrices overlap in a \(2\times 2\) block and add there. The disk adds its own \(2\times 2\) block at its node and the bearings add the stiffness \(k_{\mathrm{b}}\) to the diagonal.

The two planes and their combination are shown in figure 24.61. The plane \(xy\) has its own matrices \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\), and so does the plane \(xz\). They are joined by the gyroscopic coupling, which has a plus sign in one direction and a minus in the other. With \(\vek q = \vek d_{\mathrm{v}} + \mathrm{i}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{w}}\) the two planes become one complex equation with the term \(-\mathrm{i}\,\Omega\,\mat G\dot{\vek q}\).

Theorem 24.29 Assembly of a rotor from elements (sestavljanje rotorja)

Let the shaft be divided into \(n\) elements of lemma 24.27 with selection matrices \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\) (definitions 7.10 and 7.11), let the nodes carry disks and bearings of definition 24.28, and in rigid bearings the displacement at the node is zero (we omit the corresponding rows and columns). Let The elements are blocks on the diagonal, the selection matrices put them in place, and the disk and bearings are extra terms.

\[\mat K = \sum_{\mathrm{e}=1}^{n}\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}} + \sum_{\text{bearings}} k_{\mathrm{b}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}^\T , \quad \mat M = \sum_{\mathrm{e}=1}^{n}\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{e}}\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}} + \sum_{\text{disks}}\mat Z_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{d}}\mat Z_{\mathrm{j}} , \quad \mat G = \sum_{\mathrm{e}=1}^{n}\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat G_{\mathrm{e}}\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}} + \sum_{\text{disks}}\mat Z_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\mat G_{\mathrm{d}}\mat Z_{\mathrm{j}} , \tag{24.29}\]

where \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the unit column at the displacement of node \(j\) and \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{j}}\) the selection matrix of \((p_{\mathrm{j}}, p_{\mathrm{j}}')\). Then:

  1. The kinetic energy of the rotor is, up to a constant, \(T = \tfrac12\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{v}}^\T\mat M\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{v}} + \tfrac12\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{w}}^\T\mat M\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{w}} - \Omega\,\vek d_{\mathrm{v}}^\T\mat G\,\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{w}}\), and the strain energy is \(U = \tfrac12\vek d_{\mathrm{v}}^\T\mat K\vek d_{\mathrm{v}} + \tfrac12\vek d_{\mathrm{w}}^\T\mat K\vek d_{\mathrm{w}}\). We add up the energies over the elements, which the selection moves onto the same global column.
  2. Lagrange's equations for forces \(\vek f_{\mathrm{v}}\) and \(\vek f_{\mathrm{w}}\) in the planes are The planes are \(xy\) and \(xz\), and they are joined by the gyroscopic coupling with opposite signs.
    \[\mat M\ddot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{v}} + \Omega\,\mat G\,\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{w}} + \mat K\vek d_{\mathrm{v}} = \vek f_{\mathrm{v}} , \qquad \mat M\ddot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{w}} - \Omega\,\mat G\,\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{v}} + \mat K\vek d_{\mathrm{w}} = \vek f_{\mathrm{w}} . \tag{24.30}\]
  3. For \(\vek q = \vek d_{\mathrm{v}} + \mathrm{i}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{w}}\) and \(\vek f = \vek f_{\mathrm{v}} + \mathrm{i}\,\vek f_{\mathrm{w}}\) the two equations are one complex equation: Both are one equation in complex form.
    \[\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} - \mathrm{i}\,\Omega\,\mat G\,\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = \vek f . \tag{24.31}\]
  4. The matrix \(\mat K\) is symmetric and positive definite if the bearings hold the shaft (at least two different bearings or two prescribed displacements). The matrix \(\mat M\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite, and positive definite if the shaft has mass. The matrix \(\mat G\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite. Therefore the matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}\mat 0 & \mat G \\ -\mat G & \mat 0\end{pmatrix}\) of the real form is skew-symmetric, and the equations have the form of theorem 24.21, so all frequencies are real. If the bearings hold the shaft, the energy has a single lowest position, but without bearings the free shaft forms a trough of zero energy. For \(\mat G\) the energy is already zero for a shift without tilt.
  5. The unbalance of the disk at node \(j\) (definition 24.6) gives in \(\vek f\), at the displacement \(p_{\mathrm{j}}\), the term \(m\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\,\Omega^2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\,\Omega t}\) (up to a phase angle), as in theorem 24.7. Unbalance is a mass with an eccentricity on the disk.
Idea

We add up the energy element by element as for the beam, then compute Lagrange's equations for \(\vek d_{\mathrm{v}}\) and \(\vek d_{\mathrm{w}}\) separately and join them. We add over the elements, then separately for the planes and combine them.

Proof

We must show that the energy is a sum over the elements, that both real equations follow from it, that these combine, and that the matrices have the properties of item 4.

  1. By theorem 12.9, item 1, \(\vek d_{\mathrm{v},\mathrm{e}} = \mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{v}}\) and \(\vek d_{\mathrm{v}}^\T\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat A\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{v}} = \vek d_{\mathrm{v},\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat A\vek d_{\mathrm{v},\mathrm{e}}\) for every matrix \(\mat A\), and likewise for \(\vek d_{\mathrm{w}}\) and for the mixed term \(\vek d_{\mathrm{v}}^\T\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat G_{\mathrm{e}}\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{w}}\). The sum over the elements of lemma 24.27 with the disks (kinetic energy of the disk from lemma 24.15) and the springs \(\tfrac12 k_{\mathrm{b}}(v_{\mathrm{j}}^2 + w_{\mathrm{j}}^2)\) is item 1. The selection matrix picks four rows of the element from the column, and neighbouring elements overlap.
  2. Lagrange's equations (theorem 8.99) for the coordinate \(d_{\mathrm{v},\mathrm{I}}\) are \(\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\,\partial T/\partial\dot d_{\mathrm{v},\mathrm{I}} - \partial T/\partial d_{\mathrm{v},\mathrm{I}} + \partial U/\partial d_{\mathrm{v},\mathrm{I}} = f_{\mathrm{v},\mathrm{I}}\). From item 1: \(\partial T/\partial\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{v}} = \mat M\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{v}}\), \(\partial T/\partial\vek d_{\mathrm{v}} = -\Omega\,\mat G\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{w}}\) and \(\partial U/\partial\vek d_{\mathrm{v}} = \mat K\vek d_{\mathrm{v}}\). This is the first equation (24.30). This is the equation of plane \(xy\).
  3. For \(\vek d_{\mathrm{w}}\): \(\partial T/\partial\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{w}} = \mat M\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{w}} - \Omega\,\mat G^\T\vek d_{\mathrm{v}}\) and \(\mat G^\T = \mat G\), so \(\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\) of it is \(\mat M\ddot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{w}} - \Omega\,\mat G\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{v}}\). The term \(T\) does not contain \(\vek d_{\mathrm{w}}\), so \(\partial T/\partial\vek d_{\mathrm{w}} = \vek 0\), and \(\partial U/\partial\vek d_{\mathrm{w}} = \mat K\vek d_{\mathrm{w}}\). This is the second equation. This is the equation of plane \(xz\) with the opposite sign of the coupling.
  4. We add the first equation to the second multiplied by \(\mathrm{i}\): \(\mat M(\ddot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{v}} + \mathrm{i}\ddot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{w}}) + \Omega\,\mat G\,(\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{w}} - \mathrm{i}\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{v}}) + \mat K\,(\vek d_{\mathrm{v}} + \mathrm{i}\vek d_{\mathrm{w}}) = \vek f_{\mathrm{v}} + \mathrm{i}\vek f_{\mathrm{w}}\). Because \(\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{w}} - \mathrm{i}\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{v}} = -\mathrm{i}\,(\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{v}} + \mathrm{i}\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{w}}) = -\mathrm{i}\dot{\vek q}\), this is equation (24.31). Adding the second plane is the combination into one.
  5. The matrices \(\mat K\), \(\mat M\), \(\mat G\) are by equation (24.29) sums of real symmetric matrices, hence symmetric. For \(\mat K\): \(\vek d^\T\mat K\vek d = \sum_{\mathrm{e}}\int EI\,(v_{\mathrm{h}}'')^2\,\mathrm{d}x + \sum k_{\mathrm{b}}\,v_{\mathrm{j}}^2 \ge 0\) (theorem 12.9, item 3). If it is zero, then \(v_{\mathrm{h}}'' = 0\) on every element, so \(v_{\mathrm{h}}\) is a polynomial of degree at most one on the whole beam (continuity of the slope) that is zero at two points or has a prescribed displacement, hence it is zero, and \(\vek d = \vek 0\). For \(\mat M\): \(\vek d^\T\mat M\vek d \ge \sum_{\mathrm{e}}\int\rho A\,v_{\mathrm{h}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x \ge 0\) (lemmas 12.43 and 13.92, step 5 of the first), if it is zero then \(v_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\) on every element (continuous nonnegative integrand), so \(\vek d = \vek 0\). For \(\mat G\): \(\vek d^\T\mat G\vek d = 2\sum_{\mathrm{e}}\int\rho I\,(v_{\mathrm{h}}')^2\,\mathrm{d}x + \sum_{\text{disks}} J_{\mathrm{p}}\,\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}^2 \ge 0\), where \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the slope in \(\vek d\) at the node of the disk (equation (13.98)). The matrices are sums of real symmetric terms, and their positivity is the condition that the bearings hold the shaft, otherwise the energy is zero along the trough.
  6. The real form of equation (24.30) with \(\vek x = (\vek d_{\mathrm{v}}, \vek d_{\mathrm{w}})\) is \(\hat{\mat M}\ddot{\vek x} + \Omega\,\hat{\mat G}\dot{\vek x} + \hat{\mat K}\vek x = \vek f\) with blocks \(\hat{\mat G} = \begin{pmatrix}\mat 0 & \mat G \\ -\mat G & \mat 0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\hat{\mat G}^\T = -\hat{\mat G}\) because of \(\mat G^\T = \mat G\), and with \(\hat{\mat M}\), \(\hat{\mat K}\) symmetric and positive definite. Step 5 fulfils the assumptions of theorem 24.21. Item 5 of the theorem is the unbalance force of the disk, which by theorem 24.7 has the form \(m\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\,\Omega^2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\), and which by the definition \(\vek f = \vek f_{\mathrm{v}} + \mathrm{i}\vek f_{\mathrm{w}}\) we place at the displacement of the disk node. The block \(\hat{\mat G}\) is the coupling of the two planes with opposite signs.

Source: FPGL (section 5.7, PDF pp. 214 to 215, equation 5.109) assembles the same matrices element by element and with selection matrices and omits the rows for rigid bearings. The proof of the theorem is not from the source.

The positivity of the matrices is shown in figure 24.62. A free shaft without bearings can shift or tilt without bending, and the energy is zero along the trough. When the bearings hold the shaft, zero energy occurs only at one position at the bottom of the bowl. A shift without tilt has zero energy for \(\mat G\), so \(\mat G\) is only semidefinite.

The theorem says that the whole rotor is described by the same complex equation as the Jeffcott rotor, only with a column \(\vek q\) in place of the number \(p\) and with matrices in place of numbers: \(m\to\mat M\), \(k\to\mat K\), and the term \(-\mathrm{i}\,\Omega\,\mat G\dot{\vek q}\) brings the gyroscopic coupling. For rotor R1 with \(n = 16\) elements, \(\vek q\) is a column of 32 complex unknowns (17 nodes times two, minus two displacements at the bearings), which is 64 real ones. We look for the whirl frequencies as solutions \(\vek q = \vek\varphi\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}\), that is \((\mat K + \Omega\,\omega\,\mat G - \omega^2\mat M)\,\vek\varphi = \vek 0\), and \(\omega > 0\) means forward whirl, \(\omega < 0\) backward (definition 24.3). This is a quadratic eigenvalue problem in \(\omega\). We solve it numerically by an extension to a matrix of twice the size (the states and their derivatives), which chapter 20 treats as the state form. Everything that the book proves uses only theorem 24.21 or the synchronous whirl of section 24.4. The column \(\vek q\) has two complex numbers for each node, and \(\omega > 0\) is whirl forward, \(\omega < 0\) is backward.

24.5.4 A test: five numbers that we already know

The model is correct if it gives results that are already known, and we make the test on rotors R1 and R2 (the disk at \(0{,}25\) m from the left bearing). All calculations are SymPy and NumPy, in the script outlines/ch-rotorska-dinamika/num-05.py. Figure 24.63 shows the deviations, the rows 1 to 5 from the top down. On the axis is the relative deviation in percent. The first three tests and the fourth lie at zero, and for the fifth the mesh lies just below the Rayleigh limit.

Example 24.30

Rotors R1 and R2 with \(n = 16\) shaft elements, as in figure 24.54 with more nodes, and \(\Omega\) as needed. Synchronous forward whirl, that is \(\omega = \Omega\) in equation (24.31), gives \((\mat K - \Omega^2(\mat M - \mat G))\,\vek\varphi = \vek 0\) (section 24.4).

test element source value elsewhere
R1, massless shaft, rigid bearings 1483,2 rev/min Jeffcott rotor, section 24.1 1483,2
R2, massless shaft, at rest 1906 and 8793 rev/min model with four degrees of freedom, section 24.4 1906 and 8793
R2, massless shaft, critical speed 2046 rev/min the same section (thin disk, a single section) 2046
R1, springs \(2\cdot 10^6\) N/m, massless shaft 1303,0 rev/min non-isotropic case, section 24.2 1303
R1, with shaft mass 1415,96 rev/min Rayleigh with shape factor \(17/35\) 1415,98

The first three entries hit exactly the values that are proved in sections 24.1 and 24.4 for a model without shaft mass. The fourth entry is the same number as for the same spring in section 24.2: in the bearing the springs of the shaft and of the bearing are connected in series, which gives \(k_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1/(1/k + 1/(2k_{\mathrm{b}}))\), and \(\sqrt{k_{\mathrm{eff}}/m}\) equals \(1303{,}0\) rev/min, as in the constructed case. For \(k_{\mathrm{b}} = 10^7\) and \(10^8\) N/m it is \(1441{,}2\) and \(1478{,}8\) rev/min, which again agrees with the same formula and shows that the rigid bearing (\(1483{,}2\)) is obtained as a limit. For the same spring \(2\cdot 10^6\) N/m but with shaft mass it is \(1235{,}3\) rev/min. All three lie at zero, and so does the fourth.

The fifth entry shows what the shaft mass adds. By theorem 13.81 the Rayleigh quotient with the shape of the static deflection under a central force is an upper bound for the true frequency. The static shape under a midspan force has an effective shaft mass of \(17/35\) of its mass (SymPy), which gives \(\omega = \sqrt{k/(m + (17/35)\,m_{\mathrm{s}})} = 148{,}281\) 1/s, that is \(1415{,}98\) rev/min, which is \(4{,}53\) % below the value without shaft mass. The mesh of elements is below this bound: for \(n = 2, 4, 8, 16\) the first natural speed at rest is \(1415{,}88\), \(1415{,}84\), \(1415{,}84\), \(1415{,}83\) rev/min, and without rotary inertia \(1415{,}94\), \(1415{,}90\), \(1415{,}90\), \(1415{,}90\), so always below \(1415{,}98\). The critical speed in synchronous whirl is \(1416{,}00\) rev/min for \(n = 2\) and \(1415{,}96\) rev/min for \(n = 4, 8, 16\). The difference between it and the value at rest is only \(0{,}009\) %, because the disk at midspan does not tilt in the first mode (\(v' = 0\) at the middle by symmetry), so \(J_{\mathrm{t}}\) and \(J_{\mathrm{p}}\) do not appear and only the contribution of the shaft remains. The mesh is below the limit given by the Rayleigh quotient.

A mesh of two elements is already within \(0{,}007\) % of Rayleigh and within \(0{,}004\) % of the mesh with sixteen elements. The reason is the shape: the static deflection under a central force is cubic piece by piece, so it lies in the space of the Hermite functions of the elements (section 24.5.2, definition 12.3), and the Rayleigh quotient is obtained already with a coarse mesh. Figure 24.64 shows the reason. The shaft is simply supported at its ends, and at the middle it is loaded by the force \(F\). The static deflection under a central force is made of two cubic pieces that meet at the nodes, exactly as the mesh builds it.

24.5.5 A test on a uniform shaft

For R1 the influence of the shaft hides in the margin of \(0{,}009\) %, because the disk at midspan covers its influence. For a shaft without disks it is visible. We take a simply supported shaft without a disk, that is a uniform shaft of length \(L = 1\) m and diameter 40 mm, and for it we can compute the exact solution in closed form. This solution is the yardstick for the mesh and at the same time a counterexample to the rule of chapter 13: rotary inertia always lowers the frequency, by theorem 13.89. In a turning rotor this does not hold for forward whirl. The disk at the middle hides the influence of the shaft.

The shaft is shown in figure 24.65. The shaft lies on two bearings and spins about its axis. The first shape is a half-sine, along which the shaft whirls.

Lemma 24.31 Uniform rotating shaft (enakomerna vrteča se gred)

A simply supported round shaft of length \(L\) with constant \(E\), \(\rho\), \(A\), \(I\) turns with \(\Omega\). Let \(\beta = n\pi/L\) (here \(n = 1, 2, \ldots\) is the number of the mode, not the number of elements), \(\omega_{\mathrm{EB}} = \beta^2\sqrt{EI/(\rho A)}\) and \(\varepsilon = \beta^2 I/A\), and let \(\varepsilon < 1\) (the radius of gyration \(\sqrt{I/A}\) of definition 13.88, \(\varepsilon = (n\pi\sqrt{I/A}/L)^2\)). The equations of motion of the Rayleigh model of a rotating shaft are \(\rho A\,v_{\mathrm{tt}} - \rho I\,v_{\mathrm{xxtt}} + EI\,v_{\mathrm{xxxx}} - 2\rho I\,\Omega\,w_{\mathrm{xxt}} = 0\) and \(\rho A\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} - \rho I\,w_{\mathrm{xxtt}} + EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} + 2\rho I\,\Omega\,v_{\mathrm{xxt}} = 0\) with the boundary conditions \(v = v_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) and \(w = w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) at both ends. Then: The shaft is simply supported, of length \(L\), and spins.

  1. The complex function \(p = v + \mathrm{i}\,w = P\sin(\beta x)\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}\) (\(P \ne 0\), \(\omega\) real) solves both equations and both conditions exactly when The first shape is a half-sine, along which the shaft whirls.
    \[(1 + \varepsilon)\,\omega^2 - 2\varepsilon\,\Omega\,\omega - \omega_{\mathrm{EB}}^2 = 0 . \tag{24.32}\]
  2. Equation (24.32) has one positive root (forward whirl) and one negative (backward whirl), \(\omega_\pm = \big(\varepsilon\,\Omega \pm \sqrt{\varepsilon^2\Omega^2 + (1 + \varepsilon)\,\omega_{\mathrm{EB}}^2}\big)/(1 + \varepsilon)\). At \(\Omega = 0\) they are \(\pm\,\omega_{\mathrm{EB}}/\sqrt{1 + \varepsilon}\) (theorem 13.89, item 2), and as \(\Omega\) grows the forward frequency grows and the absolute value of the backward frequency falls. At \(\Omega = 0\) the two frequencies are equal in size, and as \(\Omega\) grows the forward one rises and the backward one falls in absolute value.
  3. Synchronous forward whirl, \(\omega_+ = \Omega\), occurs exactly at \(\Omega = \omega_{\mathrm{EB}}/\sqrt{1 - \varepsilon}\), which is the critical speed (definition 24.8). It is higher than \(\omega_{\mathrm{EB}}/\sqrt{1 + \varepsilon}\) by the factor \(\sqrt{(1 + \varepsilon)/(1 - \varepsilon)}\) and higher than the Euler-Bernoulli value \(\omega_{\mathrm{EB}}\). Synchronous whirl is the crossing of the blue curve with the line.
Idea

We get the equations of motion as in theorem 13.86, except that in the action the third term is gyroscopic. The function \(\sin\beta x\) solves all spatial derivatives, so only the quadratic equation in \(\omega\) remains. The sine shape solves all the spatial derivatives.

Proof

We must show that the assumed form is a solution exactly for equation (24.32), that this equation has roots as item 2 says, and that item 3 follows from \(\omega = \Omega\).

  1. The kinetic energy of a piece of shaft is by lemma 24.27 (the limit from step 4) \(\int\big[\tfrac12\rho A(v_{\mathrm{t}}^2 + w_{\mathrm{t}}^2) + \tfrac12\rho I(v_{\mathrm{xt}}^2 + w_{\mathrm{xt}}^2) - 2\rho I\,\Omega\,v_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xt}}\big]\mathrm{d}x\) up to a constant, and the strain energy is \(\tfrac12\int EI\,(v_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + w_{\mathrm{xx}}^2)\,\mathrm{d}x\). The action is their difference integrated over time. The energy is an integral along the shaft, as the limit of columns.
  2. The variation \(v \to v + \alpha\eta\) (\(\eta\) and \(\eta_{\mathrm{x}}\) continuous, \(\eta = 0\) at \(x = 0, L\) and at \(t_1\), \(t_2\)) gives by steps 1 to 5 of the proof of theorem 13.86 the same result as for the Rayleigh beam, except that an additional term \(-2\rho I\,\Omega\int\!\!\int\eta_{\mathrm{x}}\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t\) comes along. Integrating by parts in \(x\) it equals \(+2\rho I\,\Omega\int\!\!\int\eta\,w_{\mathrm{xxt}}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t\), because the bracket \([\eta\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}]_0^L\) is zero (\(\eta = 0\) at the ends). So \(R_{\mathrm{v}} = -\rho A\,v_{\mathrm{tt}} + \rho I\,v_{\mathrm{xxtt}} - EI\,v_{\mathrm{xxxx}} + 2\rho I\,\Omega\,w_{\mathrm{xxt}}\) and the first equation is \(R_{\mathrm{v}} = 0\). The natural boundary condition that step 8 of the same theorem gives is \(v_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\), since the additional term contributes nothing at the ends. The variation is a displaced curve next to the true one, their difference is \(\eta\), and at the ends it is zero.
  3. The variation \(w \to w + \alpha\zeta\): the term \(-2\rho I\,\Omega\,v_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) gives, by parts in \(t\) (because \(\zeta = 0\) at \(t_1\), \(t_2\)) and then in \(x\), the term \(-2\rho I\,\Omega\int\!\!\int\zeta\,v_{\mathrm{xxt}}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t\), so \(R_{\mathrm{w}} = -\rho A\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} + \rho I\,w_{\mathrm{xxtt}} - EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} - 2\rho I\,\Omega\,v_{\mathrm{xxt}}\). This is the second equation, and the boundary condition is \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\). For \(w\) the same holds, \(\zeta\) is again a variation with zeros at the ends.
  4. The complex equation: we add the first equation to the second multiplied by \(\mathrm{i}\). The terms with \(\Omega\) give \(-2\rho I\,\Omega\,(w_{\mathrm{xxt}} - \mathrm{i}\,v_{\mathrm{xxt}}) = -2\rho I\,\Omega\,(-\mathrm{i})\,(v_{\mathrm{xxt}} + \mathrm{i}\,w_{\mathrm{xxt}}) = 2\mathrm{i}\,\rho I\,\Omega\,p_{\mathrm{xxt}}\), so \(\rho A\,p_{\mathrm{tt}} - \rho I\,p_{\mathrm{xxtt}} + EI\,p_{\mathrm{xxxx}} + 2\mathrm{i}\,\rho I\,\Omega\,p_{\mathrm{xxt}} = 0\). Adding the two equations is the combination of two planes into one.
  5. We insert \(p = P\sin(\beta x)\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}\). We have \(p_{\mathrm{tt}} = -\omega^2p\), \(p_{\mathrm{xxtt}} = \beta^2\omega^2p\), \(p_{\mathrm{xxxx}} = \beta^4p\) and \(p_{\mathrm{xxt}} = -\mathrm{i}\,\beta^2\omega\,p\). The conditions \(p = p_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) at \(x = 0, L\) hold because \(\sin(n\pi) = 0\). The equation gives \(\big(-\rho A\,\omega^2 - \rho I\,\beta^2\omega^2 + EI\,\beta^4 + 2\rho I\,\Omega\,\beta^2\omega\big)\,p = 0\). Division by \(\rho A\) with \(\varepsilon = \beta^2I/A\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{EB}}^2 = EI\beta^4/(\rho A)\) gives \(-(1 + \varepsilon)\,\omega^2 + 2\varepsilon\,\Omega\,\omega + \omega_{\mathrm{EB}}^2 = 0\), which is equation (24.32). Since \(\sin(\beta x)\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}\) is nonzero everywhere except at isolated points, this is also a necessary condition (item 1). The sine keeps its shape in the equation, because a derivative only multiplies it, and at the ends it is zero.
  6. Item 2: the product of the roots of the quadratic equation is \(-\omega_{\mathrm{EB}}^2/(1 + \varepsilon) < 0\), so one root is positive and one negative, and \(\omega_\pm\) are as in the formula. At \(\Omega = 0\) they are \(\pm\,\omega_{\mathrm{EB}}/\sqrt{1 + \varepsilon}\). The derivative \(\mathrm d\omega_\pm/\mathrm d\Omega = \big(\varepsilon \pm \varepsilon^2\Omega/\sqrt{\varepsilon^2\Omega^2 + (1 + \varepsilon)\omega_{\mathrm{EB}}^2}\big)/(1 + \varepsilon)\), and since the fraction with the root in its denominator is smaller than \(\varepsilon\) for every \(\Omega\) (the root is larger than \(\varepsilon\,\Omega\)), the derivative for \(\omega_+\) is positive (the forward frequency grows) and for \(\omega_-\) also positive, so the negative \(\omega_-\) grows towards zero and its absolute value falls. One root is forward and one backward.
  7. Item 3: \(\omega = \Omega\) in equation (24.32) gives \((1 + \varepsilon - 2\varepsilon)\,\Omega^2 = \omega_{\mathrm{EB}}^2\), so \(\Omega^2 = \omega_{\mathrm{EB}}^2/(1 - \varepsilon)\). For \(\varepsilon < 1\) this is one positive solution, and \(\omega_- < 0 < \Omega\) never coincides with \(\Omega > 0\). This is the crossing of the blue curve with the line.

Source: The proof is not from the source. FPGL (section 6.8.1, PDF p. 295, equation 6.67) sets up the critical speeds of a rotor as an eigenvalue problem for \(\Omega\), in which under synchronous excitation the gyroscopic matrix enters together with the mass matrix under the same factor \(\Omega^2\), which is our \(\mat M - \mat G\). Item 2 at rest is theorem 13.89.

The variation is shown in figure 24.66. The horizontal axis is \(x\), and the ends of the shaft are at \(0\) and \(L\). We shift the deflection \(v\) into a new curve. Their difference is \(\alpha\eta\), which is zero at the ends. Lower right, the inset shows \(\eta\) alone as a function of \(x\).

Meaning: rotary inertia has two effects on a shaft, and they have opposite signs in synchronous forward whirl. Without turning it lowers the frequency by the factor \(1/\sqrt{1 + \varepsilon}\) (as for the beam), and the gyroscopic term adds \(+2\varepsilon\,\Omega\,\omega\) in forward whirl, so that the total effect is \((1 + \varepsilon - 2\varepsilon) = 1 - \varepsilon\) with the opposite sign. This is the same that we saw for the disk in the value \(J_{\mathrm{t}} - J_{\mathrm{p}}\) (section 24.4): for the disk \(J_{\mathrm{p}} = 2J_{\mathrm{t}}\) for a thin disk, and for a thin slice of shaft similarly \(\rho I_{\mathrm{p}} = 2\rho I\), so for synchronous whirl \(\rho I - 2\rho I = -\rho I\). In figure 24.67 the line is the critical speed for forward whirl, which the blue curve reaches earlier than at rest.

Figure 24.67 shows the shape of the curves. We draw the axes: on the horizontal one the spin speed \(\Omega\) in units of \(\omega_{\mathrm{EB}}\), on the vertical one the whirl frequency \(\omega\). The dashed line \(\omega = \Omega\) is synchronous whirl. The blue curve is forward whirl (\(\omega_+\)), the orange one is backward whirl (\(\omega_-\), negative because it whirls in the direction opposite to the spin). The intersection of the blue curve with the line is the critical speed. For the real shaft the effect is about two hundred times smaller (\(0{,}2/(9{,}87\cdot 10^{-4}) = 203\)) (\(\varepsilon = 9{,}87\cdot 10^{-4}\) for \(d = 40\) mm, \(L = 1\) m) and would not be visible, so for the figure \(\varepsilon = 0{,}2\) is taken (a short thick shaft) and this is stated in the title. With this \(\varepsilon\) the frequency at \(\Omega = 0\) is \(0{,}913\,\omega_{\mathrm{EB}}\), at \(\Omega = 0{,}5\,\omega_{\mathrm{EB}}\) it is \(1{,}000\) forward and \(-0{,}833\) backward, at \(\Omega = 2\,\omega_{\mathrm{EB}}\) it is \(1{,}305\) forward and \(-0{,}639\) backward, and the intersection is at \(1{,}118\,\omega_{\mathrm{EB}}\).

For the real shaft (R1 without the disk, \(d = 40\) mm, \(L = 1\) m) the numbers from the script are: \(\omega_{\mathrm{EB}} = 494{,}744\) 1/s, that is \(4724{,}5\) rev/min, \(\varepsilon = 9{,}8696\cdot 10^{-4}\), at rest \(4722{,}13\) rev/min (as in chapter 13), critical speed \(4726{,}79\) rev/min, which is \(0{,}049\) % above \(\omega_{\mathrm{EB}}\) and \(0{,}099\) % above the value at rest. At \(3000\) rev/min the forward frequency is \(4725{,}09\) and the backward \(4719{,}17\) rev/min, at \(6000\) rev/min \(4728{,}05\) and \(4716{,}21\), at \(12\,000\) rev/min \(4733{,}97\) and \(4710{,}31\). The model is the Rayleigh one, which holds as long as \(\varepsilon \ll 1\), that is the wavelength is much larger than the radius of gyration \(\sqrt{I/A} = 10\) mm. For the second mode (\(n = 2\) in lemma 24.31) \(\varepsilon = 3{,}95\cdot 10^{-3}\) and the critical speed is \(18\,935{,}2\) rev/min. In figure 24.67 the blue and orange curves for the real shaft are barely apart.

The mesh of elements confirms this and shows how fast it converges (table). Without the gyroscopic term (only \(\mat M\) with rotary inertia, \(\mat G = \mat 0\)) the mesh would give for synchronous whirl the equation \(\mat K\vek\varphi = \Omega^2\mat M\vek\varphi\), which is the same as the equation at rest, so \(4722{,}13\) rev/min, below \(\omega_{\mathrm{EB}}\) and not above it. The gyroscopic term is therefore not a small correction: without it the critical speed has the wrong sense of shift. The first and second critical speeds are shown in figure 24.68.

Figure 24.68 shows these numbers on a logarithmic scale. We draw the axes, horizontally the number of elements \(n\) (we double it), vertically the deviation. The blue line is the first critical speed, the orange one the second. With every doubling of \(n\) the deviation falls by the factor \(15{,}2\), \(15{,}8\), \(15{,}95\), so towards \(16 = 2^4\), which the triangle with slope \(-4\) shows on the logarithmic scale (an observation from these numbers, we give no proof for the rotor, for the nodes of a beam there is a similar proof in theorem 12.14). The second critical speed has at \(n\) the same deviation as the first at \(n/2\), because the wave of the second mode has twice as many half-waves and at the same \(n\) only half as many elements per half-wave. So we must adapt the mesh to the mode: for an error below \(0{,}01\) % eight elements suffice for the first and sixteen for the second mode (table), for the third more.

What have we shown? A mesh of beam elements with the complex equation (24.31) gives the Jeffcott rotor, the four degrees of freedom of the disk (section 24.4) and a rotor with shaft mass, and it agrees with the closed form of the uniform shaft, which cannot be proved with the Euler-Bernoulli beam formula alone. The matrices are three, real and symmetric, and therefore theorem 24.21 holds for every rotor that we assemble. In section 24.6 we use them for the critical speeds of a rotor with several disks, and in section 24.8 for balancing. The mesh gives the first and second critical speeds, which approach the closed form, and the crossing with the synchronous line.

24.6 Critical speeds of a rotor with several masses

For the Jeffcott rotor we found the critical speed as the peak of the response to unbalance (definition 24.8): at \(1483\) rev/min the motion of the disk centre is \(25\) times the eccentricity \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\). A rotor with an off-centre disk or with several masses has several such speeds, and the definition by a peak has three weaknesses (FPGL, §6.7, PDF p. 293). The first is that the peak depends on where the unbalance sits on the rotor, and we do not know that in advance because it arises in manufacture. The second is that it depends on which quantity we measure (displacement of the disk, displacement of the bearing, force in the bearing), because different quantities peak at different speeds. The third is that a local peak may lie at a speed that is not a property of the rotor and never harms the machine. We therefore want a definition that does not depend on the unbalance or on the measured quantity, and a calculation that finds all critical speeds of the rotor from the matrices we already have from sections 24.3 and 24.5. The section answers four questions: which speeds are critical (theorem 24.33), what shape the shaft has at each (definition 24.36), how the critical speeds change when the bearings get softer (theorem 24.37), and what happens when the rotor is run through a critical speed quickly (lemma 24.38). Such a peak is the blue curve in the figure, and at the dashed vertical line the response is unbounded.

The name critical speed (kritična hitrost) comes from the fact that at it a small unbalance can cause a motion that is critical for the machine, that is, so large that it damages it (FPGL, PDF p. 293 speaks of "problematic levels" of motion). Figure 24.73 shows the example this section treats: the response of rotor \(R_2\) (disk at \(0{,}25\) m from the left bearing, section 24.4) to unbalance, at all speeds from zero to \(9000\) rev/min.

24.6.1 Which speed is critical

A rotor has an excitation whose frequency depends on the spin speed \(\Omega\), and natural frequencies that by section 24.4 also depend on \(\Omega\). A critical speed is therefore the intersection of two curves that both move with \(\Omega\), and not merely the natural frequency of some stationary system (FPGL, PDF p. 294). First we name the axes: the horizontal one is the spin speed \(\Omega\), the vertical one the natural frequency \(\omega\), both in 1/min. Then we name the excitation we have and the natural frequency. In the figure the excitation is the line \(\omega = \Omega\), the natural frequencies are the curves for forward and backward whirl, and a critical speed is where the line meets a curve.

Definition 24.32 Critical speed, formal definition (kritična hitrost, formalna definicija)

A rotor turns at a constant speed \(\Omega > 0\) (1/s) and carries an excitation that is a sum of components with frequencies \(\omega_{\mathrm{f}}(\Omega)\) (each component is sinusoidal with its own frequency, for unbalance it is \(\Omega\)). A natural frequency of an axisymmetric rotor on bearings of equal stiffness in both planes at speed \(\Omega\) is a real number \(\omega\) at which the equation of motion without excitation has a nonzero solution \(\vek p(t) = \vek\varphi\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}\) (the whirl is forward for \(\omega > 0\) and backward for \(\omega < 0\), definition 24.3). The speed \(\Omega\) is critical if at it the frequency of one excitation component equals one natural frequency of the rotor at the same speed: \(\omega_{\mathrm{f}}(\Omega) = \omega\). In the figure these are the excitation line and a natural-frequency curve, which meet.

Source: FPGL §6.7 (PDF p. 293-294): the critical speed is "the speed of rotation of the machine at which one of the frequency components of the excitation coincides with a natural frequency of the system". As a property of the system the definition does not depend on the distribution of the excitation or on the measured quantity.

The definition removes all three weaknesses, because only two frequencies enter it, the excitation and the natural one, and not the amplitudes of the excitation, the place of the unbalance or the measured quantity. We pay for this on the other side: the definition also finds speeds that do not harm the machine, as we will see at the second critical speed of rotor \(R_1\) in section 24.6.4 (FPGL, PDF p. 293). No amplitude appears in the figure, only the line and the natural-frequency curves that cross.

For the unbalance of an axisymmetric rotor (section 24.2) there is a single excitation component, a force of frequency \(\Omega\) that turns in the same direction as the shaft (FPGL, PDF p. 294). In the complex notation \(p = v + \mathrm{i}w\) this is \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\), so the critical speed here means the natural frequency \(\omega = +\Omega\): synchronous forward whirl. For bearings with different stiffness in the two planes we get the natural frequencies from the equation of each plane separately, and the Jeffcott rotor then has two critical speeds, \(\omega_{\mathrm{v}}\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{w}}\) (lemma 24.11). This force is the line \(\omega = +\Omega\), so the critical speed is its crossing with a forward natural frequency.

24.6.2 The rotor in complex form

The model is the same as in sections 24.3 to 24.5, with the same named idealizations (section 24.5): the shaft and the disks are written with a finite number of degrees of freedom, the shaft axis is \(x\), at every node there are a displacement and a slope in the two planes \(v\) and \(w\), the spin speed \(\Omega\) is constant, the axisymmetric rotor rests on bearings of equal stiffness in both planes, and there is no damping yet (section 24.7 adds it). A constant \(\Omega\) means that the motor holds the speed whatever the response of the rotor is. This holds while the rotor runs steadily, but not in a run-up, where the speed rises and the peak is lower, for \(R_1\) from \(0{,}96\) to \(0{,}59\) of the steady peak (section 24.6.6). Let \(\vek v\) be the column of displacements and slopes in the plane \(v\) and \(\vek w\) the same column in the plane \(w\). Assembly by theorem 24.29 gives matrices of the same order \(n\): the mass matrix \(\mat M\) (symmetric, positive definite, it also contains the rotary inertia of the shaft and the transverse moment of inertia \(J_{\mathrm{t}}\) of the disks), the matrix of polar inertias \(\mat G_{\mathrm{p}}\) (symmetric, positive semidefinite, on the slopes it has the polar moments of inertia \(J_{\mathrm{p}}\) of the disks, on the shaft twice the rotary inertia, because \(\rho I_{\mathrm{p}} = 2\rho I\)) and the stiffness matrix \(\mat K\) (symmetric, positive definite, because the bearings hold the rotor). The disk is as in theorem 24.17: in the plane \(v\) the term is \(J_{\mathrm{t}}\,\ddot v' + \Omega J_{\mathrm{p}}\,\dot w'\), and in the plane \(w\) it is \(J_{\mathrm{t}}\,\ddot w' - \Omega J_{\mathrm{p}}\,\dot v'\). For all nodes together we get two real equations In panel (a) the shaft rests on two bearings and carries the disk, the axis \(x\) runs along the shaft, and a node has a displacement and a slope in the plane \(v\).

\[\mat M\ddot{\vek v} + \Omega\,\mat G_{\mathrm{p}}\,\dot{\vek w} + \mat K\vek v = \vek f_{\mathrm{v}} , \qquad \mat M\ddot{\vek w} - \Omega\,\mat G_{\mathrm{p}}\,\dot{\vek v} + \mat K\vek w = \vek f_{\mathrm{w}} . \tag{24.33}\]

We multiply the second equation by \(\mathrm{i}\) and add the two. For the complex column \(\vek p = \vek v + \mathrm{i}\,\vek w\) we have \(\dot{\vek w} - \mathrm{i}\,\dot{\vek v} = -\mathrm{i}\,(\dot{\vek v} + \mathrm{i}\,\dot{\vek w}) = -\mathrm{i}\,\dot{\vek p}\), hence

\[\mat M\ddot{\vek p} - \mathrm{i}\,\Omega\,\mat G_{\mathrm{p}}\,\dot{\vek p} + \mat K\vek p = \vek f_{\mathrm{v}} + \mathrm{i}\,\vek f_{\mathrm{w}} . \tag{24.34}\]

The unbalance of each disk \(j\) is a mass \(m_{\mathrm{j}}\) with eccentricity \(a_{\mathrm{u},\mathrm{j}}\) at an angle \(\delta_{\mathrm{j}}\) to the plane \(v\) and we write it as the complex number \(u_{\mathrm{j}} = m_{\mathrm{j}} a_{\mathrm{u},\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\delta_{\mathrm{j}}}\) (definition 24.6). Its force on the disk is by section 24.2 \(\Omega^2 u_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) in the displacement of the \(j\)-th disk, so the right-hand side of equation (24.34) is the column \(\Omega^2\,\vek u\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) with components \(u_{\mathrm{j}}\) at the displacements of the disks and zeros elsewhere. In the cross-section (b) the unbalance is a mass at the eccentricity \(a_{{\mathrm{u},\mathrm{j}}}\) at the angle \(\delta_{\mathrm{j}}\) to the plane \(v\). The arrow \(\Omega\) shows the direction of spin.

Free whirl with frequency \(\omega\) is a solution \(\vek p = \vek\varphi\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}\) of equation (24.34) without the right-hand side. Inserting it gives \(\big(-\omega^2\mat M + \omega\,\Omega\,\mat G_{\mathrm{p}} + \mat K\big)\vek\varphi = \vek 0\). The sign of \(\omega\) gives the direction of the whirl: for \(\omega > 0\) the shaft whirls forward (in the sense of the spin), for \(\omega < 0\) backward. For \(\omega = \Omega\) we have in addition \(-\Omega^2\mat M + \Omega^2\mat G_{\mathrm{p}} = -\Omega^2(\mat M - \mat G_{\mathrm{p}})\), and it is this difference that decides the critical speeds. We denote it \(\mat D = \mat M - \mat G_{\mathrm{p}}\). It is symmetric, but it need not have a sign: a disk that is thin (\(J_{\mathrm{p}} > J_{\mathrm{t}}\)) has \(J_{\mathrm{t}} - J_{\mathrm{p}} < 0\) on the slope. In panel (c) forward whirl circles in the direction of spin and backward whirl against it.

On notation (D15): \(\Omega\) is the spin speed, the same as the forcing frequency in chapter 9, \(\omega\) is the whirl frequency (the bold \(\boldsymbol\omega\) in chapter 8 is the angular velocity vector and does not appear here), \(p = v + \mathrm{i}w\) is the complex displacement (not the pressure of chapter 11), \(\mat G_{\mathrm{p}}\) is the matrix of polar inertias (the shear modulus is the italic \(G\)), and \(J_{\mathrm{p}}\) and \(J_{\mathrm{t}}\) are the polar and transverse moments of inertia of the disk.

24.6.3 Critical speeds as an eigenproblem

Now we can compute the critical speeds. From equation (24.34) with \(\omega = \Omega\) it follows that \((\mat K - \Omega^2\mat D)\vek\varphi = \vek 0\), a generalized eigenproblem, but with a difficulty: \(\mat D\) need not have a sign. In the usual eigenproblem (theorem 10.21) the mass matrix is positive definite, all eigenvalues are \(\omega^2 > 0\) and each gives a frequency. Now the role of the mass is taken by the positive definite \(\mat K\) and the role of the stiffness by \(\mat D\), which may be indefinite. Let us test the swap of roles. In panel (a) the numbers \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\) lie on an axis, negative ones give no critical speed and positive ones give \(\Omega = 1/\sqrt{{s}}\).

Theorem 24.33 Synchronous critical speeds of a rotor (sinhrone kritične hitrosti rotorja)

Let \(\mat M\), \(\mat G_{\mathrm{p}}\) and \(\mat K\) be real symmetric matrices of order \(n\), \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) positive definite and \(\mat G_{\mathrm{p}}\) positive semidefinite, and \(\mat D = \mat M - \mat G_{\mathrm{p}}\). Then there exist real numbers \(s_1 \le \dots \le s_{\mathrm{n}}\) (in s\(^2\)) and real columns \(\vek\varphi_1, \dots, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\) with \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat K\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}} = 1\) for \(r = s\) and \(0\) otherwise and \(\mat D\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = s_{\mathrm{r}}\,\mat K\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\), and for a speed \(\Omega > 0\) (positive \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\) give critical speeds):

  1. Equation (24.34) without the right-hand side has a solution \(\vek p = \vek\varphi\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) with \(\vek\varphi \ne \vek 0\) (synchronous forward whirl) if and only if \((\mat K - \Omega^2\mat D)\vek\varphi = \vek 0\), and this holds if and only if \(\Omega^2 = 1/s_{\mathrm{r}}\) for some \(r\) with \(s_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\). A solution exists only for a positive \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\).
  2. Hence the critical speeds for unbalance (definition 24.32) are the numbers \(\Omega_{\mathrm{r}} = 1/\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{r}}}\) for all \(r\) with \(s_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\), and their number is the number of distinct positive \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\). If \(\mat D\) is positive definite, all \(s_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\) and each gives a critical speed. On the axis this is the number of positive \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\), and a thin disk has fewer than a cylinder.
Proof

We must show that the equation \((\mat K - \Omega^2\mat D)\vek\varphi = \vek 0\) splits along the eigenvectors of the pair \((\mat D, \mat K)\) into \(n\) scalar equations from which we read the critical speeds. The splitting is an expansion in a basis in panel (b), and each equation has its own factor.

  1. The spectral theorem (theorem 10.21) holds for a pair of a symmetric matrix and a positive definite matrix. Take it with \(\mat D\) in the role of its \(\mat K\) and with our \(\mat K\) in the role of its \(\mat M\). It gives numbers \(s_1 \le \dots \le s_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(\mat K\)-orthonormal \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) with \(\mat D\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = s_{\mathrm{r}}\mat K\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\). These are the numbers and columns of the theorem. These are the columns \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) and the numbers \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\).
  2. The columns \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) are linearly independent, since from \(\sum c_{\mathrm{r}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek 0\) multiplication by \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\mat K\) gives \(c_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\). Every column \(\vek\varphi\) is therefore a combination \(\vek\varphi = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} c_{\mathrm{r}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\). The figure shows a column as a combination of independent columns.
  3. We insert into \((\mat K - \Omega^2\mat D)\vek\varphi = \vek 0\) and use \(\mat D\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = s_{\mathrm{r}}\mat K\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\): \(\sum_{\mathrm{r}} c_{\mathrm{r}}(1 - \Omega^2 s_{\mathrm{r}})\,\mat K\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek 0\). Multiplication by \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\) gives \(c_{\mathrm{j}}(1 - \Omega^2 s_{\mathrm{j}}) = 0\) for every \(j\). Each factor \(1 - \Omega^2 s_{\mathrm{r}}\) multiplies its own \(c_{\mathrm{r}}\).
  4. A nonzero solution \(\vek\varphi\) therefore exists if and only if \(1 - \Omega^2 s_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\) for some \(j\), that is \(s_{\mathrm{j}} = 1/\Omega^2 > 0\). Then the solutions are the combinations of the columns with the same \(s_{\mathrm{j}}\). This is the first claim in both directions. The factor is zero only at the zero of the line with \(s_{\mathrm{j}} > 0\), and the line with \(s_{\mathrm{j}} < 0\) has none.
  5. A solution \(\vek p = \vek\varphi\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) of equation (24.34) without the right-hand side satisfies after insertion \((-\Omega^2\mat M + \Omega^2\mat G_{\mathrm{p}} + \mat K)\vek\varphi = \vek 0\), that is \((\mat K - \Omega^2\mat D)\vek\varphi = \vek 0\). Conversely every solution of this equation gives a solution of the free motion, because the derivation is reversible. By definition 24.32 the speed is critical if and only if \(\omega = \Omega\) coincides with a natural frequency, which is the second claim. This is the condition that the excitation line and a natural-frequency curve meet.
  6. If \(\mat D\) is positive definite, then \(s_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat D\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\) for every \(r\) (from \(\mat D\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = s_{\mathrm{r}}\mat K\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) after multiplication by \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\)), so every \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\) gives a critical speed. All \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\) lie on the positive half-axis.

Source: The proof is not from the source. FPGL §6.8.1 (PDF p. 295): in synchronous whirl the transverse inertia of the disk becomes \(J_{\mathrm{t}} - J_{\mathrm{p}}\) and the rotary inertia of the shaft becomes \(-\rho I\).

We proved the theorem only for a pair of matrices, and all the conclusions are arithmetic with the numbers \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\). Each \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\) carries one critical speed if it is positive and none if it is negative or zero. Let us test it on rotor \(R_2\). In panel (a) the axis of the factor against \(\Omega^2\) shows the factor of a positive \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\) with its zero and the factor of a negative one, which has none, and in panel (b) a response term with a pole and a bounded term. The positive \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\) lie on the axis.

Rotor \(R_2\), four-coordinate model. The disk has mass \(m = 49{,}009\) kg, \(J_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}9802\) kg m\(^2\) and \(J_{\mathrm{t}} = 0{,}5003\) kg m\(^2\) and sits at \(0{,}25\) m from the left bearing of a steel shaft with \(EI = 24\,630\) N m\(^2\) and \(L = 1\) m. The shaft is massless, the coordinates are the displacement \(v\) and the slope \(v'\) of the disk (section 24.4). The stiffness matrix at the disk is \(\mat K = \begin{bmatrix} 4{,}9041\cdot10^6 & -1{,}0509\cdot10^6 \\ -1{,}0509\cdot10^6 & 3{,}9408\cdot10^5 \end{bmatrix}\) (N/m, N, N m), the mass matrix is \(\mat M = \mathrm{diag}(49{,}009,\ 0{,}5003)\) and the polar one is \(\mat G_{\mathrm{p}} = \mathrm{diag}(0,\ 0{,}9802)\). So \(\mat D = \mathrm{diag}(49{,}009,\ -0{,}4799)\): the first entry is the mass, the second is \(J_{\mathrm{t}} - J_{\mathrm{p}}\), negative. The eigenproblem \(\mat D\vek\varphi = s\mat K\vek\varphi\) gives (computed with Python, NumPy, num-06.py) \(s_1 = -1{,}3037\cdot10^{-6}\) s\(^2\) and \(s_2 = 2{,}1780\cdot10^{-5}\) s\(^2\). By theorem 24.33 there is one critical speed, \(\Omega = 1/\sqrt{s_2} = 214{,}28\) 1/s, that is \(2046{,}2\) rev/min, and \(s_1 < 0\) gives none. For \(R_2\) one \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\) on the axis is negative.

Figure 24.73 shows the response of rotor \(R_2\) to the unbalance force acting on the disk, without damping (blue curve). Vertically is the displacement \(|v|\) of the disk in mm on a logarithmic axis, horizontally the spin speed \(n\) in rev/min. At \(2046\) rev/min it has a vertical dashed line at which the response grows beyond all bounds (equation of theorem 24.34 below). Everywhere else it is finite.

The figure also shows what the theorem promises: of the four speeds at which something coincides for \(R_2\) (\(1771\), \(1906\), \(5501\) and \(8793\) rev/min), none is critical. Two are dashed grey lines, two are dotted grey lines. Each of them is also a test of the theorem, which says when a natural frequency is not a critical speed, and we treat each separately (rule 48). First the response by modes, which we need for both.

Theorem 24.34 Unbalance response by modes (odziv na neuravnoteženost po oblikah)

In the setting of theorem 24.33 let \(\Omega > 0\) and \(\Omega^2 \ne 1/s_{\mathrm{r}}\) for every \(r\) with \(s_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\). Let \(\vek u\) be the complex unbalance column of section 24.6.2. Then equation (24.34) with the right-hand side \(\Omega^2\vek u\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) has exactly one solution of the form \(\vek p = \vek P\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) (circular forward whirl with frequency \(\Omega\)), namely

\[\vek P = \Omega^2\sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{n}\frac{\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\vek u}{1 - \Omega^2 s_{\mathrm{r}}}\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} . \tag{24.35}\]

A term with \(s_{\mathrm{r}} \le 0\) has the denominator \(1 + \Omega^2|s_{\mathrm{r}}| \ge 1\) and is finite at every speed. For \(s_{\mathrm{r}} < 0\) its coefficient is smaller in absolute value than \(|\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\vek u|/|s_{\mathrm{r}}|\) at all speeds, for \(s_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\) it grows like \(\Omega^2\). A term with a positive \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\) has a pole, a term with a negative one has none.

Proof

We must show that the expression is a solution and that it is the only one. Insertion of \(\vek p = \vek P\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) gives \((\mat K - \Omega^2\mat D)\vek P = \Omega^2\vek u\) (the same calculation as in step 5 of theorem 24.33, only with the right-hand side). The solution is unique because the factor is not zero.

  1. We expand \(\vek P = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} c_{\mathrm{r}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) (theorem 24.33, step 2). The complex \(c_{\mathrm{r}}\) are the only unknowns, because the \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) are real and independent. The expansion is a combination of the basis.
  2. Multiplication of the equation by \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\) and \(\mat D\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = s_{\mathrm{r}}\mat K\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) give, as in step 3 of the theorem, \(c_{\mathrm{j}}(1 - \Omega^2 s_{\mathrm{j}}) = \Omega^2\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\vek u\).
  3. Since \(1 - \Omega^2 s_{\mathrm{j}} \ne 0\) by assumption for \(s_{\mathrm{j}} > 0\) and \(\ge 1\) for \(s_{\mathrm{j}} \le 0\), \(c_{\mathrm{j}}\) is uniquely determined, and this is (24.35). For \(s_{\mathrm{j}} < 0\) we have \(\Omega^2/(1 + \Omega^2|s_{\mathrm{j}}|) < 1/|s_{\mathrm{j}}|\), which gives the bound of the coefficient. For a positive \(s_{\mathrm{j}}\) the zero is not the chosen speed, for a nonpositive one the factor is at least \(1\).

Source: The proof is not from the source. The form is the same as the response by modes of theorem 10.66, but with the matrix \(\mat D\) without sign instead of a positive definite mass matrix.

The theorem says how the unbalance of an individual disk excites an individual mode: with the weight \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\vek u\). For \(R_2\) these two numbers are \(1{,}0315\cdot10^{-7}\) and \(1{,}6871\cdot10^{-6}\) kg\(^{1/2}\) m s (the unit follows from the normalization \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat K\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = 1\), for \(\vek u = (m a_{\mathrm{u}},\ 0)\) with \(a_{\mathrm{u}} = 0{,}05\) mm) and the response at \(1800\) rev/min is the sum of the term with \(s_2 > 0\), which gives \(0{,}1825\) mm, and the term with \(s_1 < 0\), which gives \(0{,}0001\) mm, together \(0{,}1827\) mm. Direct solution of the \(2\times 2\) system gives the same value \(0{,}182653\) mm (calculation, num-06.out). The weight multiplies a curve with a pole or a bounded curve.

Test 1: a natural frequency at rest is not always a critical speed. Without spin \(R_2\) has the natural frequencies \(1906\) and \(8793\) rev/min (\(31{,}77\) and \(146{,}55\) Hz). If we neglect the gyroscopic term (\(J_{\mathrm{p}} = 0\) in \(\mat G_{\mathrm{p}}\), \(\mat D = \mat M\)), these are also the critical speeds. With the gyroscopic term only one remains, \(2046\) rev/min. The reason is that \(J_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}9802 > J_{\mathrm{t}} = 0{,}5003\): the difference \(J_{\mathrm{t}} - J_{\mathrm{p}}\) is negative. By the spectral theorem (theorem 10.21) for the pair \((\mat D, \mat K)\), \(s_1\) is the smallest and \(s_2\) the largest value of the quotient \(\vek x^\T\mat D\vek x/\vek x^\T\mat K\vek x\). The column \(\vek x = (0,\ 1)\) (slope only) gives \(\vek x^\T\mat D\vek x = -0{,}4799 < 0\), so \(s_1 < 0\). The column \((1,\ 0)\) (displacement only) gives \(49{,}009 > 0\), so \(s_2 > 0\). As figure 24.73 says, the response at \(8793\) rev/min is not unbounded and there is not even a peak (dotted line on the right). For a disk at midspan (\(k_{\mathrm{C}} = 0\), section 24.4) displacement and slope do not couple and the equation of pure tilt \(-J_{\mathrm{t}}\omega^2 + J_{\mathrm{p}}\Omega\omega + k_{\mathrm{R}} = 0\) shows the same: at \(\omega = \Omega\) it gives \(\Omega^2(J_{\mathrm{p}} - J_{\mathrm{t}}) = -k_{\mathrm{R}}\), which for \(J_{\mathrm{p}} > J_{\mathrm{t}}\) and \(k_{\mathrm{R}} > 0\) has a negative right-hand side and a positive left-hand side, so there is no solution. For \(R_2\) we have \(k_{\mathrm{C}} \ne 0\) and only the conclusion from \(s_1 < 0\) holds: the upper forward curve of frequencies never reaches the line \(\omega = \Omega\), because a crossing would give a second critical speed, and it grows with \(\Omega\) faster than this line (\(146{,}55\) Hz at rest, \(271{,}04\) Hz at \(6000\) rev/min, section 24.4, lemma 24.26).

Let us compare with a disk for which the theorem promises two speeds. A cylinder of the same mass \(49{,}009\) kg and length \(0{,}4\) m has radius \(70{,}7\) mm, \(J_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}1225\) kg m\(^2\) and \(J_{\mathrm{t}} = 0{,}7147\) kg m\(^2\), so \(J_{\mathrm{t}} - J_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}5922 > 0\) and \(\mat D\) is positive definite. We idealize the cylinder as a rigid body attached at one point of the shaft at \(0{,}25\) m: the massless shaft stays the same and the cylinder does not stiffen it over its length of \(0{,}4\) m. The natural frequencies at rest are \(1876\) and \(7476\) rev/min. The eigenvalues of the pair are \(s = 1{,}3770\cdot10^{-6}\) and \(2{,}5447\cdot10^{-5}\) s\(^2\), the critical speeds are \(1893\) and \(8138\) rev/min. Both natural frequencies at rest therefore have their partner in synchronous forward whirl. For the thinner disk they do not. For the cylinder both \(s\) are positive, for the thin disk one is negative.

Test 2: backward whirl is not excited by unbalance. The unbalance turns forward, but it is not necessary that the whirl backward would coincide with it as well. In the figure the unbalance circles forward and backward whirl backward.

Corollary 24.35 Unbalance does not excite backward whirl (neuravnoteženost ne vzbuja vrtinčenja nazaj)

In the setting of theorem 24.33 equation (24.34) without the right-hand side has a solution \(\vek p = \vek\varphi\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) with \(\vek\varphi \ne \vek 0\) (synchronous backward whirl) if and only if \(\big(\mat K - \Omega^2(\mat M + \mat G_{\mathrm{p}})\big)\vek\varphi = \vek 0\). If at such a speed \(\Omega^2 \ne 1/s_{\mathrm{r}}\) for every \(r\) with \(s_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\), the response to unbalance at it is finite, as equation (24.35) says. In the figure the crossings of the line \(\omega = -\Omega\) with the backward natural frequencies are without a peak, since the excitation lies only on the line \(\omega = +\Omega\).

Proof

We must show the first claim by insertion, the second is theorem 24.34. Insert backward whirl.

  1. Insertion of \(\vek p = \vek\varphi\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) gives \(\ddot{\vek p} = -\Omega^2\vek p\) and \(\dot{\vek p} = -\mathrm{i}\Omega\,\vek p\). The term \(-\mathrm{i}\Omega\,\mat G_{\mathrm{p}}\dot{\vek p}\) is therefore \(-\mathrm{i}\Omega\cdot(-\mathrm{i}\Omega)\,\mat G_{\mathrm{p}}\vek p = -\Omega^2\mat G_{\mathrm{p}}\vek p\).
  2. The equation becomes \((-\Omega^2\mat M - \Omega^2\mat G_{\mathrm{p}} + \mat K)\vek\varphi = \vek 0\), which is the claim.
  3. The response to unbalance has the form \(\vek P\,\mathrm{e}^{+\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) and the matrix in it is \(\mat K - \Omega^2\mat D\), not \(\mat K - \Omega^2(\mat M + \mat G_{\mathrm{p}})\). If its determinant is not zero, \(\vek P\) is finite by theorem 24.34. The response lies on the line \(\omega = +\Omega\), and the crossings for backward whirl on the other.

Source: FPGL §6.7 (PDF p. 294): in an axisymmetric rotor on isotropic bearings unbalance does not excite the modes that whirl backward, although their natural frequencies are computed as critical speeds.

For \(R_2\) we have \(\mat M + \mat G_{\mathrm{p}} = \mathrm{diag}(49{,}009,\ 1{,}4805)\) and the backward whirl coincides with the speed at \(1771{,}1\) and \(5501{,}0\) rev/min (grey dashed lines in figure 24.73). The response to unbalance is \(0{,}1594\) mm at \(1771\) rev/min, \(0{,}0621\) mm at \(1500\) rev/min and \(0{,}3340\) mm at \(1900\) rev/min, rising smoothly towards the peak at \(2046\) rev/min. The reason lies in the work of the force: the unbalance force \(F = F_{\mathrm{v}} + \mathrm{i}F_{\mathrm{w}}\) on a circular motion with \(\vek p = P\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) has the power \(F_{\mathrm{v}}\dot v + F_{\mathrm{w}}\dot w = \mathrm{Re}(\bar F\dot p)\) and for \(F \propto \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) this is proportional to \(\mathrm{e}^{-2\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\), its average over a revolution is zero, so the force supplies no energy to the backward motion. For forward motion this power is constant. The condition is that the rotor is axisymmetric and the bearings have equal stiffness in both directions: for different stiffnesses \(k_{\mathrm{v}} \ne k_{\mathrm{w}}\) we found in section 24.2 ellipses and backward orbits under forward excitation. Here the assumption of isotropy thus supports the claim.

Circular orbits and the fact that unbalance does not excite backward whirl are properties of the model, not rules: for an unsymmetric rotor or bearings there are no circular orbits and a backward mode can be excited as well (FPGL, §6.9, PDF p. 299). The drawn circular orbits hold only for an axisymmetric rotor, otherwise they become ellipses.

24.6.4 Shapes at the critical speeds

A critical speed only says at which speed a peak occurs. For design we must also know what shape the shaft has then: where the motion is largest and where it stands still, and what the slope of the disk is. We name it by what it shows: the shape the shaft takes (mode shape), as with the mode shapes of chapter 10. In the figure the shape is a curve, the disk shows the slope, and a node is where the shaft stands still.

Definition 24.36 Mode shape at a critical speed (oblika pri kritični hitrosti)

Let \(\Omega_{\mathrm{r}} = 1/\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{r}}}\) be a critical speed from theorem 24.33 and \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) a real column with \((\mat K - \Omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\mat D)\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek 0\) (a column of \(n\) numbers, displacements and slopes of the nodes, determined up to multiplication by a nonzero number). The mode shape at a critical speed is this column together with the motion \(\vek p(t) = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega_{\mathrm{r}} t}\) that it describes: every point of the shaft has displacements \(v = \varphi\cos\Omega_{\mathrm{r}} t\) and \(w = \varphi\sin\Omega_{\mathrm{r}} t\) with one real number \(\varphi\) per point. The column \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) is the shape curve with the slope of the disk and a node.

Source: FPGL §6.9 (PDF p. 299): the mode shape at a critical speed is obtained by setting the spin speed to the critical one and computing the right eigenvector.

Because \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) is real, all points of the shaft have the same phase: the displacement of a point is \(\varphi(x)\) in a plane that is turned about the bearing axis by the angle \(\Omega_{\mathrm{r}} t\). The curve \(\varphi(x)\) (between the nodes it is interpolated with Hermite functions, definition 12.1) is thus a plane curve that turns as a whole with the spin speed, and each of its points describes a circle of radius \(|\varphi(x)|\). Only the points with \(\varphi(x) = 0\) (nodes) stand still. In the figure the shape curve is planar, the node stands still, and the other points describe circles.

Figure 24.74 shows four shapes obtained with the finite element model (\(n = 8\) elements, section 24.5) and with the mass of the shaft: rotor \(R_1\) (disk at midspan) and \(R_2\) (disk at \(0{,}25\) m), each at the first and second forward critical speed. Let us draw it as an eigenvector: first the bearing axis (dashed), at the ends the bearings (triangles), then the shape curve (blue), on which the disk (thick line, drawn perpendicular to the tangent of the curve, because the disk stays perpendicular to the shaft axis), and where the curve crosses the axis, the node (circle).

For \(R_1\) the first shape (top left, \(1416\) rev/min) is nearly the shape of the shaft in one half wave \(\sin(\pi x/L)\) (the largest difference is \(0{,}018\) of the largest displacement), the disk at midspan does not tilt (slope \(0\)). So the gyroscopic term of the disk does not act on it. The gyroscopic term of the shaft remains (lemma 24.27) and raises it from \(1415{,}8\) rev/min at rest (section 24.5) to \(1416{,}0\) rev/min, by \(0{,}008\) %. The second shape (top right, \(28\,384\) rev/min) has a node at midspan, where the disk sits, and the disk tilts there with slope \(0{,}836\) per metre of normalized displacement. It is just this slope that lifts it from \(7002\) rev/min at rest to \(28\,384\) rev/min, because the disk is thin and \(J_{\mathrm{p}} > J_{\mathrm{t}}\) (section 24.5, numbers from that section). This is also an example of a critical speed that does not harm the machine. An unbalance on the disk gives a column \(\vek u\) with a component only at the displacement of the disk, which is zero in the second shape, so \(\vek\varphi^\T\vek u = 0\) for this shape and its term in equation (24.35) is zero at every speed. The response around \(28\,384\) rev/min therefore stays bounded, although this speed is critical by definition 24.32. For \(R_2\) the disk is markedly tilted already at the first shape (bottom left, \(1896{,}2\) rev/min, slope \(2{,}09\) per metre): the disk is not at midspan, so it is at a place where the curve has a slope. At the second shape (bottom right, \(12\,817\) rev/min) the shaft has a node at \(0{,}295\) m, just right of the disk, the disk has displacement \(-0{,}059\) and slope \(0{,}635\) per metre.

The four-coordinate model estimated the first critical speed of \(R_2\) at \(2046{,}2\) rev/min, the finite element model with the mass of the shaft at \(1896{,}2\) rev/min, \(7{,}3\) % lower. The difference is the mass and inertias of the shaft, which has \(20{,}0\) % of the mass of the disk: for \(R_1\) the same shaft lowered the frequency by \(4{,}53\) % (section 24.1), for \(R_2\) by more. In the first shape of \(R_2\) the disk moves only by \(0{,}80\) of the largest displacement, for \(R_1\) by the whole largest displacement. So for \(R_2\) the shaft carries a larger share of the moving mass. Compare the first shape of \(R_2\), where the disk moves only \(0{,}80\), with the first shape of \(R_1\), where it moves the full displacement.

24.6.5 The map of critical speeds

The stiffness of the bearings of a machine is often not known exactly: it depends on how the bearings are made and also on how the machine is fixed (FPGL, §6.10, PDF p. 299-300). The designer wants to know how the uncertainty of this stiffness affects the critical speeds, and whether a critical speed falls into the working range for an unknown stiffness. The answer is the critical speed map (zemljevid kritičnih hitrosti): the critical speeds as functions of the stiffness. First a theorem that says in which direction the first one goes. On the map this is the critical speed against the stiffness.

Theorem 24.37 Support stiffness and the first critical speed (togost podpor in prva kritična hitrost)

Let \(\mat M\), \(\mat G_{\mathrm{p}}\) and \(\mat K\) be as in theorem 24.33 and let there be a column \(\vek y\) with \(\vek y^\T\mat D\vek y > 0\) for \(\mat D = \mat M - \mat G_{\mathrm{p}}\). Then the first (lowest) critical speed is \(\Omega_1\) and

\[\Omega_1^2 = \min\left\{\frac{\vek x^\T\mat K\vek x}{\vek x^\T\mat D\vek x} : \vek x^\T\mat D\vek x > 0\right\} . \tag{24.36}\]

If we add stiffness: \(\mat K' = \mat K + \Delta\mat K\) with \(\Delta\mat K\) symmetric and positive semidefinite (for example springs of the bearings), the first critical speed is \(\Omega_1' \ge \Omega_1\). On the map the first curve does not fall with more stiffness, and its \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\) is the largest on the axis.

Proof

We must show that the first critical speed is read off the largest \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\), and that this follows from the largest Rayleigh quotient, from which the dependence on \(\mat K\) is visible at once.
