The largest \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\) is the right end, which \(\Omega = 1/\sqrt{{s}}\) turns into the lowest critical speed.

  1. We apply the spectral theorem (theorem 10.21) to the pair \((-\mat D, \mat K)\): the smallest eigenvalue is the smallest value of \(-\vek x^\T\mat D\vek x\) among the columns with \(\vek x^\T\mat K\vek x = 1\). It is \(-s_{\max}\), where \(s_{\max}\) is the largest of the numbers \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\) of theorem 24.33. So for every \(\vek x\) we have \(\vek x^\T\mat D\vek x \le s_{\max}\,\vek x^\T\mat K\vek x\) (both sides are homogeneous of degree \(2\)) and equality holds at the corresponding \(\vek\varphi\). This is the largest \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\) on the axis.
  2. For \(\vek y\) from the assumption, \(0 < \vek y^\T\mat D\vek y \le s_{\max}\,\vek y^\T\mat K\vek y\), so \(s_{\max} > 0\). By theorem 24.33 the lowest critical speed is \(\Omega_1 = 1/\sqrt{s_{\max}}\). So \(s_{\max}\) lies on the positive half-axis.
  3. For \(\vek x\) with \(\vek x^\T\mat D\vek x > 0\) the quotient \(\vek x^\T\mat K\vek x/\vek x^\T\mat D\vek x \ge 1/s_{\max}\) by step 1, and equality holds at \(\vek\varphi\) with \(s_{\max}\). So \(1/s_{\max} = \Omega_1^2\) is the minimum, which is (24.36). The largest \(s\) gives the smallest speed, the first critical one.
  4. For \(\mat K' = \mat K + \Delta\mat K\) we have \(\vek x^\T\mat K'\vek x = \vek x^\T\mat K\vek x + \vek x^\T\Delta\mat K\vek x \ge \vek x^\T\mat K\vek x\) for every \(\vek x\), because \(\Delta\mat K\) is positive semidefinite. For every \(\vek x\) with \(\vek x^\T\mat D\vek x > 0\) the quotient with \(\mat K'\) is therefore at least as large as with \(\mat K\), and so is its minimum. So \(\Omega_1'^2 \ge \Omega_1^2\). Added stiffness lifts the first curve of the map.

Source: The proof and the minimum principle of the quotient for critical speeds are not from the source. Critical speeds as an eigenvalue problem: FPGL §6.8 (PDF p. 295).

For \(R_1\) with bearing springs, each of stiffness \(k_{\mathrm{b}}\), we get the first critical speed from the finite element model (\(n = 8\), with the mass of the shaft, num-06.py): \(519{,}4\), \(1108{,}6\), \(1373{,}8\), \(1411{,}6\), \(1415{,}5\) rev/min at \(k_{\mathrm{b}} = 10^5\), \(10^6\), \(10^7\), \(10^8\), \(10^9\) N/m, with the limit \(1416{,}0\) for rigid bearings. The theorem says that they grow, but not how fast. The answer is given by an estimate with the mass of the disk, without the mass of the shaft: the shaft of stiffness \(k = 1{,}1822\cdot10^6\) N/m is in series with two bearing springs that act in parallel (\(2k_{\mathrm{b}}\)), so the total stiffness is \(1/(1/k + 1/(2k_{\mathrm{b}}))\) and the critical speed is reduced by the factor \(1/\sqrt{1 + k/(2k_{\mathrm{b}})}\) against the value with rigid bearings. At \(k_{\mathrm{b}} = 10^7\) N/m we have \(k/(2k_{\mathrm{b}}) = 0{,}059\) and the factor is \(0{,}972\). Applied to \(1416{,}0\) rev/min with rigid bearings it gives \(1376\) rev/min, the finite elements give \(1373{,}8\) rev/min. The bearings are therefore essential when \(k_{\mathrm{b}}\) is comparable to \(k/2 = 5{,}9\cdot10^5\) N/m, and unimportant when \(k_{\mathrm{b}} \gg k\): at \(3{,}16\cdot10^7\) N/m the first critical speed is already \(1402{,}2\) rev/min, within \(1\,\%\) of the limit. In the figure the shaft is a spring \(k\), each bearing a spring \(k_{\mathrm{b}}\), the disk a mass, and the equivalent chain gives the factor. A dashed arrow marks the replacement of the top by the chain.

Figure 24.76 shows the map for \(R_1\): horizontally the stiffness \(k_{\mathrm{b}}\) of each bearing spring, vertically the critical speed \(n\), both on logarithmic axes. The first curve (blue) grows from \(519\) to \(1416\) rev/min and for \(k_{\mathrm{b}} \gtrsim 10^7\) N/m levels off at the dashed limit for rigid bearings. The second and third curves are different at low stiffness: at \(k_{\mathrm{b}} = 10^5\) N/m the second is \(3440\) rev/min, the third \(7607\) rev/min, and at \(10^9\) N/m they are \(28\,300\) and \(30\,249\) rev/min, and even there they are still \(0{,}3\) % and \(0{,}3\) % below \(28\,384\) and \(30\,339\) rev/min. The second stays sensitive even at large stiffnesses, as its growth from \(27\,543\) at \(10^8\) N/m to \(28\,300\) at \(10^9\) N/m shows. At low stiffness the second has an understandable reason: the rotor tilts as a rigid body on the bearing springs. The estimate from the rotation of a rigid rotor about midspan, \(\Omega^2 = k_{\mathrm{b}} L^2/(2J)\) with \(J = m_{\mathrm{shaft}}L^2/12 + J_{\mathrm{t}} - J_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}3369\) kg m\(^2\) (shaft mass \(9{,}802\) kg, difference \(J_{\mathrm{t}} - J_{\mathrm{p}} = -0{,}4799\) kg m\(^2\) from section 24.6.3), gives at \(10^5\) N/m \(3679\) rev/min against \(3440\) rev/min from finite elements, \(7\) % more, because the estimate does not know the bending of the shaft, which lowers the frequency. The estimate of the first, \(\sqrt{2k_{\mathrm{b}}/(m + m_{\mathrm{shaft}})}\), is the quotient (24.36) for the rigid translation \(\vek x\) (all displacements equal to \(1\), slopes zero, the shaft does not bend: \(\vek x^\T\mat K\vek x = 2k_{\mathrm{b}}\), \(\vek x^\T\mat D\vek x = m + m_{\mathrm{shaft}}\)). By theorem 24.37 it is therefore an upper bound: at \(10^5\) N/m \(556{,}9\) rev/min against \(519{,}4\) rev/min, \(7\) % more.

We proved the theorem only for the first critical speed. That all three curves grow is shown by the figure, but a proof for the second and third needs a theorem on maxima over subspaces, which the book does not yet have. The difference \(J_{\mathrm{t}} - J_{\mathrm{p}}\) is negative for \(R_1\), and still the rotor has the critical speeds \(n_2\) and \(n_3\). Only one \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\) is negative: with rigid bearings the finite element model has \(16\) degrees of freedom in one plane, and of the \(16\) numbers \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(15\) are positive (computed with Python). For soft bearings the estimate above shows the reason: the transverse inertia of the shaft \(m_{\mathrm{shaft}}L^2/12 = 0{,}817\) kg m\(^2\) is larger than \(J_{\mathrm{p}} - J_{\mathrm{t}} = 0{,}4799\) kg m\(^2\), so \(J = 0{,}3369\) kg m\(^2 > 0\). All three curves, first, second and third, rise.

24.6.6 Run-up through a critical speed

A rotor in operation runs above the first critical speed, so on its way from rest it must pass through it. For \(R_1\) the steady peak is \(a_{\mathrm{u}}/(2\zeta) = 1{,}250\) mm at \(\zeta = 0{,}02\), but this holds only for a rotor that runs at the critical speed for a long time. In run-up the speed rises and the amplitude may not have time to grow to the steady value. Section 9.8.3 tested this for a machine on pads with steady values in a slow run-up, now we ask how slow it must be for that to be true (FPGL, §6.11, PDF p. 302-305). In the figure the steady curve reaches the peak, and a fast run-up stays lower.

We write the equation of motion. The spin speed rises with a constant angular acceleration \(\dot\Omega\) (1/s\(^2\)), the angle of rotation of the shaft is \(\gamma(t)\) with \(\dot\gamma = \Omega(t)\) and \(\ddot\gamma = \dot\Omega\). In the plane with axes \(v\) and \(w\) and origin \(O\) on the bearing axis, the disk centre is at \(p\), with the centre of mass and the angle \(\gamma\), which grows with the acceleration \(\dot\Omega\).

Lemma 24.38 Equation of run-up of the Jeffcott rotor (enačba zagona Jeffcottovega rotorja)

A Jeffcott rotor (definition 24.1) with disk mass \(m\), stiffness \(k\), external damping \(c\) and unbalance \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\) turns with the angle \(\gamma(t)\) and the angular velocity \(\Omega = \dot\gamma\). The disk centre has the complex displacement \(p = v + \mathrm{i}w\), the centre of mass of the disk is at distance \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\) from the centre in the direction of the angle \(\gamma\). Then

\[m\ddot p + c\dot p + k\,p = m\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\,(\Omega^2 - \mathrm{i}\dot\Omega)\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\gamma} . \tag{24.37}\]

For \(\dot\Omega = 0\) this is the equation of section 24.2. In the figure there are the shaft force and the centre of mass at \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\) from the centre.

Proof

We must show the equation of motion of the centre of mass of the disk. We neglect the weight as in section 24.2 (the linear model adds it as a constant displacement). The motion of the centre of mass is the sum of the centre and the eccentricity.

  1. The centre of mass of the disk has the position \(z = p + a_{\mathrm{u}}\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\gamma}\) (the centre and a turn by \(a_{\mathrm{u}}\) in the direction \(\gamma\)). This is the sum of the centre and the eccentricity.
  2. The second derivative in time is \(\ddot z = \ddot p + a_{\mathrm{u}}(\mathrm{i}\ddot\gamma - \dot\gamma^2)\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\gamma}\), because \(\dot{(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\gamma})} = \mathrm{i}\dot\gamma\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\gamma}\).
  3. In the plane of rotation the disk is acted on only by the force of the shaft, which is at the centre (\(-kp - c\dot p\): elastic and damping). Newton's law for the centre of mass of a rigid body (theorem 8.82) says \(m\ddot z = -kp - c\dot p\). The force is the arrow towards the axis.
  4. We insert step 2: \(m\ddot p + m a_{\mathrm{u}}(\mathrm{i}\dot\Omega - \Omega^2)\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\gamma} = -kp - c\dot p\), which gives (24.37).

Source: The proof is not from the source. FPGL §6.11 (PDF p. 302) gives equation (24.37) in dimensionless form for a constant acceleration.

The additional term \(-\mathrm{i}\dot\Omega\) is small at our accelerations: the ratio \(\dot\Omega/\Omega^2\) at \(\Omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(\dot\Omega = 100\) 1/s\(^2\) is \(0{,}0041\), so \(0{,}4\) % of the main term \(\Omega^2\). We integrated the equation for \(R_1\) (\(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 155{,}32\) 1/s, \(\zeta = 0{,}02\), \(a_{\mathrm{u}} = 0{,}05\) mm) numerically (Runge-Kutta of fourth order, step \(1/80\) of the period) from \(0{,}5\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) to \(1{,}5\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) with constant acceleration and a start from the steady state at \(0{,}5\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\). This is a numerical observation, not a theorem. The three runs in the figure are slow, medium and fast.

\(\dot\Omega\) (1/s\(^2\)) \(\dot\Omega/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\) largest \(\lvert p\rvert\) (mm) share of the steady peak at \(\Omega/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\)
\(5\) \(2{,}07\cdot10^{-4}\) \(1{,}201\) \(0{,}961\) \(1{,}016\)
\(20\) \(8{,}29\cdot10^{-4}\) \(1{,}045\) \(0{,}836\) \(1{,}044\)
\(100\) \(4{,}15\cdot10^{-3}\) \(0{,}738\) \(0{,}590\) \(1{,}118\)

Figure 24.78 shows all three runs: horizontally the ratio \(r = \Omega/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), vertically \(|p|\) in units of the steady peak. We drew first the steady curve (grey, peak \(1{,}250\) mm, drawn as \(1\) on the dashed horizontal), for which the rotor at each moment is in the steady state at the current speed. Then the three run-ups: the slow one (\(\dot\Omega = 5\) 1/s\(^2\), \(48\) rev/min per second) is still close to the steady curve and reaches \(96\) % of the peak, the middle one (\(\dot\Omega = 20\), \(191\) rev/min per second) \(84\) %, the fast one (\(\dot\Omega = 100\), \(955\) rev/min per second) only \(59\) %. A faster run-up lowers the peak.

We notice two things and each needs an explanation. The first is that the peak is below the steady one. The amplitude of a system with damping \(\zeta\) follows a changing force with a delay of the order of the time constant \(1/(\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}}) = 0{,}322\) s (after that time the amplitude of a free oscillation falls by the factor \(\mathrm{e}\), chapter 9). The resonance peak has a width in frequency \(2\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 6{,}21\) 1/s (width at half power, theorem 9.74). At acceleration \(\dot\Omega\) the rotor crosses this width in the time \(2\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}}/\dot\Omega\), and the ratio of this time to the time constant is \(2\zeta^2\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2/\dot\Omega\): for \(\dot\Omega = 5\) it is \(3{,}86\), for \(20\) it is \(0{,}96\), for \(100\) it is \(0{,}19\). In the first the amplitude has time to grow, in the last it does not, and falls to \(59\) %. The ratios are numbers for this rotor, not a law: the explanation is an estimate of the order of magnitude, not a proof. In the figure the peak of the fast run is below the steady curve and the line \(1\).

The second is that the peak is at a higher speed than \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) (\(1{,}016\), \(1{,}044\), \(1{,}118\)), to the right of the dashed vertical \(r = 1\). The amplitude never grows at the moment when the speed is at \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), but keeps climbing and reaches the peak when the speed is already higher: the difference is the way the rotor covers in the time of the delay. After the peak the amplitude oscillates (ripples to the right of the peak in the figure), because the free oscillation with frequency \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) that remains from the transient adds to the forced oscillation with frequency \(\Omega\) and their difference of frequencies grows with time (beating, chapter 9). On the axis \(r\) the ripples are sparser at higher acceleration. The beat phase gathered since the crossing is \(\dot\Omega t^2/2 = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2(r - 1)^2/(2\dot\Omega)\), where \(t = (\Omega - \omega_{\mathrm{n}})/\dot\Omega\) is the time since the crossing: at the same speed less time has passed since the crossing and the phase is smaller. At \(\dot\Omega = 5\) 1/s\(^2\) there are no ripples, because the free part dies out meanwhile.

A practical rule (FPGL, §6.11, PDF p. 302-305): the run-up through a critical speed should be as fast as possible, because the peak is reduced and the rotor spends fewer revolutions at a high amplitude, and the critical speed should be well damped. For very large machines, such as power plant turbines, the run-up takes about \(20\) minutes and the response is almost steady, which is computed in the frequency domain (FPGL, PDF p. 305). For our rotor the steady peak \(1{,}25\) mm and the \(0{,}96\) from the table at \(\dot\Omega = 5\) 1/s\(^2\) show that in a slow run-up the steady calculation is enough, and in a fast one it overestimates the peak by \(1/0{,}59 - 1 = 69\) %. It shows the peak of the fast and the slow run against the steady peak.

24.6.7 What we have shown

We connected two definitions of the critical speed: the peak of the response from section 24.2 is, for light damping, near the speed at which the excitation and natural frequencies coincide (definition 24.32), and the latter does not depend on the unbalance. For the unbalance of an axisymmetric rotor on isotropic bearings it equals the eigenproblem \((\mat K - \Omega^2\mat D)\vek\varphi = \vek 0\) (theorem 24.33, proved from the spectral theorem), and only positive \(s_{\mathrm{r}}\) give critical speeds: for a thin disk there are fewer of them than natural frequencies, as \(R_2\) and the cylinder showed. Backward whirl is not excited by unbalance (corollary 24.35), but only for an isotropic rotor. The shape at a critical speed is a plane curve that turns with the rotor (definition 24.36, figure 24.74), the first critical speed does not fall with larger bearing stiffness (theorem 24.37, figure 24.76), and run-up lowers the peak by the ratio of the time of crossing the resonance to the time constant (numerical observation, figure 24.78).

24.7 Internal damping and instability

In sections 24.1 and 24.2 the shaft was free of losses. The damping \(c\) in the equation of the response to unbalance (theorem 24.7) acted on the disk centre from the surroundings, as air drag or as friction in the bearings. A real shaft, however, loses energy by itself. The shaft material, friction in the bolted joints between its parts and a laminated build of the rotor (a rotor stacked from thin sheets) turn part of the work into heat at every contraction and stretch (FPGL, PDF p. 336). A fibre of the shaft that bends and straightens again as the shaft turns goes through one cycle of loading and unloading. For a steady deflection of a shaft that turns with angular speed \(\Omega\) this is one cycle per revolution, so \(\Omega/(2\pi)\) cycles per second, and for a whirl (definition 24.3) of frequency \(\omega\) the motion of the fibre relative to the shaft is slower or faster by \(\omega\).

We draw the bent shaft with a fibre: the upper fibre is stretched, the lower one compressed, and when the shaft turns through half a revolution they swap. So the fibre is stretched once and compressed once in one cycle. Stress against strain of the fibre traces a loop, the hysteresis loop, because strain lags behind stress. The area of the loop is the work lost to heat in one cycle.

We want to know what this loss does to the rotor. The thought that damping always calms the motion is wrong here: above the first critical speed (definition 24.8) internal damping can drive the motion. The section settles the question on the rotor of section 24.1, in the example R1 (steel shaft of diameter 40 mm, bearings 1 m apart, a steel disk 400 × 50 mm at midspan, \(m = 49{,}009\) kg, \(k = 1{,}1822\cdot 10^6\) N/m, \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 155{,}32\) 1/s, 1483 rev/min). Because a treatment in fixed axes would hide the nature of internal damping, we first write the motion in axes that turn with the shaft.

From history

Steam turbines gave engineers several vibration troubles, among them the whirl of a shaft with a disk. The influence of hysteresis on the whirl of a shaft was treated by A. L. Kimball (TIMO, PDF p. 358). Hysteresis (Greek hysteresis, lagging behind) is the lag of strain behind stress: in every cycle of loading and unloading part of the work is lost in the material. Hysteresis in a shaft is therefore one source of what we call internal damping (FPGL, PDF p. 336 lists material damping among the sources).

Kimball's question is ours: what does internal damping do to the whirl. We already know that by theorem 24.7 the disk moves on a circle under unbalance and that this solution is always possible by itself. Now we ask whether such a solution is also stable.

The model is the Jeffcott rotor (definition 24.1) with the following named idealizations. The shaft is massless and round (isotropic), the bearings are rigid and short, the angular speed \(\Omega\) is constant and prescribed, the displacements are small so that the equations are linear. The internal damping is viscous, that is proportional to velocity. FPGL stresses that modelling internal damping is difficult and that the viscous model is taken as an illustration (PDF p. 336). A different law can give a different threshold or none, so theorem 24.43 holds only for the viscous law.

We draw the disk on the shaft between the bearings, turning with angular speed \(\Omega\). The internal damping \(c_{\mathrm{i}}\) is a damper in the shaft that turns with it, the external \(c_{\mathrm{e}}\) a damper between the disk and the fixed surroundings.

24.7.1 Axes that turn with the shaft

The internal force of the shaft depends on how the shaft deforms, that is on the displacement of the disk centre relative to the shaft material. The material turns. So we need coordinates in which the shaft is at rest.

Figure 24.81 builds them. First we draw the fixed axes \(v\) and \(w\) in the plane of the disk, as in section 24.1. In this plane lies the disk centre \(P\), whose position we write with the complex number \(p = v + \mathrm{i}\,w\) (definition 9.24, see also D2 in the introduction of the chapter on notation), and the arrow \(p\) runs from the bearing axis \(O\) to \(P\). Then on the cross-section of the shaft we draw the axes \(\xi\) and \(\eta\): they are fixed to the shaft and turn with it. The shaft turns with constant angular speed \(\Omega\), so at time \(t\) the axes are rotated by the angle \(\Omega t\) relative to \(v\) and \(w\). Finally from the point \(P\) we drop perpendiculars onto the turning axes: their feet are \(\xi\) and \(\eta\), the coordinates of the disk centre in the axes that turn with the shaft. We write \(q = \xi + \mathrm{i}\,\eta\).

The first question is what the kinetic energy of the disk is if we take \(\xi\) and \(\eta\) as coordinates. By theorem 8.97 the kinetic energy in these coordinates has three parts, \(T_2 + T_1 + T_0\), of second, first and zeroth degree in the velocities, and chapter 8 promised that turning systems would show transport and Coriolis forces. Here the promise is kept.

Lemma 24.39 The Jeffcott rotor in rotating axes (Jeffcottov rotor v vrtečih se oseh)

The Jeffcott rotor without damping has a disk of mass \(m\) and a shaft of stiffness \(k\) (definition 24.1) and turns with constant angular speed \(\Omega\). Let \(q = \xi + \mathrm{i}\,\eta\) be the coordinate of the disk centre in the axes that turn with the shaft (figure 24.81). Then \(p = q\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\), the kinetic energy of the disk centre is \(T = T_2 + T_1 + T_0\) with

\[T_2 = \tfrac12 m(\dot\xi^2 + \dot\eta^2) , \quad T_1 = m\Omega(\xi\dot\eta - \eta\dot\xi) , \quad T_0 = \tfrac12 m\Omega^2(\xi^2 + \eta^2) , \tag{24.38}\]

and the equations of motion are

\[\begin{aligned} m\ddot\xi - 2m\Omega\,\dot\eta + (k - m\Omega^2)\,\xi &= 0 , \\ m\ddot\eta + 2m\Omega\,\dot\xi + (k - m\Omega^2)\,\eta &= 0 . \end{aligned} \tag{24.39}\]

Written together as one complex equation (the first equation plus the second multiplied by \(\mathrm{i}\)) they give

\[m\ddot q + 2\mathrm{i}\,m\Omega\,\dot q + (k - m\Omega^2)\,q = 0 . \tag{24.40}\]

Substituting \(q = p\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) returns \(m\ddot p + k p = 0\).

Proof

We must show that the kinetic energy and the Lagrange equations in the coordinates \(\xi\), \(\eta\) give the stated equations and that they agree with the equation in the fixed axes.

  1. A point with coordinates \((\xi, \eta)\) in the axes rotated by \(\Omega t\) has in the fixed axes \(v = \xi\cos\Omega t - \eta\sin\Omega t\) and \(w = \xi\sin\Omega t + \eta\cos\Omega t\) (figure 24.81, projections on \(v\) and \(w\)). These are the real and imaginary parts of the product \((\xi + \mathrm{i}\,\eta)(\cos\Omega t + \mathrm{i}\sin\Omega t)\), so \(p = q\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) by definition 9.33.
  2. By the product rule and theorem 9.34 (point 3), \(\dot p = (\dot q + \mathrm{i}\Omega\,q)\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\). Since a turn through the angle \(\Omega t\) does not change a length, that is \(|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}| = 1\) (point 2 of the same theorem), \(|\dot p|^2 = |\dot q + \mathrm{i}\Omega\,q|^2 = (\dot\xi - \Omega\eta)^2 + (\dot\eta + \Omega\xi)^2\), because \(\dot q + \mathrm{i}\Omega q = (\dot\xi - \Omega\eta) + \mathrm{i}(\dot\eta + \Omega\xi)\).
  3. Besides the motion of its centre the disk only turns about its own axis, and its contribution \(\tfrac12 J_{\mathrm{p}}\Omega^2\) by theorem 8.92 does not depend on \(\xi\), \(\eta\) and does not appear in the Lagrange equations (the derivative of a constant is zero). So \(T = \tfrac12 m|\dot p|^2\). We expand both squares of step 2: \(T = \tfrac12 m(\dot\xi^2 + \dot\eta^2) + m\Omega(\xi\dot\eta - \eta\dot\xi) + \tfrac12 m\Omega^2(\xi^2 + \eta^2)\). The term with two velocities is \(T_2\), with one \(T_1\), with none \(T_0\), which is (24.38).
  4. The potential energy of the shaft is \(V = \tfrac12 k|p|^2 = \tfrac12 k(\xi^2 + \eta^2)\), because \(|p| = |q|\) (step 2, \(|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}| = 1\)) and the shaft is round: the energy depends only on the size of the deflection, not on its direction.
  5. For \(\xi\) by theorem 8.101 with \(\mathcal L = T - V\): \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial\dot\xi = m\dot\xi - m\Omega\eta\), its time derivative is \(m\ddot\xi - m\Omega\dot\eta\), and \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial\xi = m\Omega\dot\eta + m\Omega^2\xi - k\xi\). The difference is \(m\ddot\xi - 2m\Omega\dot\eta - m\Omega^2\xi + k\xi = 0\), the first equation of (24.39). For \(\eta\): \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial\dot\eta = m\dot\eta + m\Omega\xi\), derivative \(m\ddot\eta + m\Omega\dot\xi\), \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial\eta = -m\Omega\dot\xi + m\Omega^2\eta - k\eta\), and the difference is the second equation.
  6. The first equation plus \(\mathrm{i}\) times the second: the terms with \(\Omega\dot{}\) are \(2m\Omega(-\dot\eta + \mathrm{i}\dot\xi) = 2\mathrm{i}\,m\Omega(\dot\xi + \mathrm{i}\dot\eta) = 2\mathrm{i}\,m\Omega\,\dot q\), which gives (24.40).
  7. From \(q = p\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) it follows that \(\dot q = (\dot p - \mathrm{i}\Omega p)\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) and \(\ddot q = (\ddot p - 2\mathrm{i}\Omega\dot p - \Omega^2 p)\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) (point 3 of theorem 9.34 twice). We substitute into (24.40) and divide by \(\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\): \(m\ddot p - 2\mathrm{i}m\Omega\dot p - m\Omega^2 p + 2\mathrm{i}m\Omega\dot p + 2m\Omega^2 p + kp - m\Omega^2 p = m\ddot p + kp\).

Source: The proof is not from the source. The split \(T = T_2 + T_1 + T_0\) into transport and complementary (Coriolis or gyroscopic) forces: GR (1.36)-(1.40) (PDF pp. 46 to 47). Step 7 and SymPy checked that the equation in the rotating axes agrees with equation (24.40) without damping in the fixed axes.

The lemma says what the turning of the axes brings, and each term has its cause.

We draw the axes \(\xi\) and \(\eta\) that turn with the shaft and in them the disk centre with its velocity. The shaft pulls it toward the axis with the elastic force, the turning of the axes pushes it away with the centrifugal force and sideways with the Coriolis force, perpendicular to the velocity.

  • The term \(-m\Omega^2\xi\) is a transport force (it comes from \(T_0\)): in turning axes the disk needs, to move on a circle, an acceleration toward the centre of \(\Omega^2\) per unit of radius, and since an observer in these axes turns together with the disk, he feels his acceleration toward the centre as a force \(m\Omega^2 q\) away from the centre. We call it the centrifugal force (Latin centrum and fugere, to flee from the centre). It reduces the effective stiffness from \(k\) to \(k - m\Omega^2\).
  • The terms \(\mp 2m\Omega\dot\eta\) and \(\pm 2m\Omega\dot\xi\) (the term \(T_1\)) are a force proportional to velocity and turned by a right angle relative to it. We call it the Coriolis force (after Coriolis) or the gyroscopic force. Because the coefficients are skew-symmetric (\(+2m\Omega\) and \(-2m\Omega\)), the power is \(\dot\xi\cdot 2m\Omega\dot\eta - \dot\eta\cdot 2m\Omega\dot\xi = 0\): the force does no work. The gyroscopic matrix of the disk from section 24.3 (lemma 24.19) has the same structural property, only here the cause is the turning of the coordinates, not the tilt of the disk.

The first consequence is the same as for the critical speed. At \(\Omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) we have \(k - m\Omega^2 = 0\) and equations (24.39) allow rest in the turning axes at every \(q \neq 0\): the disk centre turns with the shaft at exactly the same angular speed, on a circular orbit. In a synchronous forward whirl \(q\) is constant, because the orbit turns together with the axes. This is the speed at which, in the turning axes, the balance between the elastic and the centrifugal force holds.

24.7.2 Internal and external damping

When then does internal damping act? The shaft loses energy when its fibre deforms, that is when the disk centre moves relative to the turning axes.

Definition 24.40 Internal and external damping (notranje in zunanje dušenje)

Let the Jeffcott rotor be as in lemma 24.39. Internal damping is a force of the shaft on the disk centre proportional to the velocity of the centre relative to the turning axes: in components of the turning axes \(F_\xi = -c_{\mathrm{i}}\dot\xi\), \(F_\eta = -c_{\mathrm{i}}\dot\eta\), in complex form \(F^{\mathrm{vrt}}_{\mathrm{i}} = -c_{\mathrm{i}}\dot q\), with a coefficient \(c_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\) in N s/m. External damping is a force of the surroundings (bearings, air) on the disk centre proportional to the velocity of the centre relative to the fixed axes: \(F_{\mathrm{e}} = -c_{\mathrm{e}}\dot p\) with \(c_{\mathrm{e}} \ge 0\). We write both coefficients with the damping ratios (definition 9.5) \(\zeta_{\mathrm{e}} = c_{\mathrm{e}}/(2m\omega_{\mathrm{n}})\) and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{i}} = c_{\mathrm{i}}/(2m\omega_{\mathrm{n}})\), where \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \sqrt{k/m}\).

Source: FPGL §7.5 (PDF pp. 336 to 337): damping in the rotor (\(c_{\mathrm{i}}\)) and damping outside the rotor (\(c_{\mathrm{e}}\), in bearings and foundation, also air drag), (7.58) for the force \(-c_{\mathrm{i}}\) times the velocity in the turning axes. The name is by where the force acts: internal acts inside the turning part, external between it and the surroundings.

What does the condition "relative to the turning axes" mean in the fixed axes in which we shall compute? By step 2 of lemma 24.39 the velocity of the centre relative to the turning axes is \(\dot q\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t} = \dot p - \mathrm{i}\Omega p\): from the velocity \(\dot p\) of the centre we subtract the velocity \(\mathrm{i}\Omega p\) that a point fixed to the shaft at the same place would have (the vector \(p\) rotated forward by a right angle and multiplied by \(\Omega\)).

Lemma 24.41 Equation of the rotor with internal and external damping (enačba rotorja z notranjim in zunanjim dušenjem)

The Jeffcott rotor with the dampings of definition 24.40 and angular speed \(\Omega\) has in the fixed axes the equation of motion

\[m\ddot p + (c_{\mathrm{e}} + c_{\mathrm{i}})\,\dot p - \mathrm{i}\,\Omega c_{\mathrm{i}}\,p + k p = 0 . \tag{24.41}\]

Written out in the components \(p = v + \mathrm{i}\,w\) these are the equations

\[\begin{aligned} m\ddot v + (c_{\mathrm{e}} + c_{\mathrm{i}})\dot v + \Omega c_{\mathrm{i}}\,w + k v &= 0 , \\ m\ddot w + (c_{\mathrm{e}} + c_{\mathrm{i}})\dot w - \Omega c_{\mathrm{i}}\,v + k w &= 0 . \end{aligned} \tag{24.42}\]
Proof

We must show that the force of internal damping in the fixed axes is \(-c_{\mathrm{i}}(\dot p - \mathrm{i}\Omega p)\) and that it is to be added to the right-hand side of the equation without damping.

  1. Without damping the Lagrange equations in the coordinates \(v\), \(w\) with \(T = \tfrac12 m(\dot v^2 + \dot w^2)\) and \(V = \tfrac12 k(v^2 + w^2)\) give by theorem 8.101 \(m\ddot v + kv = Q_{\mathrm{v}}\) and \(m\ddot w + kw = Q_{\mathrm{w}}\). For a virtual displacement \((\delta v, \delta w)\) of the disk centre the work of a force \((F_{\mathrm{v}}, F_{\mathrm{w}})\) is \(F_{\mathrm{v}}\delta v + F_{\mathrm{w}}\delta w\), so \(Q_{\mathrm{v}} = F_{\mathrm{v}}\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{w}} = F_{\mathrm{w}}\). With \(F = F_{\mathrm{v}} + \mathrm{i}F_{\mathrm{w}}\) we have \(m\ddot p + kp = F\).
  2. The components of a vector in the turning and in the fixed axes are related like the coordinates of a point (step 1 of lemma 24.39): \(F_{\mathrm{v}} + \mathrm{i}F_{\mathrm{w}} = (F_\xi + \mathrm{i}F_\eta)\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\). For the internal force therefore \(F_{\mathrm{i}} = -c_{\mathrm{i}}\dot q\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\), and by step 2 of the lemma \(\dot q\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t} = \dot p - \mathrm{i}\Omega p\). So \(F_{\mathrm{i}} = -c_{\mathrm{i}}(\dot p - \mathrm{i}\Omega p)\) (SymPy confirms the same).
  3. The external force is \(F_{\mathrm{e}} = -c_{\mathrm{e}}\dot p\) by definition. We insert \(F = F_{\mathrm{e}} + F_{\mathrm{i}}\) in step 1 and move to the left: \(m\ddot p + c_{\mathrm{e}}\dot p + c_{\mathrm{i}}\dot p - \mathrm{i}\Omega c_{\mathrm{i}} p + kp = 0\), which is (24.41).
  4. We split into real and imaginary parts: \(-\mathrm{i}\Omega c_{\mathrm{i}}(v + \mathrm{i}w) = \Omega c_{\mathrm{i}} w - \mathrm{i}\Omega c_{\mathrm{i}} v\), so the real part brings \(+\Omega c_{\mathrm{i}} w\) and the imaginary part \(-\Omega c_{\mathrm{i}} v\), which is (24.42).

Source: FPGL §7.5 (PDF pp. 336 to 337), (7.58) to (7.62): the same equation written with \(u\), \(v\) and in matrix form. The proof by steps is not from the source.

Let us read equations (24.42). Besides the usual damping \(c_{\mathrm{e}} + c_{\mathrm{i}}\) they have a term \(\pm\Omega c_{\mathrm{i}}\): a force on the disk that is proportional to the displacement but perpendicular to it. It has the structural property of a stiffness matrix with a skew-symmetric part, and this part grows with \(\Omega\) (FPGL, PDF p. 348). The skew-symmetric part of the stiffness is the one that does not conserve energy: a force perpendicular to the displacement that accompanies it can supply work to the disk instead of taking it. Let us see what this means for the orbit.

Figure 24.83 shows it for a disk on a circular orbit, whirled forward with frequency \(\omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\). We draw the orbit around the axis \(O\) and on it the disk centre \(P\). On \(P\) act first the elastic force of the shaft \(F_{\mathrm{k}}\), directed toward the axis, of size \(k|p|\). Then the external force \(F_{\mathrm{e}}\), always opposite to the velocity, that is against the direction of the whirl, so we draw it tangentially backward. The internal force \(F_{\mathrm{i}} = -c_{\mathrm{i}}(\dot p - \mathrm{i}\Omega p)\) depends on the difference of two velocities, which we draw below: \(\dot p\) of the disk centre and \(\mathrm{i}\Omega p\) of the point of the shaft at the same place. At \(\Omega = \omega\) (left) they are equal, the relative velocity is zero and there is no internal force: the centre turns with the shaft as a whole, the fibre does not change its deformation and no energy is dissipated. At \(\Omega = 4\omega\) (right) the shaft runs ahead of the whirl, the point of the shaft at the same place moves four times faster, the relative velocity \(\dot p - \mathrm{i}\Omega p\) points backward, and the force \(F_{\mathrm{i}}\) therefore points forward, in the direction of the whirl. The shaft thus drags the disk forward by friction and above the whirl frequency drives it instead of braking it.

A computation confirms this. On a circular orbit \(p = P\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}\) we have \(\dot p = \mathrm{i}\omega p\). The external force is \(-c_{\mathrm{e}}\mathrm{i}\omega p\), along the velocity in the opposite sense, the internal one \(-c_{\mathrm{i}}\mathrm{i}(\omega - \Omega)p = c_{\mathrm{i}}(\Omega - \omega)\,\mathrm{i}p\), along the velocity (\(\mathrm{i}p\) points forward) if \(\Omega > \omega\). The power of these forces is the scalar product of force and velocity. The sum of the damping forces is \(-c_{\mathrm{e}}\dot p - c_{\mathrm{i}}\dot p + \mathrm{i}\Omega c_{\mathrm{i}} p = \big(c_{\mathrm{i}}\Omega - (c_{\mathrm{e}} + c_{\mathrm{i}})\omega\big)\,\mathrm{i}p\). So it lies on the tangent and has in the forward direction, the direction of \(\mathrm{i}p\) of length \(|p|\), the component \(\big(c_{\mathrm{i}}\Omega - (c_{\mathrm{e}} + c_{\mathrm{i}})\omega\big)|p|\). The velocity \(\dot p = \mathrm{i}\omega p\) points the same way with size \(\omega|p|\), and the elastic force \(-kp\) is perpendicular to it and does no work. So the power is

\[\mathcal P = \big(c_{\mathrm{i}}\Omega - (c_{\mathrm{e}} + c_{\mathrm{i}})\,\omega\big)\,\omega\,|p|^2 . \tag{24.43}\]

It is positive at \(\Omega > \omega(1 + c_{\mathrm{e}}/c_{\mathrm{i}})\). The orbit gains more energy than it loses and its amplitude grows. The energy does not come from nothing: the drive that holds \(\Omega\) constant (which is why we took \(\Omega\) as prescribed) must turn the shaft against the friction of the fibre, and through the force \(F_{\mathrm{i}}\) on figure 24.83 on the right (pointing forward) that work passes into the whirl. At \(\omega \approx \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) the threshold is \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}(1 + c_{\mathrm{e}}/c_{\mathrm{i}})\). So from the law of work (power is force times velocity) we arrived at a number that the theorem below proves from the roots.

One consequence holds at once and links this section with section 24.2.

Corollary 24.42 Internal damping does not affect the response to unbalance (notranje dušenje ne vpliva na odziv na neuravnoteženost)

Let the rotor of lemma 24.41 also have the unbalance force \(m a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) on the right (definition 24.6). If \(c_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\) or \(\Omega \ne \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), one solution is the circular orbit \(p = P\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\), with an amplitude that depends only on the external damping:

\[P = \frac{m a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2}{k - m\Omega^2 + \mathrm{i}\,c_{\mathrm{e}}\Omega} . \tag{24.44}\]

This is the response of theorem 24.7 with \(c = c_{\mathrm{e}}\).

Proof

We must show that \(c_{\mathrm{i}}\) drops out of the equation.

  1. We insert \(p = P\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) into (24.41) with the right-hand side \(m a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\). Since \(\dot p = \mathrm{i}\Omega p\) and \(\ddot p = -\Omega^2 p\), we get \(\big(-m\Omega^2 + \mathrm{i}\Omega(c_{\mathrm{e}} + c_{\mathrm{i}}) - \mathrm{i}\Omega c_{\mathrm{i}} + k\big)P = m a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2\).
  2. The terms \(\mathrm{i}\Omega c_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(-\mathrm{i}\Omega c_{\mathrm{i}}\) cancel, and \((k - m\Omega^2 + \mathrm{i}c_{\mathrm{e}}\Omega)P = m a_{\mathrm{u}}\Omega^2\) remains, which is (24.44).

Source: The proof is not from the source. The same reason as for figure 24.83 on the left: at \(\omega = \Omega\) there is no internal force.

For R1 at \(\zeta_{\mathrm{e}} = 0{,}02\) and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{i}} = 0{,}01\) we have \(|p| = 4{,}1886\), \(25{,}0000\) and \(5{,}6394\,a_{\mathrm{u}}\) at \(\Omega = 0{,}9\), \(1\) and \(1{,}1\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), and we obtain the same numbers if we set \(c_{\mathrm{i}}\) to zero (computation in num-07.py). The response of section 24.2 thus stays as it was. The consequence does not say, however, that the orbit is stable: this solution makes sense only if a disturbance around it does not grow, and that is decided by the theorem in the next part.

24.7.3 The stability threshold

From the law of work we guessed for the threshold \(\Omega_{\mathrm{s}} = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}(1 + c_{\mathrm{e}}/c_{\mathrm{i}})\). The theorem proves it without the approximation \(\omega \approx \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), with the zeros of the characteristic polynomial of equation (24.41).

The zeros lie in the complex plane. We draw the real and imaginary axes, the left half-plane where solutions decay and the right one where they grow. The zero \(s_-\) stays on the left at every \(\Omega\). The zero \(s_+\) moves to the right as \(\Omega\) grows and crosses the imaginary axis at \(\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) when \(\Omega = \Omega_{\mathrm{s}}\).

Theorem 24.43 Stability threshold of the Jeffcott rotor with internal damping (meja stabilnosti Jeffcottovega rotorja z notranjim dušenjem)

Let \(m > 0\), \(k > 0\), \(c_{\mathrm{e}} \ge 0\) and \(c_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\) and let \(\Omega\) be real. Let \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \sqrt{k/m}\) and the threshold

\[\Omega_{\mathrm{s}} = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\Big(1 + \frac{c_{\mathrm{e}}}{c_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big) . \tag{24.45}\]

The characteristic polynomial of equation (24.41) is \(\chi(s) = m s^2 + (c_{\mathrm{e}} + c_{\mathrm{i}})s + k - \mathrm{i}\,\Omega c_{\mathrm{i}}\). Its zeros are \(s_\pm = \big(-(c_{\mathrm{e}} + c_{\mathrm{i}}) \pm \sqrt\Delta\big)/(2m)\), where \(\Delta = (c_{\mathrm{e}} + c_{\mathrm{i}})^2 - 4m(k - \mathrm{i}\,\Omega c_{\mathrm{i}})\) and \(\sqrt\Delta\) is the complex root with nonnegative real part (for real \(\Delta < 0\), which happens only at \(\Omega = 0\), the one with positive imaginary part). Then \(\operatorname{Re}s_- < 0\) at every \(\Omega\) and:

  1. The equilibrium \(p = 0\) is asymptotically stable (definition 9.52 for the coordinates \(v\), \(w\)) if and only if \(|\Omega| < \Omega_{\mathrm{s}}\).
  2. For \(|\Omega| > \Omega_{\mathrm{s}}\) we have \(\operatorname{Re}s_+ > 0\) and the equilibrium is not stable (definition 8.130).
  3. At \(\Omega = \Omega_{\mathrm{s}}\) we have \(s_+ = \mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\): the solution \(\varepsilon\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t}\) neither decays nor grows. For \(\Omega > 0\) the zero \(s_+\) has a positive imaginary part, which is a forward whirl (definition 24.3), and \(s_-\) a negative one, a backward whirl.
Proof

We must show that the sign of \(\operatorname{Re}s_+\) is decided by the comparison of \(|\Omega|\) and \(\Omega_{\mathrm{s}}\). First we reduce stability to the zeros through the characteristic polynomial, then we compute them.

  1. Equation (24.41) is a linear equation of order 2 with constant complex coefficients for a complex function \(p\). By theorem 9.44 all solutions have the form \(p = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} p_{\mathrm{k}}(t)\,\mathrm{e}^{\sigma_{\mathrm{k}} t}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}\) the zeros of the polynomial \(\chi\), \(p_{\mathrm{k}}\) polynomials of degree less than the multiplicity of the zero, and by the choice of coefficients we reach any initial values. If both zeros have a negative real part, every term \(t^j\mathrm{e}^{\sigma t}\) tends to zero, and so does its derivative, so \(p\) and \(\dot p\) tend to zero for every start. The coefficients of the polynomials \(p_{\mathrm{k}}\) are linear functions of the initial values \(p(0)\) and \(\dot p(0)\) (the solution of a system of two linear equations from theorem 9.44). Since every term decays and is therefore bounded, there is a number \(C\) with \(|p(t)| + |\dot p(t)| \le C\,(|p(0)| + |\dot p(0)|)\) for all \(t \ge 0\). A small start therefore stays small, the equilibrium is stable (definition 8.130) and, with the limit zero, asymptotically stable. If \(\operatorname{Re}\sigma_{\mathrm{k}} \ge 0\) for some zero, then \(p = \varepsilon\,\mathrm{e}^{\sigma_{\mathrm{k}} t}\) is a solution (since \(\chi(\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}) = 0\)) with \(|p(0)| = \varepsilon\) and \(|p(t)| = \varepsilon\,\mathrm{e}^{(\operatorname{Re}\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}) t}\), which at \(\operatorname{Re}\sigma_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\) does not tend to zero and at \(\operatorname{Re}\sigma_{\mathrm{k}} > 0\) grows without bound for arbitrarily small \(\varepsilon\). The equilibrium is then not asymptotically stable and at \(\operatorname{Re}\sigma_{\mathrm{k}} > 0\) not even stable.
  2. We write \(c = c_{\mathrm{e}} + c_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\), \(A = c^2 - 4mk\) and \(B = 4m\Omega c_{\mathrm{i}}\). The zeros are \(s_\pm = (-c \pm \sqrt\Delta)/(2m)\) with \(\Delta = A + \mathrm{i}B\), which is the \(\Delta\) of the theorem. We write the root of the theorem as \(\sqrt\Delta = a + \mathrm{i}b\) with \(a \ge 0\). From \(a^2 - b^2 = A\) and \(2ab = B\) we get \(b^2 = a^2 - A\) and \(4a^2(a^2 - A) = B^2\), so \(x = a^2\) is a zero of the polynomial \(x^2 - Ax - B^2/4\) with \(x \ge 0\) and \(x \ge A\) (because \(b^2 = x - A \ge 0\)). The zeros of this polynomial are \(\big(A \pm \sqrt{A^2 + B^2}\big)/2\). The zero with the minus is \(\ge 0\) only if \(\sqrt{A^2 + B^2} \le A\), and \(\ge A\) only if \(\sqrt{A^2 + B^2} \le -A\). Both hold together only at \(A = B = 0\), where the two zeros are equal. Hence \(a^2 = \big(A + \sqrt{A^2 + B^2}\big)/2\).
  3. The real parts of the zeros are \(\operatorname{Re}s_\pm = (-c \pm a)/(2m)\). The zero with the minus has \(\operatorname{Re}s_- = -(c + a)/(2m) < 0\) at every \(\Omega\), because \(c > 0\) and \(a \ge 0\). For the zero with the plus: \(\operatorname{Re}s_+ < 0\) exactly when \(a < c\), and since \(c > 0\) and \(a \ge 0\) this is the same as \(a^2 < c^2\), that is \(\sqrt{A^2 + B^2} < 2c^2 - A = c^2 + 4mk\). Both sides are positive, so this is the same as \(A^2 + B^2 < (c^2 + 4mk)^2\), that is \(B^2 < (c^2 + 4mk)^2 - (c^2 - 4mk)^2 = 16\,m k c^2\). With \(B^2 = 16 m^2\Omega^2 c_{\mathrm{i}}^2\) this is \(\Omega^2 < (k/m)(c/c_{\mathrm{i}})^2\), so \(|\Omega| < \omega_{\mathrm{n}} c/c_{\mathrm{i}} = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}(1 + c_{\mathrm{e}}/c_{\mathrm{i}}) = \Omega_{\mathrm{s}}\). The same steps with \(=\) and \(>\) instead of \(<\) give \(\operatorname{Re}s_+ = 0\) at \(|\Omega| = \Omega_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(\operatorname{Re}s_+ > 0\) at \(|\Omega| > \Omega_{\mathrm{s}}\). On figure 24.86 the threshold is where the curve crosses zero (case \(\zeta_{\mathrm{e}} = 0{,}02\)).
  4. Points 1 and 2 of the theorem follow from steps 1 and 3.
  5. At \(\Omega = \Omega_{\mathrm{s}} > 0\) we have \(\operatorname{Re}s_+ = 0\), so \(s_+ = \mathrm{i}\sigma\) with real \(\sigma\). We insert into \(\chi(s) = 0\): the real part \(-m\sigma^2 + k = 0\) and the imaginary part \(c\sigma - \Omega c_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\). The first gives \(\sigma = \pm\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), the second \(\sigma = \Omega c_{\mathrm{i}}/c = \omega_{\mathrm{n}} > 0\). So \(s_+ = \mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) and the solution \(\varepsilon\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t}\) of step 1 has constant \(|p| = \varepsilon\).
  6. At \(\Omega > 0\) we have \(B > 0\), so \(a > 0\) (if \(a = 0\) then \(B = 2ab = 0\)) and \(b = B/(2a) > 0\). The imaginary parts of the zeros are \(\pm b/(2m)\), so \(\operatorname{Im}s_+ > 0\) and \(\operatorname{Im}s_- < 0\). A solution \(\mathrm{e}^{st}\) with \(\operatorname{Im}s > 0\) is \(p = \mathrm{e}^{(\operatorname{Re}s) t}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\operatorname{Im}s) t}\), which turns in the same direction as the turning of the shaft (forward, definition 24.3), because \(\Omega > 0\).

Source: FPGL (7.72) and (7.73) (PDF p. 338): \(\zeta_{\mathrm{i}} R = \zeta_{\mathrm{e}} + \zeta_{\mathrm{i}}\) and stability for \(\Omega < \omega_{\mathrm{n}}(1 + \zeta_{\mathrm{e}}/\zeta_{\mathrm{i}})\), which is the same, because \(c_{\mathrm{e}}/c_{\mathrm{i}} = \zeta_{\mathrm{e}}/\zeta_{\mathrm{i}}\). FPGL proves it with the Routh-Hurwitz criterion or from the zeros, here we name it and do not use it. The proof by steps is not from the source.

Let us test the theorem on R1 with \(\zeta_{\mathrm{e}} = 0{,}02\) and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{i}} = 0{,}01\), so \(c_{\mathrm{e}} = 304{,}5\) N s/m and \(c_{\mathrm{i}} = 152{,}2\) N s/m. The threshold is \(\Omega_{\mathrm{s}} = 3\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 465{,}95\) 1/s, that is 4449 rev/min, three times the first critical speed. At \(0{,}99\,\Omega_{\mathrm{s}}\) we have \(s_+ = -0{,}0466 + 155{,}32\,\mathrm{i}\) 1/s and at \(1{,}01\,\Omega_{\mathrm{s}}\) we have \(+0{,}0466 + 155{,}32\,\mathrm{i}\) 1/s, so the real part changes sign and the zero stays at almost the same frequency \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\). A rotor just above the threshold whirls forward with frequency \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) and not \(\Omega\), so subsynchronously, and its amplitude is multiplied by \(\mathrm{e}^{0{,}0466\,t}\). Growth is this slow because 1 % above the threshold is little. Figure 24.85 shows the difference at 20 % from the threshold.

In the figure the coordinate axes \(v\) and \(w\) are common, the start is on a circle of radius 1,15 cm. At \(\Omega = 0{,}8\,\Omega_{\mathrm{s}}\) the orbit shrinks and in 0,8 s only 47 % of the initial amplitude remains. At \(\Omega = 1{,}2\,\Omega_{\mathrm{s}}\) the orbit widens to 211 %. In the linear model the amplitude grows without bound, as \(\mathrm{e}^{0{,}93\,t}\). What happens at large amplitudes is decided by nonlinearities that we do not treat.

The threshold of stability is determined by the ratio \(c_{\mathrm{e}}/c_{\mathrm{i}}\) and not by the size of \(c_{\mathrm{i}}\). Figure 24.86 shows the real part of the zero \(s_+\) as a function of \(\Omega/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) for \(\zeta_{\mathrm{i}} = 0{,}01\) and three external dampings.

We draw the axes: \(\Omega/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) on the horizontal and \(\operatorname{Re}s_+\) on the vertical. First the case \(\zeta_{\mathrm{e}} = 0{,}02\): the line starts at \(-4{,}66\) 1/s, that is \(-(\zeta_{\mathrm{e}} + \zeta_{\mathrm{i}})\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), because at \(\Omega = 0\) the rotor is not turning and both kinds of damping act as usual, and it crosses zero at the threshold at 3. The case \(\zeta_{\mathrm{e}} = 0{,}05\) starts lower (\(-9{,}32\)) and crosses zero at 6, the case \(\zeta_{\mathrm{e}} = 0\) at 1, that is at the first critical speed. The grey dashed line is the rotor with \(\zeta_{\mathrm{e}} = 0{,}02\) and no internal damping: its real part is \(-\zeta_{\mathrm{e}}\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = -3{,}106\) 1/s at every speed and never crosses zero. All three curves with \(\zeta_{\mathrm{i}} = 0{,}01\) are almost parallel with slope \(\zeta_{\mathrm{i}}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\). The reason is equation (24.43): the growth of the amplitude has the rate \(\mathcal P\) divided by the energy \(m\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2|p|^2\) of the orbit, so \(2\operatorname{Re}s_+ \approx \mathcal P/(m\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2|p|^2)\) and

\[\operatorname{Re}s_+ \approx \zeta_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Omega - (\zeta_{\mathrm{e}} + \zeta_{\mathrm{i}})\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} \tag{24.46}\]

(with \(\omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\)). At \(\Omega = 4\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) the approximation is \(1{,}553\) 1/s, the exact value from step 3 of the theorem \(1{,}551\) 1/s. At \(7\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) it is \(6{,}21\) against \(6{,}19\) 1/s. The approximation holds for small \(\zeta\), because we wrote the energy of the orbit as for an undamped circular orbit. The theorem is exact, the approximation explains the cause.

The table collects what the reader must hold when choosing.

\(\zeta_{\mathrm{e}}\) \(\zeta_{\mathrm{i}}\) \(\Omega_{\mathrm{s}}/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) \(\Omega_{\mathrm{s}}\) (rev/min)
\(0\) \(0{,}01\) \(1\) \(1483\)
\(0{,}02\) \(0{,}02\) \(2\) \(2966\)
\(0{,}02\) \(0{,}01\) \(3\) \(4449\)
\(0{,}05\) \(0{,}01\) \(6\) \(8899\)
\(0{,}02\) \(0\) no threshold stable at all speeds

External damping does not remove the threshold, it only raises it, internal damping lowers it, and since \(\Omega_{\mathrm{s}} \ge \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) at every \(c_{\mathrm{e}} \ge 0\), the rotor is always stable below the first critical speed. For operation at \(\Omega\) we need \(c_{\mathrm{e}}/c_{\mathrm{i}} > \Omega/\omega_{\mathrm{n}} - 1\).

We now test the theorem on the cases whose hypotheses it excludes.

Example 24.44 External damping only (samo zunanje dušenje)

At \(c_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) the term \(\mathrm{i}\Omega c_{\mathrm{i}} p\) in (24.41) vanishes and the equation is the ordinary damped equation of theorem 9.53 for each plane separately. The threshold of (24.45) with \(c_{\mathrm{e}}/c_{\mathrm{i}} \to \infty\) goes to infinity, which agrees. For R1 with \(\zeta_{\mathrm{e}} = 0{,}02\) we have \(\operatorname{Re}s = -\zeta_{\mathrm{e}}\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = -3{,}106\) 1/s at every \(\Omega\) (the grey dashed line in figure 24.86), at \(\Omega = 3\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) just as at \(0\). The theorem does not apply, because it assumes \(c_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\). The reason is not that external damping guarantees stability, but that there is no term that drives the motion: the force \(\mathrm{i}\Omega c_{\mathrm{i}} p\) is the only source of energy in the equation.

Example 24.45 Internal damping only (samo notranje dušenje)

At \(c_{\mathrm{e}} = 0\) we have \(\Omega_{\mathrm{s}} = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\). R1 with \(\zeta_{\mathrm{i}} = 0{,}01\) is stable at \(\Omega = 0{,}975\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) (\(\operatorname{Re}s_+ = -0{,}0388\) 1/s) and unstable at \(1{,}025\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) (\(+0{,}0388\) 1/s). At the speed \(1{,}1\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) it is \(+0{,}155\) 1/s. The threshold is at the first critical speed: a rotor that has only internal damping is stable only below it (FPGL, PDF p. 338, the worst case). Fast growth is prevented here only by \(\zeta_{\mathrm{i}}\) being small, not by some property of the model. The example warns that "damping always helps" does not hold for a rotor that has internal damping and no external damping.

Example 24.46 Check against the source's equations (preizkus z enačbami vira)

FPGL, example 7.5.1 (PDF pp. 338 to 339), takes \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 100\) 1/s and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{e}} = \zeta_{\mathrm{i}} = 0{,}1\), so the threshold is \(\Omega_{\mathrm{s}} = 2\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) (\(R = 2\) in the source). Our equation (24.41) gives at \(R = 1{,}95\) the zeros \(-0{,}48 + 99{,}90\,\mathrm{i}\) and \(-39{,}52 - 99{,}90\,\mathrm{i}\) and at \(R = 2{,}05\) the zeros \(+0{,}48 + 100{,}10\,\mathrm{i}\) and \(-40{,}48 - 100{,}10\,\mathrm{i}\) (rad/s), which are the numbers of table 7.1 in the source. The zero that becomes unstable has a positive imaginary part, that is forward whirl, as the source text says (PDF p. 339).

The section showed three things. First, in rotating axes the kinetic energy splits into transport and Coriolis terms (lemma 24.39), because the coordinates turn. Second, internal damping is a force relative to the shaft and not to the bearings, so in fixed axes it gets a term \(-\mathrm{i}\Omega c_{\mathrm{i}} p\) perpendicular to the displacement (lemma 24.41), and the synchronous response of section 24.2 stays unchanged (corollary 24.42). Third, above \(\Omega_{\mathrm{s}} = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}(1 + c_{\mathrm{e}}/c_{\mathrm{i}})\) this term drives a forward whirl with frequency \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) (theorem 24.43). What this means for design is short: above the first critical speed the rotor should have a lot of external damping in the bearings and as little internal damping as possible, which comes for example from bolted joints and laminated rotors (FPGL, PDF p. 336).

The idealizations of the section are listed once more so that the reader knows what the theorem really covers. Viscous internal damping (the theorem holds for this law). A shaft without mass and isotropic: for a shaft with mass and more complex rotors FPGL says that internal damping shows up in finite elements as a skew-symmetric part of the stiffness that grows with \(\Omega\) (§7.7, PDF pp. 348 to 349). For the overhung rotor of FPGL, example 7.7.1 (PDF p. 350), the second eigenvalue becomes unstable between 1000 and 2000 rev/min. The section does not prove this, it cites it. Hydrodynamic bearings and asymmetric rotors are only named in the chapter.

24.8 Balancing flexible rotors (uravnoteženje podajnih rotorjev)

In section 24.2 we saw that unbalance excites a whirl of the shaft whose response grows at the critical speed. Now we ask what to do about it.

We cannot remove the unbalance, because we do not know where on the shaft it is, but we can add or remove mass at places we can reach, so that the effects add up to zero (figure 24.87). In the view from one side the hidden unbalance \(U_0\) is a vector that turns with the shaft, the added mass gives a correction \(U_{\mathrm{c}} = -U_0\) opposite to it, and their sum is zero. This is called balancing (uravnoteženje). The word has the same origin as balance: a rotor is balanced when the forces that the turning causes on its masses are in equilibrium like the pans of a scale, and the shaft feels no force that turns with it. A rotor is flexible (podajen, from "podati", to give way under load) when it visibly bends under these forces. A rigid rotor (togi rotor), which does not bend and moves as a rigid body, is balanced in two planes by the procedure of chapter 23.

Here we show why this is not enough for a flexible rotor, and derive two procedures that are: influence coefficients (vplivni koeficienti), which need no model of the shaft, and modal balancing (modalno uravnoteženje), which needs the mode shapes of the shaft. We prove both with the response of section 24.2 and the models of chapters 10 and 13.

From history

According to the source FPGL (PDF p. 358) the rotor of smaller machines is usually rigid and moves as a rigid body. In recent decades there has been a trend towards flexible rotors, which deform under the forces and moments of unbalance, and these are common in larger units, for example turbogenerators (FPGL, PDF p. 358). Many balancing techniques were introduced in the 1950s and 1960s ("1950s and 1960s"), and a historical survey, especially for modal balancing, is given by the papers of Bishop and Gladwell (1959) and Parkinson (1965, 1966, 1967) (FPGL, PDF p. 358). The source does not say what these papers proved, so we cite them only as a survey.

The question of the section is now sharper: where on a flexible shaft should we add masses, and how do we compute them from measurements. First we set up a model (section 24.8.1), then we compute the response of the flexible shaft by modes, because linearity follows from it, and every procedure stands on linearity (section 24.8.2). Then comes the influence coefficient procedure for one plane and for several planes (sections 24.8.3 and 24.8.4), and last the case in which two planes are not enough, and the modal procedure (sections 24.8.5 and 24.8.6).

24.8.1 Model: what we add and what we measure

Take a steel shaft of length \(L = 1\) m and diameter \(40\) mm, turning in two rigid short bearings (chapter 13, the same as in section 24.2). On it we choose three balance planes (ravnine uravnoteženja), transverse planes at \(0{,}1L\), \(0{,}5L\) and \(0{,}9L\), in which we can fix or remove mass. The added or removed mass, for example a bolt or a drilled hole, is a point mass \(m_{\mathrm{c}}\) at radius \(\rho_{\mathrm{c}}\). In the figure the trial mass is in plane 2. On the shaft there is a mark, a short stretch that the probe detects once per revolution, and this gives us the phase. So we do not describe the mass by clock time but by the angle from the mark. To look at one plane exactly, we step to the end of the shaft and look at it from one side. From the mark we measure the angle \(\theta_{\mathrm{c}}\) to the mass, in the sense of rotation, and the radius \(\rho_{\mathrm{c}}\) to the axis. The position of the mass is \(\rho_{\mathrm{c}}\,e^{i\theta_{\mathrm{c}}}\) in the complex plane. By section 24.2 its unbalance (neuravnoteženost, definition 24.6) is the complex number

\[U = m_{\mathrm{c}}\,\rho_{\mathrm{c}}\,e^{i\theta_{\mathrm{c}}} . \tag{24.47}\]

Why is this the right measure? The shaft turns with angular velocity \(\Omega\), so the mass on a circle of radius \(\rho_{\mathrm{c}}\) must feel a force towards the axis \(m_{\mathrm{c}}\rho_{\mathrm{c}}\Omega^2\) (Newton's second law for motion on a circle, chapter 8), and by the third law the mass pulls the shaft outwards with the same force. The force has magnitude \(|U|\Omega^2\), turns together with the mass, and so the whole exciting force that the mass causes is, in complex form, \(U\Omega^2 e^{i\Omega t}\). The magnitude and the angle of \(U\) are therefore all we need to know about the mass.

The probe stands next to the shaft, in the figure at \(0{,}3L\), and measures the displacement of its centre from the bearing axis. Since the supports are equal in all directions (isotropic), the orbit of the centre is a circle (section 24.2), and the measurement is the complex amplitude \(r\) of the circular orbit, that is \(p(t) = r\,e^{i\Omega t}\) for the complex displacement \(p = v + i w\) of section 24.1. Its angle \(\arg r\) tells by how much the centre leads the mark at the moment the mark passes the probe. The letter \(r\) here means the reading, and not the frequency ratio \(\Omega/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) of chapter 9, which we do not use in this section.

Let us first show the assumptions in figure 24.89. On the left is the plane of unbalance, on the right the plane of readings, and the arrow between them is the rule \(r = r_0 + \alpha U\), whose \(\alpha\) we shall call the influence coefficient in section 24.8.3. The hidden unbalance \(U_0\) gives the reading \(r_0\). The trial unbalance \(U_{\mathrm{t}}\) moves it to \(r_1\), by the change \(r_{\mathrm{d}}\). Twice the unbalance gives twice the change, and the sum of two unbalances gives the sum of the changes. If we add the correction \(U_{\mathrm{c}} = -U_0\), the reading falls to zero.

Figure 24.90 shows how one mode responds. On the left is the term of the series \(|C_{\mathrm{n}}|\) against \(\Omega/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\). The denominator is small near \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), and without damping the term would be infinite, with damping it stays finite. If the modal unbalance is zero, the term is zero at every \(\Omega\). On the right is the displacement at midspan of the shaft of example 24.49, the sum of all terms, and in it the term of mode 1 and the term of mode 3, which dominate at the first and the third critical speed. The run-up to the third must pass through the first.

The model has these assumptions, all named:

  • The response is linear in the unbalance: twice the unbalance gives twice the reading, and the readings of two unbalances add. This is the assumption of all balancing procedures (FPGL, PDF p. 357). With bearings of nonlinear stiffness it holds only approximately and the procedure must be repeated (FPGL, PDF p. 357). For our model we prove it in section 24.8.2.
  • The shaft is uniform with the models of chapter 13 (Euler-Bernoulli beam, rotary inertia neglected, which by section 24.5 changes the critical speed by \(0{,}049\) %).
  • The damping is modal with ratio \(\zeta_{\mathrm{n}} = 0{,}02\) in every mode (definition 10.64), which is a choice of the model and not a measurement. Internal damping is not included (section 24.7).
  • The probe and the mark are ideal, without noise. Noise we show in section 24.8.3.

24.8.2 Response of the flexible shaft by modes

Section 24.2 treated one disk on a massless shaft. The unbalance of a flexible shaft is distributed along its length, so we must first describe it (figure 24.91). The centre of mass of the cross-section at \(x\) is displaced from the geometric centre of the shaft by \(a(x)\,e^{i\Omega t}\), where \(a(x)\) is the complex eccentricity (izsrednost), that is, the displacement at the moment when the mark is on the real axis. By chapter 13 each mode \(\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}(x) = \sin(n\pi x/L)\) measures how much unbalance it feels, and the response of the shaft to a load by modes follows from theorem 13.73. Besides it, point masses are fixed in the planes, and we must count them too. So we first define how much unbalance a shape feels.

Definition 24.47 Unbalance with respect to a shape (neuravnoteženost glede na obliko)

Let a shaft of length \(L\) have mass per unit length \(\rho A\) (constant), eccentricity \(a\colon [0, L] \to \mathbb C\) (a continuous function), and let \(K\) masses with unbalances \(b_1, \dots, b_{\mathrm{K}} \in \mathbb C\) by equation (24.47) be fixed in the planes \(x_1, \dots, x_{\mathrm{K}}\). For a continuous function \(\varphi\colon [0, L] \to \mathbb R\), which we call a shape, the unbalance with respect to the shape (a complex number in kg m) is

\[U(\varphi) = \int_0^L \rho A\,a(x)\,\varphi(x)\,\mathrm{d}x + \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{K}b_{\mathrm{j}}\,\varphi(x_{\mathrm{j}}) . \tag{24.48}\]

The first term is the area under the product \(\rho A\,a\,\varphi\), the second the sum of the values of the shape in the planes of the masses, each multiplied by its mass. For \(\varphi = \varphi_{\mathrm{n}} = \sin(n\pi x/L)\) we write it \(U_{\mathrm{n}}\) and call it the modal unbalance (modalna neuravnoteženost) of mode \(n\). For \(\varphi = 1\) it is the total unbalance (from it comes the force \(\Omega^2\,U(1)\) that the rotor excites as a rigid body), and for \(\varphi = x - L/2\) it is the moment of this unbalance about the midpoint.

Source: FPGL (8.40), PDF p. 382, where it is the scalar product \(\mathbf u_\ell^{\mathsf T}\mathbf b\) of the mode and the unbalance vector. The notation with an integral and a shape \(\varphi\) is ours.

The reason for the name: for \(\varphi = 1\) and \(\varphi = x - L/2\) we get the quantities that the rigid balancing in two planes removes (chapter 23), and for \(\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\) the quantity that by the next theorem excites mode \(n\). The theorem says that these numbers alone decide the response.

Figure 24.92 shows what we shall compute. On the left is the cross-section of the shaft at \(x\): the axes \(v\) and \(w\) measure the displacements in the two planes, the displacement \(p = v + i w\) points to the geometric centre, and the centre of mass is ahead of it by \(a\,e^{i\Omega t}\). As the shaft turns, the centre describes a circular orbit of radius \(|P|\). On the right is the shaft from the side in both planes, the bending \(v\) and the bending \(w\), each loaded by the inertia force of the unbalanced masses.

Figure 24.93 shows what we do with a point mass, because the response theorem requires a continuous load. On the axis \(x\) are the plane \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) and the limits \(x_{\mathrm{j}} \pm \eta\). At the top is a triangle with base \(2\eta\) and height \(1/\eta\), its area is \(1\), and as \(\eta\) decreases it becomes narrower and taller with the same area. Below is the band \(|x - x_{\mathrm{j}}| \le \eta\) around the plane, in which the shape \(\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\) changes by at most the difference, which falls to zero as the band narrows.

Figure 24.94 shows why a series with terms smaller than \(B/n^4\) converges. We use it in step 6 of the proof below. On the left are the columns of height \(1/n^4\) and width \(1\) for \(n = 2, 3, \dots\), and column \(n\) stands over the stretch on the axis \(x\) from \(n - 1\) to \(n\). There \(x \le n\), so \(1/x^4 \ge 1/n^4\) and the column lies under the curve \(1/x^4\). The area under the curve to the right of \(x = 1\) is \(\int_1^\infty x^{-4}\,\mathrm{d}x = 1/3\), so the sum of these columns is at most \(1/3\). On the right all the terms are stacked into one column, the first term \(1\) and all the others above it, together \(1{,}0823\), which is below the bound \(1 + 1/3\).

Theorem 24.48 Response of the flexible shaft by modes (odziv podajne gredi po načinih)

Let a simply supported shaft of length \(L\) have constant \(EI > 0\) and \(\rho A > 0\), as in theorem 13.73, and let it have eccentricity \(a(x)\) and masses in planes as in definition 24.47. Let it turn with \(\Omega > 0\) and let its centre describe a circular orbit \(p(x, t) = P(x)\,e^{i\Omega t}\) with complex displacement \(p = v + i w\). Let \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = (n\pi/L)^2\sqrt{EI/\rho A}\), \(M_{\mathrm{n}} = \rho A L/2\) and \(\Omega \ne \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) for every \(n\). Then \(P(x) = \sum_{\mathrm{n}=1}^{\infty}C_{\mathrm{n}}\sin(n\pi x/L)\) with

\[C_{\mathrm{n}} = \frac{\Omega^2\,U_{\mathrm{n}}}{M_{\mathrm{n}}\,\big(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 - \Omega^2\big)} . \tag{24.49}\]

With modal damping of ratio \(\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}\) the denominator is \(M_{\mathrm{n}}(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 - \Omega^2 + 2i\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\Omega)\). The response \(P(x)\) is therefore linear in the eccentricity \(a\) and in the unbalances \(b_{\mathrm{j}}\).

Idea

The shaft has two bendings, one in each plane. We solve each with theorem 13.73 and combine them in one complex equation. The load is the inertia of the unbalanced masses.

Proof

We must show equation (24.49) for the real and imaginary parts of \(P\), then add the point masses and the damping.

  1. The centre of mass of the cross-section at \(x\) has coordinates \(v + \mathrm{Re}(a\,e^{i\Omega t})\) and \(w + \mathrm{Im}(a\,e^{i\Omega t})\), where \(v\), \(w\) are the displacements of the geometric centre in the two planes. The inertia force per unit length is mass times the acceleration of the centre of mass (theorem 8.79), and the bending term depends on the displacement of the axis (chapter 13, equation (13.42)). Hence
    \[\rho A\,v_{\mathrm{tt}} + EI\,v'''' = \rho A\,\Omega^2\,\mathrm{Re}(a\,e^{i\Omega t}) , \qquad \rho A\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} + EI\,w'''' = \rho A\,\Omega^2\,\mathrm{Im}(a\,e^{i\Omega t}) ,\]
    because \(\partial_{\mathrm{t}}^2\,\mathrm{Re}(a\,e^{i\Omega t}) = -\Omega^2\,\mathrm{Re}(a\,e^{i\Omega t})\) and this term is moved to the right.
  2. We multiply the second equation by \(i\) and add it to the first. Since the operators are real, \(p = v + i w\) is a solution of the equation \(\rho A\,p_{\mathrm{tt}} + EI\,p'''' = \rho A\,\Omega^2\,a\,e^{i\Omega t}\).
  3. We insert \(p = P(x)\,e^{i\Omega t}\). We get \(EI\,P'''' - \rho A\,\Omega^2\,P = \rho A\,\Omega^2\,a\) with \(P = P'' = 0\) at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\). This is equation (13.76) with right-hand side \(Q = \rho A\,\Omega^2\,a\). Theorem 13.73 holds for the real and for the imaginary part separately, so for the coefficients \(C_{\mathrm{n}} = \frac{2}{L}\int_0^L P\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\mathrm{d}x\) we have \(\rho A(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 - \Omega^2)\,C_{\mathrm{n}} = \frac{2}{L}\rho A\,\Omega^2\int_0^L a\,\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  4. Let the mass in plane \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) be spread over a short stretch \([x_{\mathrm{j}} - \eta, x_{\mathrm{j}} + \eta]\) with the same unbalance \(b_{\mathrm{j}}\) and with the triangular density \(g_\eta(x) = \max\big(0, \eta - |x - x_{\mathrm{j}}|\big)/\eta^2\), which is continuous, nonnegative and has integral \(1\) (a triangle with base \(2\eta\) and height \(1/\eta\)). The load \(Q = \Omega^2 b_{\mathrm{j}}\,g_\eta\) is then continuous, as theorem 13.73 requires. Its contribution to the right-hand side of step 3 is \(\frac{2}{L}\,\Omega^2 b_{\mathrm{j}}\int_0^L g_\eta\,\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}x\). Since the integral of \(g_\eta\) is \(1\), this contribution differs from \(\frac{2}{L}\,\Omega^2 b_{\mathrm{j}}\,\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}(x_{\mathrm{j}})\) by at most \(\frac{2}{L}\,\Omega^2|b_{\mathrm{j}}|\max_{|\mathrm{x} - \mathrm{x}_\mathrm{j}| \le \eta}|\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}(x) - \varphi_{\mathrm{n}}(x_{\mathrm{j}})|\). As \(\eta \to 0\) this bound tends to zero by the continuity of \(\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\), so the contribution is \(\frac{2}{L}\Omega^2 b_{\mathrm{j}}\,\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}(x_{\mathrm{j}})\).
  5. We divide step 3 by \(\rho A\,L/2 = M_{\mathrm{n}}\) and sum the contributions of the planes. The right-hand side is \(\Omega^2\,U_{\mathrm{n}}/M_{\mathrm{n}}\) with \(U_{\mathrm{n}}\) from equation (24.48), which is equation (24.49).
  6. The series converges. Since \(|\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}| \le 1\), \(|U_{\mathrm{n}}| \le \bar U = \int_0^L \rho A\,|a|\,\mathrm{d}x + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} |b_{\mathrm{j}}|\) for every \(n\). By equation (13.74) \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 = n^4\,\omega_1^2\). For all \(n\) with \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 \ge 2\Omega^2\), that is for all but finitely many, we therefore have \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 - \Omega^2 \ge \omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2/2\) and \(|C_{\mathrm{n}}| \le B/n^4\) with \(B = 2\Omega^2\,\bar U/(M_{\mathrm{n}}\,\omega_1^2)\). The sum of the bounds \(B/n^4\) is finite, so the series converges, and since \(|\sin(n\pi x/L)| \le 1\), it converges at every \(x\).
  7. Damping: with modal damping the equation of the mode is \(M_{\mathrm{n}}\ddot q_{\mathrm{n}} + 2\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}\omega_{\mathrm{n}} M_{\mathrm{n}}\dot q_{\mathrm{n}} + M_{\mathrm{n}}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 q_{\mathrm{n}} = \) force (definition 10.64), and for the response \(q_{\mathrm{n}} = C_{\mathrm{n}} e^{i\Omega t}\) the factor \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 - \Omega^2\) is replaced by \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 - \Omega^2 + 2i\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\Omega\) (theorem 9.62).
  8. The right-hand side is linear in \(a\) and \(b_{\mathrm{j}}\) and the denominators do not depend on them, so \(P\) is linear in them.

Source: Expansion by modes: theorem 13.73 (GR section 4.2.3, PDF pp. 252-253). Model of the shaft with eccentricity and unbalances in planes: FPGL section 6.3 (PDF pp. 269-275). The proof is not from the sources.

The theorem gives three things that we will need. First, the linearity that every procedure assumes is proved and not only assumed. Second, the numbers \(U_{\mathrm{n}}\) decide the response, so two equally unbalanced shafts differ only in these numbers. Third, for \(\Omega\) near \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) one term of the series dominates, because the denominator is small.

Example 24.49 A shaft with uniform eccentricity

Take a shaft without a disk (\(d = 40\) mm, \(L = 1\) m, \(E = 196\) GPa, \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³), where \(\rho A = 9{,}8018\) kg/m and \(\omega_1 = 494{,}74\) 1/s, that is \(4724\) rev/min. The eccentricity is uniform and real, \(a(x) = a_0 = 20\) μm, so the total unbalance is \(\rho A\,a_0\,L = 196{,}04\) g mm. By equation (24.48) \(U_{\mathrm{n}} = \rho A\,a_0\,L\,(1 - \cos n\pi)/(n\pi)\), because \(\int_0^L\sin(n\pi x/L)\,\mathrm{d}x = L(1 - \cos n\pi)/(n\pi)\). The even modes are zero (\(U_2 = 0\)), the odd ones give \(U_1 = \rho A a_0 L\cdot 2/\pi = 124{,}80\) g mm, \(U_3 = 41{,}60\) g mm and \(U_5 = 24{,}96\) g mm. At \(\Omega = \omega_1\) with \(\zeta = 0{,}02\) mode 1 dominates by theorem 24.48, and at midspan \(|P(L/2)| = 4a_0/(2\pi\zeta) = 0{,}6366\) mm, which with nine modes is \(0{,}6366\) mm. The displacement \(0{,}64\) mm is \(32\) times the eccentricity, since the ratio at resonance is \(4/(2\pi\zeta)\). The numbers \(U_1\) and \(U_3\) are the grey bars of figure 24.99 in section 24.8.6, the height of a bar is the number itself.

24.8.3 One plane is balanced with an influence coefficient

How do we find \(U_{\mathrm{c}}\) without knowing where the unbalance is? We measure how much the reading changes when we add a known mass, and from it we compute what mass we would have to add to make the reading vanish. The change of the reading per unit of added unbalance we call the influence coefficient, because it tells how much the added unbalance influences the reading.

Definition 24.50 Influence coefficient (vplivni koeficient)

Let a rotor have a balance plane and a probe, and let the reading \(r\) at spin speed \(\Omega\) after fixing an unbalance \(U\) in the plane be written as \(r(U) = r_0 + \alpha\,U\), where \(r_0 \in \mathbb C\) is the reading without added mass. The complex number \(\alpha\) (unit m per kg m), which does not depend on \(U\), is the influence coefficient (vplivni koeficient) of the plane and the probe at speed \(\Omega\). The notation makes sense by theorem 24.48, which proves that the reading is linear in the unbalances, and by theorem 24.7 for the disk, where \(\alpha = \Omega^2/(k - m\Omega^2 + ic\Omega)\).

Source: FPGL (8.10)-(8.13), PDF p. 364, where \(R(\Omega)\) is the response function. The content is the same, the notation is ours.

Theorem 24.51 Single-plane balancing (uravnoteženje v eni ravnini)

Let \(r(U) = r_0 + \alpha U\) by definition 24.50, and let a trial unbalance \(U_{\mathrm{t}} \ne 0\) give a reading \(r_1\) with \(r_1 \ne r_0\). Then \(\alpha = (r_1 - r_0)/U_{\mathrm{t}}\), and the only unbalance for which the reading is zero is

\[U_{\mathrm{c}} = -\,\frac{r_0}{\alpha} = -\,\frac{r_0\,U_{\mathrm{t}}}{r_1 - r_0} . \tag{24.50}\]

If the whole original unbalance \(U_0\) is in this plane, then \(U_{\mathrm{c}} = -U_0\) and the rotor is balanced at every spin speed.

Idea

The line in the complex plane \(U \mapsto r_0 + \alpha U\) is determined by two points. The first point is the reading without mass, the trial mass gives the second point, and we compute the zero of the line.

Proof
  1. From \(r_1 = r_0 + \alpha U_{\mathrm{t}}\) it follows that \(\alpha = (r_1 - r_0)/U_{\mathrm{t}}\), and \(\alpha \ne 0\) because \(r_1 \ne r_0\).
  2. Because \(\alpha \ne 0\), the equation \(r_0 + \alpha U = 0\) has exactly one solution \(U = -r_0/\alpha\). We insert \(\alpha\) from step 1 and get equation (24.50).
  3. Let all the excitation be the unbalance \(U_0\) in the plane. A rotor without any unbalance reads zero, and the reading is linear in the unbalance of the plane (theorem 24.48). So \(r_0 = \alpha\,U_0\) with the same \(\alpha\) as for the added mass, since \(U_0\) lies in the same plane. By step 2 \(U_{\mathrm{c}} = -r_0/\alpha = -U_0\). The total unbalance \(U_0 + U_{\mathrm{c}}\) is zero, so all \(U_{\mathrm{n}}\) are zero, and by theorem 24.48 the response is zero at every \(\Omega\) (for the disk by theorem 24.7).

Source: FPGL (8.14), PDF p. 364, and example 8.4.1, PDF p. 365. The proof is not from the source.

Example 24.52 The rotor R1 at 1187 rev/min

Take the rotor R1 of section 24.2: a disk of \(49{,}009\) kg at midspan with \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 155{,}32\) 1/s (\(1483\) rev/min), \(\zeta = 0{,}02\). We want to balance it at \(\Omega = 0{,}8\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), that is \(1187\) rev/min. The unbalance is in the plane of the disk, but the balancer does not know it. The readings are given by the probe. We proceed:

  1. We draw the axes of the complex readings and the axes of the unbalance. Without added mass the reading \(r_0\) is \(0{,}0885\) mm at \(24{,}9^\circ\) ahead of the mark. The hidden unbalance is \(U_0\), \(2450\) g mm at \(30^\circ\).
  2. We fix a trial mass of \(10\) g at radius \(150\) mm at \(0^\circ\), so \(U_{\mathrm{t}} = 1500\) g mm. The reading is \(r_1\) \(= 0{,}1382\) mm at \(13{,}6^\circ\).
  3. The change of the reading is \(r_{\mathrm{d}} = r_1 - r_0 = 0{,}0542\) mm at \(-5{,}1^\circ\), and the influence coefficient is \(\alpha = r_{\mathrm{d}}/U_{\mathrm{t}} = 36{,}13\) mm per kg m at \(-5{,}1^\circ\). The formula \(\Omega^2/(k - m\Omega^2 + ic\Omega)\) of section 24.2 gives the same value.
  4. The reading is to be zero, so the target is the change of reading \(-r_0\). We reach it if we turn the trial mass by \(150^\circ\) clockwise and enlarge it by \(|r_0|/|r_{\mathrm{d}}| = 1{,}634\). In the plane of the masses this is the correction \(U_{\mathrm{c}}\), \(2450\) g mm at \(-150^\circ\) (the angle between \(U_{\mathrm{t}}\) and \(U_{\mathrm{c}}\)), that is \(16{,}34\) g at radius \(150\) mm at \(-150^\circ\). Indeed \(U_{\mathrm{c}} = -U_0\).

So with exact readings the reading becomes zero. But every real measurement has an error, so we test the procedure on a wrong reading.

Figure 24.96 shows what an error does. On the left are the reading \(r_0\) and the reading \(r_1\) on the axes. The error \(\delta\) of the tip of the reading \(r_1\) is \(3\) % too large, and the phase error turns the tip by \(3^\circ\). Both shorten or turn the change \(r_{\mathrm{d}}'\) from which we compute \(\alpha\). In the middle is the remaining unbalance after the correction. On the right a small trial mass gives a short change \(r_{\mathrm{d}}\), so the same error \(\delta\) is relatively large, while larger trial masses reduced it.

Example 24.53 The first trial reading is 3 % too high

For the rotor R1 let the reading \(r_1\) be \(3\) % too large because of a probe error, \(r_1' = 1{,}03\,r_1\) (the phase is correct). By equation (24.50) we get \(U_{\mathrm{c}}'\), and the unbalance \(U_0 + U_{\mathrm{c}}' = 175\) g mm remains, which is \(7{,}1\) % of the original. The reading at \(0{,}8\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) after the correction is \(0{,}0063\) mm instead of zero. Why is the error \(2{,}4\) times larger than \(3\) %? Let \(r_1' = r_1 + \delta\) with \(\delta = 0{,}03\,r_1\) and \(r_{\mathrm{d}}' = r_{\mathrm{d}} + \delta\). Since \(r_0 = \alpha U_0\) and \(r_{\mathrm{d}} = \alpha U_{\mathrm{t}}\),

\[U_0 + U_{\mathrm{c}}' = U_0\Big(1 - \frac{r_{\mathrm{d}}}{r_{\mathrm{d}} + \delta}\Big) = U_0\,\frac{\delta}{r_{\mathrm{d}}'} , \qquad \frac{|U_0 + U_{\mathrm{c}}'|}{|U_0|} = 0{,}03\,\frac{|r_1|}{|r_{\mathrm{d}}'|} = 0{,}03 \cdot \frac{0{,}1382}{0{,}0581} = 0{,}0713 . \tag{24.51}\]

The error \(\delta\) is proportional to the reading \(r_1\), but it is divided by the small change \(r_{\mathrm{d}}'\): the trial mass of \(10\) g changes the reading by only \(0{,}61\,|r_0|\) (\(|r_{\mathrm{d}}| = 0{,}0542\) mm against \(|r_0| = 0{,}0885\) mm), so the error grows. With a trial mass of \(25\) g the remainder by equation (24.51) is \(4{,}6\) %, with \(50\) g it is \(3{,}7\) %, because the ratio \(|r_1|/|r_{\mathrm{d}}'|\) falls from \(2{,}38\) to \(1{,}53\) and \(1{,}25\). FPGL (PDF p. 364) therefore recommends a trial mass for which \(|r_{\mathrm{d}}|\) is similar to \(|r_0|\). A phase error of \(3^\circ\) with the same \(10\) g mass, however, leaves \(13{,}9\) %. A turn by \(3^\circ\), that is \(0{,}052\) rad, moves the tip of \(r_1\) by \(\delta\) with \(|\delta| = 0{,}052\,|r_1|\), which is \(1{,}75\) times more than the magnitude error of \(3\) %.
